shows.title: Free and Queer: Black Californian Roots of Gay Liberation
shows.description:
This history-driven exhibition makes the case that California, and Black Californians in particular, deserve a bigger place in the story of LGBTQ liberation than they usually get. Rather than starting the clock at Stonewall, curator Susan D. Anderson and her research team trace a much longer arc: Black queer life in California from the early twentieth century through the McCarthy era, the civil rights movement, the AIDS crisis, and on to marriage equality. The material comes largely from archives rather than art-world sources — vintage newspapers, photographs, flyers, and ephemera assembled with ONE Archives at the USC Libraries and community archivists like Lisbet Tellefsen and Alan Bell.

One throughline you can already see in the exhibition's own imagery is the Aché Project, the Bay Area's Black lesbian collective and journal founded in 1989 by Tellefsen and Pippa Fleming — its 1990s demonstration marches appear as some of the show's key images, a reminder that this is protest history as much as it is portraiture. Expect print culture and performance ephemera alongside photography, since the curators are explicit that they're treating publishing and performance as sites of political organizing, not just documentation.

It's a dense, research-heavy show rather than a survey of individual artists, which makes it a good fit for CAAM's history galleries and its mandate to fill in overlooked chapters of California's past. Anyone interested in queer history, civil rights history, or the visual culture of grassroots organizing will find a lot to sit with here, and the show's nearly year-long run gives it plenty of room to become a point of reference for the city's Black History Month and Pride programming alike.

shows.title: Things I Like
shows.description:
Patrick Wilson makes hard-edge abstract paintings the slow way: dozens of ultra-thin, translucent and opaque films of acrylic pulled across the canvas in careful sequence, each color decision keyed to the one before it. The results are geometric compositions that read as flat and luminous at once, with titles like "Free Lemons" and "Szechuan Food" arrived at through free association after the paintings are finished rather than as illustrative starting points.

There's a distinctly Southern Californian light in Wilson's palette — acid yellows, sky blues, marmalade orange, hot pink against teal — that places him in a lineage of LA hard-edge and Light and Space painting without simply repeating it. The appeal of the work is in its insistence on slowness: in an image-saturated moment, Wilson is making paintings that only give up their structure to someone willing to actually stand and look.

venue.name: Vielmetter Los Angeles
venue.about: Vielmetter Los Angeles is a contemporary art gallery in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles, located at 1700 S Santa Fe Avenue. It is owned and directed by Susanne Vielmetter and operates three exhibition spaces at that address. The gallery represents a multigenerational group of artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video, and installation, including figures such as Nicole Eisenman, Arlene Shechet, Mickalene Thomas, Wangechi Mutu, Mary Kelly, and the estate of William Pope.L. Represented artists have participated in major international biennials, museum surveys, and art fairs, and have received sustained critical attention in publications including The New York Times, Artforum, The Guardian, and Artnet. The gallery's program spans several decades of contemporary practice, with a consistent focus on socially engaged, figurative, and materially inventive work by artists based in Los Angeles, New York, and internationally.

shows.title: Paint, oil, water
shows.description:
Ann Thornycroft has been painting in Los Angeles since arriving from London and New York in the early 1970s, and this show gathers a year's worth of new abstractions built on the grid she has spent decades refining. Each canvas starts from a twelve-inch square lattice, sometimes barely visible as pencil beneath washes of poured pigment, sometimes broken into rounded triangular and vesica-shaped units that recall quilting and Pattern & Decoration painting without ever tipping into its maximalism.

What distinguishes the new work is how much further the paint has been allowed to take over. In a piece like Ancient Glass, sea-foam greens and blues churn across the canvas, all but dissolving the underlying structure into pure atmosphere. That push between the rational scaffold of the grid and the loose, wet unpredictability of poured color has always been Thornycroft's subject, and here the balance tips toward openness and vulnerability rather than the earlier control.

Thornycroft's career threads through Venice Beach's Light and Space scene (Robert Irwin once helped her secure an NEA grant) and decades of Los Angeles gallery history, without ever locking into one movement's orthodoxy. This is a chance to see a veteran abstract painter still actively pushing her own vocabulary rather than repeating it.

shows.title: Anteroom: Growing by Living Together
shows.description:
Sarah Ippolito is a scuba diver as much as a sculptor, and this small presentation in Official Welcome's Anteroom space translates that underwater looking into ceramic, wood, and metal. Two new tondos take the round format's long history — Roman shields, deschi da parto, ecology diagrams — and use it to compress the feeling of facing a coral reef wall: a dense, teeming, close-up superorganism where everything grows because it grows together.

Alongside the tondos, a large wall-mounted sculpture isolates a single plane from Ippolito's freestanding work, letting a biomorphic form hang free of the ground the way a creature might drift in open water. The palette and texture throughout lean toward the neon and crackling colors of reef life rather than any tasteful marine blue, which is the point: Ippolito treats ocean biodiversity as a subject for genuine sensory immersion rather than pretty reference.

Houston-born and now Altadena-based, Ippolito has shown at Various Small Fires and the A+D Museum, and her work carries a scientist's curiosity about nonhuman embodiment alongside a sculptor's feel for material. This is a compact but vivid entry point into a practice built on empathy for creatures most of us never get close to.

shows.title: Anton Roland Laub: Mobile Churches in Ceaușescu's Bucharest
shows.description:
In the 1980s, Nicolae Ceaușescu's "systematization" campaign flattened roughly a third of historic Bucharest to make way for the oversized avenues and government buildings of a totalitarian regime. Seven churches, deemed too significant to destroy outright, were instead jacked up, set on rails, and physically wheeled behind new apartment blocks — hidden in plain sight rather than demolished. Photographer Anton Roland Laub, who grew up amid this leveled cityscape, spent years tracking down these displaced structures and documenting how they sit today, wedged into gaps between mismatched postwar architecture.

The exhibition — Laub's first solo presentation in the United States — pairs his contemporary large-format photographs with archival material from the era of the relocations, including material from the engineer who devised the rail-lifting technique. The pictures are quiet and procedural rather than sensational: facades caught at odd angles against concrete housing, empty lots where history was erased, buildings that look stranded rather than saved. Together they form a document of a strange, little-known act of architectural survival under one of Eastern Europe's most destructive dictatorships.

This is the first chapter of a three-part project by Laub examining the final years of the Ceaușescu regime, continued in his later series Last Christmas (of Ceaușescu) and Mineriada. Guest-curated by independent curator Sonia Voss, the show rewards a slow look at how state power reshapes — and sometimes just relocates — the physical fabric of a city.

shows.title: Ivana Dama: Breathing Alarms
shows.description:
Tucked into the East German guardhouse that sits in the Wende's sculpture garden, this installation by Belgrade-born, New York-based artist Ivana Dama turns a Cold War-era surveillance structure into an instrument that visitors themselves have to play. At its center is a custom air-raid siren — historically a device that broadcasts danger to a passive public — rebuilt here so that it only sounds when someone breathes into it. That breath simultaneously spins a small aluminum zoetrope showing an animation of birds, so the piece links two very different alarm systems: the mechanical siren and the natural, and increasingly threatened, phenomenon of birdsong.

Dama developed the piece's mechanics with researchers at MIT's Center for Bits and Atoms, and the result is deceptively simple to encounter even though the engineering behind it is intricate. Rather than a spectacle, it's a quiet, participatory gesture: visitors have to lean in and exhale to make anything happen at all, turning a device built for collective alarm into something that depends on individual, bodily presence.

The work fits the guardhouse's ongoing role at the Wende as a rotating site for artists responding to themes of surveillance, borders, and state power, and it extends Dama's longer-running research into sirens and warning systems, drawing a line between the sound of Cold War civil defense and her own memories of the bombing of Belgrade in 1999.

shows.title: Eileen Cowin: Between Panic and Paradise
shows.description:
Eileen Cowin has spent five decades staging photographs and videos that look like scenes from movies you never quite saw — domestic dramas full of glances, standoffs, and unresolved tension between the people in them. This survey pulls together her experimental photographic processes, Polaroids, inkjet prints, and video work, much of it drawn from LACMA's own holdings and other Southern California museum collections, to trace how she has used cinema, literature, and painting as source material for pictures that hover between document and fiction.

What makes Cowin's work stand out among her Pictures Generation contemporaries is how personal and specifically Los Angeles it feels — the light, the domestic interiors, the sense of a life being narrated in fragments. Seeing this much of her output together offers a rare chance to track how her interest in doubling, rivalry, and role-play has evolved across changing photographic technologies, from analog Polaroids to digital video.

This is a show for anyone interested in how photography can borrow the grammar of film and theater without ever fully committing to a plot — Cowin leaves just enough ambiguity that every image reads as a still from a story you have to invent yourself.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
venue.about: LACMA is the largest art museum in the western United States, holding some 155,000 objects spanning 6,000 years of global art history. It traces its roots to the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, and Art (1910) and became an independent institution in 1961, opening on Wilshire Boulevard in 1965. The campus has grown through additions including the Anderson/Art of the Americas Building, the Pavilion for Japanese Art, BCAM, and the Resnick Pavilion, culminating in the 2026 opening of the Peter Zumthor-designed David Geffen Galleries. Located on Wilshire Boulevard in the Miracle Mile, LACMA presents rotating exhibitions across its global collection alongside public programs, education initiatives, and community partnerships, including a gallery at Charles White Elementary School.

shows.title: Fashioning Chinese Women: Empire to Modernity
shows.description:
More than seventy garments trace a century of change in Chinese women's dress, moving from the loose embroidered robes of the late Qing court through the fitted 1930s qipao to the cheongsam that became a global fashion icon by the 1960s. Drawn largely from Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Chinese American wardrobes, the pieces on view are less about fashion history in the abstract than about the women who wore them — how cut, fabric, and silhouette became ways of signaling identity through decades of political and social upheaval.

The mannequins themselves are part of the story: designer Jason Wu customized the forms specifically for this installation, giving the historic garments a contemporary staging that underscores the throughline between then and now. It is a show that rewards close looking at craftsmanship — hand embroidery, frog closures, and dye techniques — as much as it does thinking about dress as a form of quiet self-assertion for Chinese and Chinese American women across a century of dramatic change.

shows.title: Danse Macabre: Death in Print from Durer to Dix
shows.description:
Skeletons have been dancing through European printmaking since the 14th century, and this focused installation of works on paper follows that morbid, oddly playful tradition from early woodcuts up through the German Expressionists working in the shadow of World War I. The danse macabre motif — Death leading figures from every social rank in a mocking procession — gave printmakers a shorthand for mortality that could be both comic and genuinely unsettling.

Drawn entirely from LACMA's collection, the prints here span roughly four centuries, letting you watch how the same essential image — the grinning skeleton, the hourglass, the personification of Death as a dance partner nobody can refuse — gets reinvented by artists responding to plague, war, and industrial-scale violence. It's a compact but pointed show, best suited to visitors who like their art history with a little bit of gallows humor.

shows.title: Alfonso Gonzalez Jr.: In Between Stops
shows.description:
Twelve painted benches line LACMA's Kendall Concourse, each one designed by Alfonso Gonzalez Jr., a second-generation sign painter who learned rotulismo mexicano — the tradition of hand-lettered Mexican signage — from his father's shop. Instead of the ads you'd normally find on a bus bench, Gonzalez's panels carry personal messages, community references, and occasional nods to LACMA's own collection and history, turning a piece of street furniture into a small billboard for ideas that have nothing to do with selling anything.

The project sits at the intersection of fine art and vernacular craft, continuing a lineage of Los Angeles artists who've used the city's public infrastructure — benches, murals, storefronts — as exhibition space. It's a free, outdoor, easy-to-miss show that rewards visitors who slow down on their way between LACMA's buildings.

shows.title: Collecting Impressionism at LACMA
shows.description:
This is less a straightforward Impressionism show than a behind-the-scenes look at how a museum's identity gets built. It traces how paintings by Degas, Pissarro, and their contemporaries entered LACMA's collection through the taste and generosity of specific Hollywood-era donors and collectors, and asks why French Impressionism in particular has come to stand in for an entire late-19th-century visual culture that actually included printmaking, photography, fashion, and design.

The paintings themselves — landscapes, portraits, urban scenes — are the draw, but the real subject is collecting as an act of cultural self-definition: how a young museum in a young city used European "taste" to legitimize itself, and how that history is now being examined rather than simply celebrated. Anyone interested in provenance, philanthropy, and the politics of museum-building will find plenty to chew on here alongside the pretty pictures.

shows.title: Every Minute Is History: Five Views of Los Angeles
shows.artist: Laura Aguilar, Reynaldo Rivera, George Rodriguez, Patssi Valdez, Ricardo Valverde
shows.description:
Five photographers who worked in and around Los Angeles's Chicano/a communities anchor this survey, each pulling the camera toward a different corner of everyday life — Laura Aguilar's frank, body-conscious self-portraiture and documentary work with queer Latina communities, Reynaldo Rivera's nightlife and drag-bar portraits, George Rodriguez's photojournalism spanning music, sports and civil-rights history, Patssi Valdez's staged, theatrical tableaux rooted in her work with the group Asco, and Ricardo Valverde's hand-colored, experimental prints that fuse documentary and fine-art impulses.

What ties the five together is less a shared style than a shared refusal to let Chicano/a Los Angeles be photographed only from the outside. Aguilar and Valverde in particular pushed printing and color into expressive, sometimes surreal territory, while Rivera and Rodriguez worked closer to classic documentary and press photography. Seen together, the works trace roughly four decades of the city's visual history through a lens rarely centered in mainstream photography surveys.

The show opens alongside a companion exhibition of Mexican photography, and the pairing is intentional: both examine how a camera can hold a community's memory as much as its image. It's a strong, tightly focused two-gallery visit if you catch them together.

venue.name: Getty Center
venue.about: The Getty Center is one of two Los Angeles-area sites operated by the J. Paul Getty Trust, a cultural organization founded on the legacy of businessman and art collector J. Paul Getty. Located in Brentwood, the Center presents European art from the Middle Ages to today amid modern architecture and gardens with views over Los Angeles. It is one of the Trust's four programs, alongside the Getty Research Institute, Getty Conservation Institute, and Getty Foundation. The Trust's second museum site, the Getty Villa, focuses on ancient Greek and Roman antiquities in Pacific Palisades. Admission to both locations is free with a timed-entry reservation.

shows.title: Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography
shows.artist: Manuel Álvarez Bravo, Lola Álvarez Bravo, Manuel Carrillo, Antonio Reynoso, Héctor García, Mariana Yampolsky, Rodrigo Moya, Pedro Meyer, Graciela Iturbide, Yolanda Andrade, Pablo Ortiz Monasterio, Cecilia Salcedo Méndez, Flor Garduño
shows.description:
Nearly a century of Mexican photography, told through thirteen photographers whose work moves from the socially engaged modernism of Manuel and Lola Álvarez Bravo in the late 1920s and '30s through to the more conceptual, documentary-adjacent practices of figures like Graciela Iturbide and Pablo Ortiz Monasterio decades later. The pictures come almost entirely from a single source — a twenty-five-year run of gifts to the Getty from collectors Daniel Greenberg and Susan Steinhauser — which gives the show an unusually coherent backbone even as it ranges across generations and approaches.

The exhibition borrows its structure from Octavio Paz's 1982 book "Instante y revelación," which paired his poetry with Álvarez Bravo's photographs; here the galleries are organized around lines from a related Paz poem, using the poet's language as a loose armature for grouping the images rather than a strict chronology. Expect the recognizable high points of Mexican modernist photography alongside less-familiar later work, including Iturbide's color studies and Ortiz Monasterio's more recent digital-era photographs.

It's being shown deliberately in tandem with "Every Minute Is History," the Getty's concurrent survey of Chicano/a photographers in Los Angeles, and the two together make an argument about the visual dialogue between Mexico City and LA that's worth taking in as a pair.

shows.title: Lost. Found. Returned.
shows.description:
A small, focused provenance-research exhibition built around a single drawing: a nude study by the German Symbolist Otto Greiner, acquired by Dresden's Kupferstich-Kabinett in 1894 and marked "lost" after the Second World War before turning up, decades later, in the Getty Research Institute's own holdings. Rather than presenting a broad survey, the show walks through the detective work — archival sleuthing, condition and provenance clues — that let researchers trace the drawing's wartime disappearance and confirm its identity ahead of its return to Germany.

It's a quieter show than the Getty's big loan exhibitions, but it's a genuinely interesting look at how provenance research actually works, useful for anyone curious about the mechanics of restitution rather than just its headlines.

shows.title: Stendahl's World: Marketing Ancient Mexico and Modern Art in Los Angeles
shows.description:
Drawn from the Getty Research Institute's Stendahl Art Galleries archive, this show is a portrait of a single, unusually influential Los Angeles dealer rather than of any one artist. Earl Stendahl spent decades selling California Impressionism and introducing European modernists like Diego Rivera, Marc Chagall and Picasso to Southern California buyers before pivoting, in the mid-1930s, to marketing pre-Hispanic Mexican antiquities — a shift that reshaped the market for ancient American art on the West Coast.

The material here is archival rather than art-historical in the usual sense: photographs, gallery correspondence, sales records and publicity materials that show how Stendahl built demand through traveling shows, department-store tie-ins, celebrity collectors and even Hollywood product placement. The exhibition doesn't shy from the uglier consequences of that marketing success, noting the looting of Mexican archaeological sites that accompanied the boom in demand he helped create.

It's less a visual spectacle than a case study in taste-making, useful for anyone interested in how the market for "ancient" art gets built by very modern hands.

shows.title: The Making of a Medieval Manuscript
shows.description:
A process-focused show pulled from the Getty's own manuscript holdings, walking through the four stages that went into producing a book by hand in pre-modern Europe: preparing animal skin into parchment, then writing, painting and binding it. Rather than organizing around a single theme or artist, the curators use roughly a dozen manuscripts — including biblical and Qur'anic pages worked in tempera, gold leaf and ink — to illustrate each technical stage in turn.

It's a good primer for anyone who loves illuminated manuscripts but has never quite understood how the physical objects were actually made, with close attention paid to material and craft rather than iconography alone.

shows.title: Five Centuries of Works on Paper: The Grunwald Center at 70, Part II
shows.description:
The second half of a two-part anniversary show marking seventy years of UCLA's Grunwald Center for the Graphic Arts, one of the country's major repositories of prints, drawings, photographs and artists' books. Housed at the Hammer since 1994, the collection began with a 1956 gift from Los Angeles collector Fred Grunwald and has grown into a holding of more than 45,000 works spanning the Renaissance to the present.

This installment leans into that range: Dürer woodcuts and Piranesi etchings sit alongside Hiroshige's Edo-period landscapes, Degas and Manet prints, and a run of twentieth-century material that includes Käthe Kollwitz, Egon Schiele, Picasso and Matisse. The photography side of the collection gets real attention too, with Ansel Adams and Imogen Cunningham running into more conceptually driven work by Robert Heinecken, James Welling and Catherine Opie. Contemporary names — Julie Mehretu, James Turrell, Alison Saar, Kara Walker — round out the picture, making the point that the Grunwald's holdings didn't stop accumulating at some tasteful historical cutoff.

It's a survey show in the best sense: less an argument than an occasion to look closely at seventy-plus individual objects, many of them rarely on view, drawn entirely from a single institution's collection.

venue.name: Hammer Museum
venue.about: The Hammer Museum is a UCLA-affiliated contemporary art museum in Westwood, Los Angeles, founded by Armand Hammer and opened in November 1990. Since a 1994 partnership agreement, it has been operated by UCLA, absorbing the collections of the Wight Art Gallery and the Grunwald Center for the Graphic Arts as well as the Franklin D. Murphy Sculpture Garden. Directors have included Henry Hopkins, Ann Philbin (1999–2024), and current director Zoë Ryan (from 2025). The museum is known for its Made in L.A. biennial, the ongoing Hammer Projects series, and an active calendar of lectures, film, and public programs. Admission is free.

shows.title: Inventing America: The Comic Book Revolution
shows.description:
This sprawling survey traces the American comic book from its Depression-era beginnings through the turn of the millennium, using original art, vintage covers, and rare production artifacts to show how a disposable pulp medium became a mirror for the national psyche. The show leans hard on the fact that so many of the medium's founding artists and writers were immigrants and outsiders — many of them Jewish — whose own experience of displacement and reinvention shaped the archetypes (the orphaned alien who becomes a savior, the mild-mannered outcast with a secret power) that are now global shorthand for American myth-making.

Expect to see the medium's marquee names — Superman, Wonder Woman, Captain America, Spider-Man, Black Panther, Archie, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles — alongside pencil roughs and character studies that reveal the working process behind the finished page. The installation photos show gallery walls given over to mural-scale blow-ups of classic covers, a reminder that these images functioned as genuinely mass culture long before "graphic novel" became a respectable term.

Rather than a nostalgia trip, the exhibition frames comics as historical documents: stand-ins for anxieties about war, civil rights, and the changing shape of American identity across six decades. It's a good pick for anyone who grew up on these characters and wants the fuller, stranger story behind their creation, and it runs long enough (through February 2027) that there's no rush to catch it.

shows.title: Mountain Spirits: Rice and Indigeneity in the Northern Luzon Highlands, Philippines
shows.dates_note: Venue page gives the closing only as "January, 2027" with no specific day; saved as Jan 31, 2027 pending confirmation.
shows.description:
This exhibition looks at the Ifugao people of the northern Luzon highlands in the Philippines, whose terraced rice fields — carved into mountainsides over centuries and recognized by UNESCO — are as much spiritual infrastructure as agricultural engineering. Rather than treating the terraces as a scenic backdrop, the show insists they're a living, working culture: a place where farming, ritual, and kinship are inseparable.

The galleries bring together carved guardian figures, ritual bowls, woven textiles, and traditional farming tools alongside video and soundscape installations that situate the objects in their landscape and social context. It's a materials-rich show that rewards slow looking — the carvings especially carry the kind of formal power that made Philippine highland sculpture influential well beyond its region.

What makes this show worth the trip is its refusal to freeze Ifugao culture in the past tense: the framing throughout is that these terraces and traditions are ongoing, not museum relics, and the video work by Paul Connor reinforces that sense of a still-living practice. Paired with the Fowler's other current exhibitions on textile monuments and African art provenance, it rounds out a strong season on land, memory, and material culture.

shows.title: "This Land Is ..." Exhibition
shows.description:
Timed to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, this sprawling group exhibition uses the Huntington's own library, art, and botanical holdings to ask what "land" has meant in the American imagination — as property, as promise, as home, and as a site of dispossession. The show's title nods to Woody Guthrie's "This Land Is Your Land," and the trailing ellipsis is doing real work: everything here complicates the anthem's easy claim.

The material ranges wildly, from an early printed copy of the Declaration itself and a George Washington land grant to a Langston Hughes poem and a well-worn guitar, alongside historical photographs, maps, and artwork that trace westward expansion, Indigenous displacement, and the country's contested relationship to its own territory. It's less a single argument than a layered conversation, moving from the Atlantic coast to the Pacific and from the colonial period into the present.

It's an ambitious, research-heavy show best suited to visitors happy to slow down and read; the payoff is a far more textured picture of American land history than the marketing bunting around most 250th-anniversary programming tends to offer.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Sanctified Steel
shows.description:
Jacqueline Valenzuela paints the garage as a kind of chapel. Her first solo show with Craig Krull Gallery gathers densely worked panels — built up from oil and automotive paint, faux fur, jeweled and pompom trim, gold leaf, and even found personal objects like votive candles — that frame lowrider culture in the visual language of Catholic devotion. Many pieces borrow the shape of the nicho, the small shadow-box altar used to honor saints and lost loved ones, and repurpose it to hold portraits of cars, women, and family memory instead.

Valenzuela, who grew up in East Los Angeles and has spent years working alongside painters and fabricators in an auto body shop, treats restoration and customization as acts of care and inheritance rather than mere craft. Recurring appearances of the Virgen de Guadalupe tie the individual stories in the show — a red Corvair remembered with marigolds and candlelight, a friend's crudely spray-painted car in "Just Like Candy" — to a larger tradition of veneration and cultural pride, including the reclaimed concept of rasquachismo, making the most of what's at hand.

The result is a body of work that insists lowrider culture and fine-art materials belong in the same sentence: chrome-shop bravado rendered with the patience and symbolism of an altarpiece. It's a striking, tactile show, heavy with texture and personal narrative, and a strong introduction to an artist building a wider reputation for centering women's experience within a famously male-coded car culture.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 4-6pm (in conjunction with Bergamot Station's Fall Open House); Artist Talk Saturday, September 19, 11am

shows.title: Walking Venice
shows.description:
Craig Krull, better known in Los Angeles as a gallerist, turns his own camera on the neighborhood that raised him. Walking Venice collects small-format archival pigment prints made during meandering daily walks he began during the pandemic — a return to the alleys, canals, and boardwalk he first roamed as a kid in the early 1970s and later lived beside as a young gallery hand in the 1980s.

The pictures favor palimpsest and decay over postcard landmarks: piles of discarded furniture and street debris arranged, almost sculpturally, by the people who live among them; architectural fragments; the funky, unbothered texture of alleys like Speedway that gentrification hasn't managed to scrub clean. Krull cites the deliberate, meditative walking-as-art practices of Richard Long and Roger Ackling as a touchstone, and the photographs — intimate, often just 4x5 inches printed onto larger sheets — read like a diary of attention rather than a survey of sights.

At the center of the gallery Krull has installed Memento, a tower of mismatched concrete breeze blocks planted with sweet alyssum — a quiet sculptural coda to a show that's ultimately about one person's decades-long, still-unfolding relationship with a single square mile of Los Angeles.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 4-6pm (in conjunction with Bergamot Station's Fall Open House); Artist Talk Saturday, September 19, 11am

shows.title: ADRIAN: Designing Hollywood, Dressing America
shows.description:
Gilbert Adrian was the costume designer who built MGM's glamour machine in the 1930s and '40s, and this exhibition is a chance to see just how much engineering went into that glamour up close. The ASU FIDM Museum is pulling more than fifty ensembles and accessories from its own deep costume-history collection, supplemented by loans from private collectors, to trace Adrian's path from Hollywood soundstage to his own Wilshire Boulevard couture salon.

What made Adrian's work so enduring wasn't just spectacle — it was structural. His sharp shoulders and bias-cut gowns for stars like Joan Crawford and Jean Harlow reshaped what American ready-to-wear looked like once department stores started knocking off his silhouettes nationwide. The show promises pieces connected to more than 200 film productions, including costumes tied to The Wizard of Oz, alongside sketches and ephemera that show the design process behind the finished garments.

For a museum with free admission and no advance booking, this is a rare opportunity to get close to Golden Age costume design outside a film archive. Fashion history and film history collide here, and the installation itself — mannequins under the museum's soft gallery light — is worth the trip even before you start reading the wall text.

venue.name: ASU FIDM Museum
venue.address_detail: Museum entrance on ground floor, ASU California Center Grand
hours: Wed - Sat 10:00am to 5:00pm (open only during exhibitions)

shows.title: Whispers: Women, Animals and Chimeras
shows.description:
Elika Hedayat's Whispers gathers a menagerie of hybrid figures — women fused with animals, chimeric bodies that slip between the human and the mythic — into what reads as a meditation on femininity refracted through folklore. The imagery draws on a long tradition of composite creatures in Persian and broader Middle Eastern storytelling, where animal-headed women and shape-shifting bodies carry warnings, protections, and desires that couldn't be spoken plainly.

Rendered with a soft, almost illustrative touch, the works feel intimate rather than monumental — more whispered confidences than declarations, true to the title. It's the longest-running of the three shows the gallery opens this week, giving it room to be the anchor exhibition through much of September and into October.

Seen together with Hiva Alizadeh's botanical abstractions and Anali Taherian's spare Storyless, Hedayat's chimeras complete a loose trilogy of shows built around inherited image-worlds — pattern, silence, and myth — all filtered through women's perspectives.

venue.name: Aabee Bleue Project
venue.about: Aabee Bleue Project is a contemporary art space in Downtown Los Angeles that builds connections among cultures, communities, and contemporary artistic practices. Through exhibitions, conversations, and public programs, the gallery introduces contemporary artists from Iran, the Middle East, and beyond to new audiences and contexts. It was founded by Sabrina Younesi and Narges Hamzianpour, and developed alongside Niloufar Binafard, who serves as Artist Liaison and Art Advisor. The program is driven by curiosity, collaboration, and a desire to create dialogue between artists, ideas, and communities, using art as a means to build cross-cultural dialogue, challenge perspectives, and create spaces for discovery.

shows.title: Creative Continuities: Family, Pride, and Community in Native Art
shows.artist: John Pepion, Brocade Stops Black Eagle, Jessa Rae Growing Thunder
shows.description:
Three contemporary Plains Indian artists — Blackfeet painter John Pepion, Crow (Apsáalooke) artist Brocade Stops Black Eagle, and Dakota/Nakoda beadworker Jessa Rae Growing Thunder — were invited to curate sections of the Autry's Native American collection through their own cultural lenses. Rather than a conventional survey of historic objects, the show pairs beadwork, garments, and regalia made by past generations with new works and commentary from these three "culture bearers," organized around the ideas of Knowing, Creating, and Transference.

The result is a conversation across time: a 19th-century Miniconjou Lakota pipe bag or a Crow beaded vest sits alongside contemporary pieces like Pepion's ink-on-antique-map painting Our Land, making the case that Plains Native art-making is a living, continuous practice rather than a closed chapter of history. A Blackfeet tipi, fully assembled inside the gallery, anchors the installation and comes with its own audio guide.

This is one of the more thoughtfully collaborative exhibitions in the Autry's collection galleries — instead of anthropologists or curators speaking for Native material culture, the artists whose communities made these objects get to frame their meaning directly. It runs for over a year and a half, so there's no rush, but it rewards a slow look at beadwork and garment craftsmanship that's easy to walk past on autopilot.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: Broken Sleeps
shows.description:
Fiona Connor has spent years making exacting, deadpan replicas of overlooked civic and social infrastructure — noticeboards, drinking fountains, storefront gates — objects whose surfaces carry the residue of public use. Broken Sleeps, her third solo show with Château Shatto, marks a turn in that practice: rather than faithfully reproducing an existing object down to its scars, these new sculptures are built through what the gallery describes as material translation, letting the source object loosen into something more poetic and less strictly documentary.

Connor's work has always lived in the gap between sculpture and readymade, asking viewers to look twice at things designed to be invisible. This show promises to push that inquiry further, trading precision-replica fidelity for a looser, more interpretive kind of object-making — a meaningful development for an artist whose reputation was built on exactness.

Given Connor's track record — her work has been included in major museum surveys and she is one of the gallery's longest-running artists — this is a show worth catching close to its opening, before word spreads.

venue.name: Château Shatto
venue.about: Château Shatto is a contemporary art gallery based in Los Angeles that represents an international group of artists working across painting, sculpture, video, and installation. Its roster includes Aria Dean, Fiona Connor, Van Hanos, Helen Johnson, C.B. Evans, Cécile B. Evans, and the late Jacqueline de Jong, alongside a growing list of emerging names, with photographer John Divola joining the program in 2026. The gallery frequently presents artists' work at international institutions such as the Hammer Museum, Renaissance Society, ICA London, and Serralves Museum, and participates in art fairs including Art Basel and FIAC/OFFICIELLE. Its exhibitions and programming, including screenings and curated group shows, reflect an interest in conceptually driven, research-based practices spanning painting, sculpture, moving image, and site-specific installation.

shows.title: Carroll Dunham
shows.description:
Carroll Dunham has spent five decades building one of contemporary painting's most instantly recognizable vocabularies — biomorphic forms, cartoonish anatomy, and hot, unmixed color pushed to the edge of abstraction — and this show at Matthew Brown's Seward Street space brings a new body of paintings, including works from his ongoing "Sharing Space" series glimpsed in the gallery's promotional image.

Dunham emerged from the downtown New York scene of the 1980s and has remained one of the most influential painters of his generation for younger figurative and abstract painters alike; his work moves fluidly between grotesque comedy and formal rigor, often mining the human body — especially figures rendered with exaggerated, almost violent simplicity — for both humor and unease.

This is a rare opportunity to see a major senior American painter's new work on the West Coast.

shows.title: Lookout Weekend
shows.description:
The Perez Bros—identical twins Alejandro and Vicente—capture the passion and precision of Los Angeles lowrider culture through painting. This exhibition of new work invites viewers into the garage in the lead-up to a car show or cruise night, featuring scenes of meticulous preparation, tuning, and polishing. The paintings are finished with high-gloss resin and reflective flake, creating a visual surface that mirrors the glossy perfection of the cars themselves and collapses the boundary between subject and medium.

The exhibition title references a 1984 dance track by Debbie Deb that soundtracked the brothers' childhood, setting a tone of hopeful anticipation. While earlier works focus on the cars themselves, this body of work introduces wider scenes, including a panoramic painting of a car show featuring more than a dozen vehicles surrounded by crowds, shade tents, and the bustling community ecosystem that gathers around them. Other works depict cars as near-celebrities, positioned on tow trucks or posed for the camera like stars on a red carpet.

The Perez Bros pull from an extensive photographic archive of the LA lowrider scene, distilling images into scenes of pure detail rendered in bright hues. Their meticulous approach to composition and finish reflects a deep knowledge of and obvious love for the cars and the culture surrounding them—a distinctly Los Angeles subject matter treated with the care of fine art painting.

venue.name: Charlie James Gallery
venue.about: Charlie James Gallery opened in 2008 in Los Angeles' Chinatown and has built a program centered on emerging and established artists with distinct, often political voices. The gallery works across painting, sculpture, textile, installation, and new media, with particular attention to marginalized perspectives and narratives touching on identity, race, gender, and broader socio-political concerns. Under gallery director Ever Velasquez, the program has become known for thoughtful, provocative curatorial approaches, including annual group exhibitions, and for close collaboration with museums and academics to help place artists' work within broader critical and historical conversations. The gallery now operates two adjoining spaces on historic Chung King Road.

shows.title: Fantasy Street / The Lifted Veil
shows.description:
Milano Chow's site-specific installation takes over a small, historically layered room inside Hollyhock House — once a child's bedroom, later a clubhouse lounge — with folding screens of graphite, ink, and photo-transfer drawings. Her invented facades borrow the vocabulary of 1920s Los Angeles (movie palaces, apartment blocks, shop windows pulled from the public library's photo archive) to build streetscapes that look documentary but exist nowhere, a fitting echo of Frank Lloyd Wright's own fabricated ornament just outside the door.

Alongside her own work, Chow has curated a companion exhibition of photographs by the late Deborah Turbeville, the fashion photographer known for hazy, fractured images that unsettled the glossy conventions of Vogue and Harper's Bazaar. The pairing sets Chow's crisp, monochrome invented architecture against Turbeville's blurred, deteriorated interiors and contact-sheet outtakes, both artists drawn to environments that feel staged, aged, or slightly unreal.

It's a smart, quiet two-hander for a house that has spent a century blurring the line between architecture and stage set — Wright designed Hollyhock House as a kind of total artwork for Aline Barnsdall, and successive artist interventions here have leaned into that theatricality. Worth the trip for anyone who wants to see contemporary drawing and vintage fashion photography in conversation inside one of LA's few UNESCO World Heritage sites, rather than in a white-box gallery.

venue.name: Hollyhock House
hours: Last entry 3:30pm; Visitor Center open 10:45am to 3:30pm

shows.title: 2026 K-Comics Origin Los Angeles: Korean Webtoon Experience Exhibition
shows.description:
This is less a gallery show than a walk-through pop-culture pavilion: the Korean Creative Content Agency and KCCLA have turned the center's second-floor art gallery into an immersive tribute to Korean webtoons, tracing roughly a century of Korean comics up through the digital-native "webtoon" format that now drives some of the biggest entertainment franchises on the planet.

Three hit series anchor the installation — All of Us Are Dead, Omniscient Reader's Viewpoint, and Solo Leveling — with large-scale graphic environments, character models, and interactive stations built around each. Rather than framing panels on a wall, the show leans into spatial installation and role-play: visitors move through recreated sets and photo-ready tableaux that translate a scrolling digital medium into a physical, room-sized experience.

It's a useful reminder that Koreatown's cultural institutions treat comics and animation as part of the same continuum as painting and calligraphy, and it's a rare chance to see original character and production art from webtoons that mostly live on phone screens blown up to mural scale. Free admission and no reservation required make it an easy add to a Wilshire museum-row afternoon.

venue.name: Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles (KCCLA)
venue.about: The Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles (KCCLA) is a public cultural institution operated by the Republic of Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, located in the Miracle Mile district at 5505 Wilshire Blvd. It functions as a hub for Korean heritage and contemporary culture in the United States, housing a library, a permanent heritage exhibition hall, a second-floor art gallery, an auditorium (Ari Hall), and a media arts wall. Programming spans traditional and contemporary Korean art exhibitions, film screenings, Korean-language classes, and community-oriented shows organized with Korean-American arts associations, alongside field trips and cultural workshops for schools and the public.

shows.title: Lollipop
shows.description:
Adam Higgins has spent the last several years painting salads — specifically, bird's-eye views of Caesar salads loaded with sardines, raw shrimp, croutons, and improbable amounts of dressing, rendered with the obsessive, all-over density of a Pollock drip painting crossed with a 17th-century Dutch still life. Lollipop, his new show at Chris Sharp Gallery, continues that project while widening its frame: recent bodies of work have folded in photographic fragments underneath the food — a Parisian street, a yacht-dotted seascape, the artist's own truck — so that the salad becomes a kind of screen or portal onto other pictures and other places.

Higgins, who earned his MFA at Yale and lives and works in Los Angeles, treats the salad-as-subject as a deadpan device: funny on its face, but built with real formal seriousness around composition, palette, and the history of still life painting. The joke never undercuts the craft — dense layering of paint, tondo and rectangular formats borrowed from culinary photography, and a persistent tension between abstraction and legible imagery.

This is Higgins's latest solo outing with the gallery that has represented him since his breakout "My Salad Years" series, a body of work that has since traveled to Paris and been featured at fairs including Independent. Expect a tightly hung gallery of oils on linen and canvas that reward close looking — the closer you get, the more the salad dissolves into pure paint.

venue.name: Chris Sharp Gallery
venue.about: Chris Sharp Gallery is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles, founded in January 2021 by writer and curator Chris Sharp, co-founder of the Mexico City project space Lulu. The program mixes emerging, mid-career, and historically overlooked artists, with a core group based in Los Angeles alongside artists working on the East Coast, in the UK, and in Europe. The gallery favors fully integrated practices in which ideas, politics, and materials are inseparable, giving weight to personal, idiosyncratic sensibilities, humor, and craft, presented with careful spatial attention. Chris Sharp serves as owner and director, supported by a small staff handling operations and exhibitions. The gallery is located on Santa Monica Boulevard and participates regularly in international art fairs.

shows.title: Sculptures
shows.description:
John Baldessari is remembered above all as a conceptual artist of language and photography, but this show at Sprüth Magers makes the case for a less-discussed side of his practice: his eye for three-dimensional, often absurdist sculpture. Best known for punning, deadpan photo-text works, Baldessari also spent decades building objects and installations that translate his visual jokes into physical space.

The show's anchor piece is "Beethoven's Trumpet (With Ear) Opus # 133" (2007), an oversized bronze horn fused to a giant white ceramic ear mounted on the wall — a sculptural pun on listening, amplification, and the absurdity of monumentalizing sound. Rendered at a scale that turns a wearable object into architecture, the piece is classic Baldessari: funny on first look, quietly unsettling the longer you sit with its scale and material contradictions (resin and fiberglass standing in for bronze weight, electronics embedded in a body that's otherwise inert).

It's a rare chance to see Baldessari's spatial and sculptural instincts foregrounded on their own, in the Los Angeles gallery scene where his photo-based conceptualism looms largest.

venue.name: Sprüth Magers
hours: Tue - Sat 11am to 6pm and by appointment
venue.about: Sprüth Magers is an international gallery for postwar and contemporary art, founded by Monika Sprüth in Cologne in 1983 and joined by Philomene Magers, whose own gallery merged with Sprüth's in 1998. Known for close, curatorially rigorous relationships with artists and museums, the gallery built its reputation on conceptual, photography-based and feminist-inflected practices, showing figures such as Rosemarie Trockel, Cindy Sherman, Barbara Kruger and John Baldessari from early on. In 2016 it opened its Los Angeles space on the Miracle Mile, its first US location, debuting with new works by Baldessari. The LA gallery continues the program's mix of longstanding conceptualists, mid-career figures and emerging voices across painting, sculpture, photography and installation.

shows.title: L-Għajn
shows.description:
Jeffrey Stuker's solo show takes its title from the Maltese word for "the eye" or "the spring" (a source of water) — a fitting double meaning for an artist whose work moves between lens-based image-making and questions of origin and perception. Stuker, a Los Angeles artist with a Yale MFA who is completing a PhD at UC San Diego, has spent the last few years exhibiting internationally, from Brussels and Milan to Rome, while also writing criticism for Artforum and other publications.

His practice tends to treat photography less as documentation than as a kind of philosophical instrument, probing how images are constructed, mediated, and read. Past shows have carried titles that nod to obscure textual and architectural sources; L-Għajn continues that interest in etymology and hidden structure, using the gallery's project history (this is Stuker's second solo outing at Ehrlich Steinberg, following 2024's "From A Defoliated Monograph") to push further into his ongoing inquiry into vision and its technologies.

Given the density of reference in Stuker's past work — from Getty Museum group shows to a MOMuS biennial appearance — this exhibition is likely to reward close, patient looking rather than a quick pass through the gallery.

shows.title: bulgaria;mexicali
shows.description:
Ramon Saturnino's new exhibition at Frankfurt Ordorica takes its title from two seemingly unrelated places — Bulgaria and Mexicali — that the artist yokes together as a way of thinking about the strange logic of borders, migration routes, and the geographic imagination. Rather than a literal travelogue, the show reads as a meditation on how place names circulate as symbols long after their specific histories are forgotten, and how an artist working in Los Angeles might hold two distant, disconnected geographies in mind at once.

Saturnino's solo outing continues that thread with a body of new work that plays with the tension between the personal and the cartographic.

shows.title: Flesh Witness
shows.artist: Bernice Akamine, Lani Asunción, Pelenakeke Brown, Crystal Z Campbell, Jisoo Chung, Sean Connelly, Kyuri Jeon, Jane Jin Kaisen, Mao Ishikawa, Slow Futures Laboratory, Stephanie Syjuco
shows.description:
Flesh Witness gathers eleven artists and collectives working across Hawai'i, Korea, Okinawa, the Philippines, and Samoa to trace how militarism has been written onto bodies, landscapes, and official archives over the past half-century. The show's title borrows from Kyuri Jeon's video piece about Korean War prisoners who were forcibly tattooed with anti-communist slogans, and that image of skin as a site of imposed history sets the tone for everything around it: photographs and film stills pulled from state archives, sculpture built from coastal materials, and new commissions that talk back to that archival record.

Organized by the diasporic Korean arts nonprofit GYOPO with scholar Amy Kahng, the exhibition spans works from the 1970s to newly commissioned pieces, including a still from Jane Jin Kaisen's film "Burial of This Order" and photography by Mao Ishikawa documenting Okinawa under US occupation. Rather than treating these histories as separate national stories, the curators line them up so the shared machinery of occupation and control becomes visible across very different Pacific and Asian geographies.

It's the kind of ambitious, research-driven group show REDCAT's gallery does well: free to enter, modest in scale, but dense with material that rewards slow looking. The opening reception on September 12 kicks off a run through mid-December, giving plenty of time to catch it alongside the fall performance season upstairs.

venue.name: Gallery at REDCAT
venue.about: REDCAT (the Roy and Edna Disney CalArts Theater) is CalArts' downtown Los Angeles center for contemporary visual and performing arts, opened in November 2003 inside the Walt Disney Concert Hall complex designed by Frank Gehry. Initiated by Roy E. Disney as a gift from the Walt Disney Company and matched by Roy and Patty Disney, it houses a 250-seat black-box theater, a 3,000-square-foot gallery, and a lounge. Through performances, exhibitions, screenings, and literary events, REDCAT presents experimental and cutting-edge work by Los Angeles-based and international artists, extending CalArts' mission of experimentation, discovery, and civic discourse to a professional venue in the city's downtown cultural corridor.

shows.title: Sit So Your Back Isn't Against The Door
shows.description:
This is the rarely-seen, most unguarded corner of Glenn Ligon's practice: his Coloring Book paintings, made after a 1999-2000 residency at the Walker Art Center where he handed out pages from Afrocentric coloring books of the late 1960s and '70s and let children scribble on them. Ligon then blew those uninhibited marks up into large-scale canvases, turning a kid's crayon work into paintings about authorship, historical memory, and who gets to narrate Black history and iconography. The bright, candy-colored surfaces read as pure fun before the harder questions underneath start to surface.

Ligon is best known for his text paintings built from James Baldwin and Zora Neale Hurston quotations, so this body of work shows a different, more collaborative and improvisational side of an artist who has spent four decades picking apart how American language and imagery encode race. The show marks the first time these paintings have been reunited in over 25 years, which alone makes it a significant occasion for anyone who has followed his career since his 2011 Whitney retrospective "AMERICA."

The exhibition opens the gallery's fall season alongside Jack Whitten's "The Numinous," reopening the Downtown LA campus after a period of installation and marking ten years since Hauser & Wirth first arrived in the Arts District. Entry is free and no booking is required.

venue.name: Hauser & Wirth Downtown Los Angeles
venue.about: Hauser & Wirth Downtown Los Angeles is the Los Angeles outpost of the international gallery founded in 1992 in Zurich by Iwan Wirth, Manuela Wirth and Ursula Hauser. The Los Angeles space opened in March 2016 in the Arts District, occupying the historic former Globe Mills flour-mill complex, restored in consultation with Selldorf Architects. The campus combines exhibition galleries with an open-air courtyard, garden and the Manuela restaurant, and hosts a robust learning and community-engagement program built around partnerships with local schools, universities and nonprofits. As part of the wider Hauser & Wirth program, the Los Angeles gallery presents historically minded surveys alongside contemporary exhibitions, drawing on the gallery's roster of more than ninety living artists and artist estates spanning painting, sculpture, photography and installation across generations and geographies.

shows.title: Jack Whitten: The Numinous
shows.description:
Following his acclaimed 2025 retrospective at MoMA, Jack Whitten gets a focused historical show at Hauser & Wirth's Downtown LA flour-mill campus, honing in on paintings and works on paper from the 1980s — a decade that began with a studio fire and ended with some of the artist's most technically audacious breakthroughs. This is deep-catalog Whitten rather than greatest-hits: the Soulspace paintings and circular acrylic reliefs that gesture toward celestial navigation, pixel-like grids that anticipate his later tesserae technique, and Site paintings cast directly from manhole covers and tire treads.

Whitten spent his career pulling abstraction away from gesture and toward material invention — peeling, casting, and layering paint until it behaved more like sculpture than pigment. This show catches him mid-transformation, fusing formal experimentation with the spiritual and political charge that runs through his work on Black identity and animist belief. It's a rewarding show for anyone who thinks they already know postwar American abstraction; Whitten's 1980s output complicates that story in the best way.

The exhibition opens September 30 alongside Glenn Ligon's concurrent show at the same location, making for a strong single visit to the gallery's reopened downtown campus.

venue.name: Hauser & Wirth Downtown Los Angeles
venue.about: Hauser & Wirth Downtown Los Angeles is the Los Angeles outpost of the international gallery founded in 1992 in Zurich by Iwan Wirth, Manuela Wirth and Ursula Hauser. The Los Angeles space opened in March 2016 in the Arts District, occupying the historic former Globe Mills flour-mill complex, restored in consultation with Selldorf Architects. The campus combines exhibition galleries with an open-air courtyard, garden and the Manuela restaurant, and hosts a robust learning and community-engagement program built around partnerships with local schools, universities and nonprofits. As part of the wider Hauser & Wirth program, the Los Angeles gallery presents historically minded surveys alongside contemporary exhibitions, drawing on the gallery's roster of more than ninety living artists and artist estates spanning painting, sculpture, photography and installation across generations and geographies.

shows.title: Carl Cheng: Nature Never Loses
shows.description:
Carl Cheng has been quietly making some of Los Angeles's most prescient art since the 1960s, and this survey — the first to trace his full six-decade career — finally gives him the wide-lens treatment. Cheng trained in both fine art and industrial design, and it shows: his work looks like it was made by an engineer moonlighting as a conceptualist, full of erosion machines, simulated landscapes, plastic "nature" specimens, and gadgets that turn ecological anxiety into something you can crank a handle to operate. Coming out of the aerospace-saturated, politically charged Los Angeles of the 1960s and 70s, he became one of the sharpest artists anywhere on the subject of humans trying (and failing) to engineer their way around nature.

The show, organized by The Contemporary Austin and previously seen at ICA Philadelphia, Bonnefanten, and Museum Tinguely, lands at ICA LA as the final stop on its international tour — fittingly, since Cheng has lived and worked in Santa Monica for most of his career and showed at the museum's predecessor, the Santa Monica Museum of Art, back in 1998. Expect around fifty works and archival materials, including his signature "erosion machines" that use pebbles, water pumps and black light to simulate geological time in real time, plus a new water-based commission made specifically for this presentation.

Paired in the same season with Amia Yokoyama's first institutional solo show in the Project Room and a new Zoe Walsh mural on the building's 7th Street façade, this is ICA LA's strongest fall lineup in some time — a chance to see an underrated LA original get his due alongside two much younger artists extending some of the same questions about bodies, technology and land.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Gathering
shows.description:
Zoe Walsh takes over ICA LA's 7th Street facade with a commissioned, site-specific mural — the museum's outdoor project slot for the fall season. Walsh, a Los Angeles painter with an MFA from Yale, builds their compositions through digital modeling, hand-cut stencils, and screen printing, layering photographs of queer community and chosen family staged in their own garden with material drawn from queer archives and topographic maps.

The resulting images read as silhouetted bodies suspended in gardens, parks, and urban landscapes — scenes that treat the city's green spaces as sites of queer intimacy reclaimed from erasure. Rather than a single fixed image, Walsh's process of superimposition and refraction keeps the picture plane unstable, so figures shimmer in and out of legibility depending on where you stand and how the light falls on the facade.

This mural extends ideas Walsh has explored in solo shows at Vielmetter and Yossi Milo, translating a studio practice built on canvas into a public-facing, weather-exposed format that will live on the building through the winter. It's a free, walk-by way to encounter an artist whose gallery work usually requires stepping inside.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Our Strange Hollows
shows.description:
Amia Yokoyama's first institutional solo show fills ICA LA's Project Room with ceramic sculpture, holography, painting, and experimental animation — a body of work that treats metamorphosis as both subject and method. Yokoyama, who trained in experimental animation at CalArts and attended Skowhegan, moves clay and light through repeated cycles of breakdown and repair, letting each material's instability stand in for the porousness of bodies and identities under pressure.

The show's title points to an interest in negative space and the underworld: hollow forms in bronze and glass become portals rather than absences, mining ancient mythologies of descent and transformation. Yokoyama has described her ceramics practice as a "dialog with earth, fire, water, and air" that carries political and ritual histories inside ordinary-seeming objects, and that same logic extends to her holographic pieces, where a fragment is built to contain the whole.

It's a compact but ambitious presentation from an artist who has shown at the Armory Center for the Arts and Jeffrey Deitch, and a good entry point for anyone curious about how sculpture and moving image can be made to behave like liquid.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Grounding Bodies, Casting Dreams
shows.description:
This is less a conventional exhibition than a live community ritual staged inside ICA LA: a collaboration between the museum's Agency of Assets youth fellowship and Hwa Records, a collective of Korean diasporic artists and healers-in-residence at the museum. Together, teenage fellows and the resident artists are building a Dol Top (돌탑), a stone tower rooted in Korean geomancy traditions meant to spiritually protect a village — here reimagined as a protective gesture for the fellowship's young participants.

Visitors are invited to participate directly, bringing a stone from home or the surrounding landscape to the front desk to add to the accumulating tower; at the close of the show, the rocks are ceremonially returned to the local Tongva/Los Angeles landscape rather than kept as artifacts. It's a project about displacement, care, and communal repair, growing out of Hwa Records' work processing the effects of anti-Asian violence and generational trauma through gathering and craft.

Worth seeing as much for the process as the object — the tower will look different depending on when you visit, and the show doubles as a showcase for the mentorship and paid-employment model that Agency of Assets runs with Downtown and East LA high schoolers.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Healing with Gold: The Art of Kintsugi on Ceramics & Beyond
shows.description:
Kintsugi — the practice of repairing broken ceramics with gold-dusted lacquer — has become such a popular metaphor in wellness culture that it's easy to forget the actual objects behind it: centuries-old tea bowls whose cracks were mended rather than hidden, turning damage into ornament. This group show at JACCC's Doizaki Gallery, curated by Japanese art historian Meher McArthur, puts those historical vessels in the same room as more than thirty contemporary works that take the kintsugi philosophy in far more varied directions.

The exhibition is organized in three parts, moving from the traditional tea-ceremony roots of gold lacquer repair through contemporary artists actively practicing the technique on ceramics, and finally to work that borrows kintsugi's logic — visible repair as a form of beauty — for painting, sculpture, textile art and installation. Artists in the show include Miya Ando, Naoko Fukumaru, Ted Meyer and Kristine Schomaker, among others, several of whom have used the idea of "golden repair" to address illness, grief, or trauma rather than literal broken pottery.

It's a modest but well-considered survey of an idea that gets invoked constantly and examined rarely — a chance to see where the actual craft tradition ends and the metaphor begins, all inside a 2,000-square-foot gallery in the heart of Little Tokyo. An opening reception and a curator's tour the following weekend offer two easy ways to catch McArthur's thinking on the show in person.

venue.name: Japanese American Cultural & Community Center (JACCC) – George J. Doizaki Gallery

shows.title: Into the Lake of Fire // ⲉ̀ϧⲟⲩⲛ ⲉ̀ϯⲗⲩⲙⲛⲏ ⲛ̀ⲭ̀ⲣⲱⲙ
shows.description:
Sherin Guirguis returns to Luis De Jesus with a suite of monoprints made during a Sam Francis Foundation fellowship in Paris, where she worked directly with Egyptian heritage objects held in French institutions. The prints use gold, faience blue, carnelian red, and ochre — pigments drawn from Egyptian art and architecture — layered on black paper so that glyphs and ritual patterns seem to float or dissolve into the surface. It's quiet, research-driven work that turns museum archives into a starting point for something personal rather than an ending point.

The title nods to a passage from the ancient funerary text long mistranslated as "The Book of the Dead," and the whole project is really about translation and mistranslation: how colonial-era archaeology flattened and renamed Indigenous Egyptian (RemenKeemi) culture, and what it looks like to work back through that record toward something closer to the original meaning. Repetition — printmaking's basic gesture — becomes a way of insisting on memory against erasure.

Guirguis is an LA-based, Cairo-born artist whose work sits in the collections of LACMA and MOCA, among others, and who has built large-scale public commissions from the Pyramids of Giza to Desert X. This is smaller, more intimate work than those outdoor pieces, made for close looking, and it rewards it — the surfaces have a jeweled, light-catching quality that's hard to get across in photos.

venue.name: Luis De Jesus Los Angeles
venue.about: Luis De Jesus Los Angeles is a contemporary art gallery founded in 2007 in San Diego by partners Luis De Jesus and Jay Wingate under the name Luis De Jesus Seminal Projects. The gallery relocated to Santa Monica in 2010, rebranding as Luis De Jesus Los Angeles, then moved to the Culver City Arts District in 2011, where it operated for a decade. Since spring 2021 it has occupied an expansive space on the edge of downtown Los Angeles's Arts District. The gallery represents a diverse roster of artists whose work engages personal, social, cultural, and aesthetic concerns, with many receiving major awards, biennial invitations, and museum acquisitions.

shows.title: Bite The Hand That Feeds You
shows.description:
Phung Huynh's third solo show at Luis De Jesus centers on an unlikely charged object: the pink donut box that has become an emblem of Cambodian refugee entrepreneurship in Southern California. Huynh, a Cambodian-Vietnamese refugee artist based in LA, draws directly onto and around these boxes in graphite, building documentary-style drawings, paintings, and sculptural installations that hold both the sweetness of the family business mythology and the exhausting, racialized labor underneath it.

The work pointedly rejects the "grateful refugee" narrative baked into American resettlement rhetoric. By reclaiming the idiom "bite the hand that feeds you" — usually deployed to silence complaint — Huynh reframes who is actually doing the feeding: immigrant and refugee labor sustaining industries that then target those same communities through immigration enforcement. It's a body of work that uses something as mundane as a donut box to talk about debt, gratitude, and who gets to tell the story of arrival.

Huynh's work sits in LACMA's and the Pacific Asia Museum's collections, and this show continues her long-running interest in using intimate, everyday materials to unpack the costs of displacement and assimilation.

shows.title: Inheritance
shows.description:
June Edmonds extends her well-known Flag series with new paintings that treat the American flag as an unstable, contested symbol rather than a fixed monument. Working in a deep, deliberately expanded palette of browns, Edmonds interrupts her "Standing Flag" compositions with abstract stains — blights, scars, phantom topographies — that read as unresolved history pushing up through the stripes.

A newer, more intimate strand of the show, the "Draped Flag" works, releases the canvas from its rectangular support entirely; cinched at the center, these loose, child-sized forms evoke hoodies and children's clothing, a direct address to the adultification and endangerment of Black youth, from Emmett Till to Tamir Rice and Trayvon Martin. It's a shift from monument to garment, from symbol to body.

Edmonds, an LA-based painter who had a mid-career survey at LMU's Laband Art Gallery in 2021 and holds a Guggenheim Fellowship, continues to use color theory — specifically the range and dignity of brown — as both formal strategy and political argument. This is her fourth show with the gallery and a clear escalation of the ideas she's been building for years.

shows.title: Camino y Paz
shows.description:
Ángeles Agrela paints and draws women whose faces are all but consumed by cascades of hair — thick, colorful, sculptural masses rendered in acrylic and pencil on paper at a scale that turns portraiture into something closer to landscape. The Granada-based Spanish artist has spent years using hair as her central subject, treating it as a stand-in for the layered, often contradictory ways femininity has been depicted across art history, from Pre-Raphaelite muses to contemporary fashion imagery.

Camino y Paz gathers new large-scale works, many nearly six feet tall, each built around a pair or single sitter whose identity is partly obscured by an exuberant tangle of pattern and color. The effect is playful but pointed: by hiding the face, the traditional site of a portrait's meaning, Agrela redirects attention to costume, gesture, and the sheer physical presence of hair as material and metaphor.

This is Agrela's first solo exhibition at Nicodim's Los Angeles space, following her inclusion in the gallery's group shows over the past several years and solo presentations in New York, Marbella, and Vancouver. Her work sits in public collections including CAC Málaga and the National Library of Spain, and this show extends a body of work that has been steadily gaining international attention.

venue.name: Nicodim Gallery
venue.about: Nicodim Gallery is a contemporary art gallery led by owner Mihai Nicodim, with spaces in Los Angeles, New York, and Bucharest. Its program centers on painting and sculpture by an international, cross-generational roster of artists, including figures from Zimbabwe, South Africa, Romania, Spain, and the United States. The gallery has built a reputation for introducing artists such as Isabelle Albuquerque, Devin B. Johnson, Adrian Ghenie, and Moffat Takadiwa to wider audiences, later supported by major institutional exhibitions and biennials. Nicodim regularly participates in international art fairs including Frieze, Art Basel, and The Armory Show, and maintains an active exhibition schedule across its three locations, reflecting a program invested in figuration, materiality, and voices from outside traditional Western art centers.

shows.title: Happy Trails
shows.description:
Sarah Miska paints horses and the people who work with them, and for her third solo show at Night Gallery she trades the English riding world of her earlier paintings for the American West. Last fall she spent six weeks painting out of a converted horse stable in Wyoming, and the resulting canvases draw on photographs she took there — cattle ranches, working horses, and the wranglers and apprentices who tend them.

The paintings are meticulous in a way that rewards close looking: individual strands of mane, the sheen of a cow's ear in the sun, the particular sun-bleached texture of denim and leather. Miska has always been interested in the intimacy between horse and rider, and here she extends that interest to the practical, unglamorous labor of ranch life — a deliberate departure from the tailored, aristocratic associations of the equestrian paintings that made her name.

What holds the show together is Miska's refusal to let Western and equestrian subject matter sit at the margins of "serious" painting. Her sculptural training shows in how she handles bodies and space, and the paintings have a voyeuristic closeness that turns grooming rituals and rough terrain into meditations on self-presentation and control.

venue.name: Night Gallery
venue.about: Night Gallery is a contemporary art gallery based in the Arts District of Los Angeles, at 2050 Imperial Street. Led by owner Davida Nemeroff, the gallery represents an international roster of emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, and installation. Its program includes solo and group exhibitions, publications, and an active presence at major international art fairs such as Frieze, Art Basel Miami Beach, The Armory Show, and NADA. Night Gallery artists have received extensive press coverage in outlets including The New York Times, Artforum, Frieze, and Hyperallergic, and its exhibitions frequently travel to museums and institutions worldwide.

shows.title: Idea of North
shows.description:
Ben Tong's second solo show at Night Gallery is built around the idea that a painting shouldn't sit still. Working in oil, Tong pushes pigment across the canvas with brushes, rags, and — distinctively — a massage gun, producing radial, semi-controlled bursts of color that behave like light passing through stained glass or wind moving through a landscape. Moons, rainbow arcs, and starlike flares recur across the work, giving the paintings a charged, almost transmitting quality.

The title borrows from Glenn Gould's 1967 radio documentary of the same name, and Tong is explicit about thinking in terms of frequency and signal — light as something that can be received rather than just depicted. It's a body of work shaped by the particular quality of Southern California sun, treating each canvas as if it were already lit from within before a single brushstroke.

Tong, an LA-based painter who previously showed The Violet Hour at the gallery, works in a mode that resists fixed concepts in favor of intuitive, doubt-tolerant process — action generating meaning rather than the reverse. Worth seeing for anyone interested in painting that treats color and surface as an active, moving field rather than a settled image.
