shows.title: Future Past Tense
shows.artist: Esperanza Cortés, Cheryl Derricotte, Karen Hampton, Asa Jackson, Fay Ku
shows.description:
Future Past Tense brings together five artists — Esperanza Cortés, Cheryl Derricotte, Karen Hampton, Asa Jackson, and Fay Ku — whose work treats personal and historical memory as material to be woven, cast, or dyed rather than simply narrated. The show spans tapestry, kiln-formed glass, beaded and clay sculpture, and graphite drawing, but the artists share a habit of using craft traditions to carry difficult inherited histories forward.

Karen Hampton's indigo tapestries grew out of a visit to the South Carolina plantation that gave her family its surname, and Asa Jackson's monumental woven pieces reference the indigo-dyed cotton once worn by enslaved laborers. Cheryl Derricotte's glass "books" with invented titles quietly needle at the erasure of Black women from professional and historical record, while Esperanza Cortés's beaded and clay sculptures draw on the folk-art and ritual traditions of the Americas to push back against colonial narratives. Fay Ku's graphite and watercolor drawings, rooted in the fables her family told after emigrating from Taiwan, add a more intimate, fantastical register to the show.

Individually, several of these artists have exhibition histories with major institutions — Hampton's work sits in the Museum of Fine Arts Boston and the Denver Art Museum, and Cortés has a concurrent show opening at New York's Hispanic Society Museum & Library this September. Together at Patricia Sweetow, their work makes a quiet case that craft media are especially suited to holding onto histories that official records tend to smooth over.

venue.name: Patricia Sweetow Gallery
venue.about: Patricia Sweetow Gallery is a contemporary art gallery that opened in San Francisco in 1997 and relocated to Downtown Los Angeles in 2022, where it now operates from South Santa Fe Avenue. The gallery is led by principal Patricia Sweetow with associate director Christal Darling. Its program centers on artists working in non-traditional materials—textile, ceramic, fiber, and craft-based practices—that challenge institutional hierarchies between 'high' and 'low' art. Exhibiting artists often draw on craft traditions to interrogate colonial structures, personal identity, and cultural memory. The gallery has participated in numerous art fairs across the U.S. and Canada and represents a roster of emerging and mid-career artists working across sculpture, painting, ceramics, and fiber art.

shows.title: In These Times: Recent Acquisitions at MOCA
shows.description:
MOCA takes stock of five years of collecting with this survey of recent purchases and gifts, organized not chronologically but thematically — rooms devoted to depictions of Los Angeles, group portraiture, new directions in abstract painting, and work obsessed with minute detail. It's the kind of show that functions as a status report on a museum's priorities: what MOCA's curators and donors have decided matters enough to acquire right now.

The roster spans generations and media, from painters like Louise Bonnet, Jacqueline Humphries, and Rebecca Morris to photographers Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Sawako Goda, sculptors Liz Larner and Diane Simpson, and artists working at the intersection of painting and social history like Andrea Bowers, Henry Taylor, and Vincent Valdez. Grouping the works by theme rather than by artist or date lets the show make quieter arguments about what recurs across a collection built by many different hands and donors over time.

For visitors who know MOCA's permanent holdings, this is a chance to see what's been added to the story since the last big collection rehang — and for those still working out what MOCA collects and why, it's as good an introduction as any to the museum's current curatorial thinking.

venue.name: MOCA Grand Avenue
venue.about: MOCA, founded in 1979, is Los Angeles's leading museum dedicated to contemporary art, built around a collection of nearly 8,000 works with deep holdings in LA-based practice alongside international art. MOCA Grand Avenue, the museum's original and flagship site in downtown LA, was designed by architect Arata Isozaki in the 1980s and opened as his first completed US project, announcing MOCA as a major architectural presence on Bunker Hill. The museum also operates The Geffen Contemporary at MOCA, a renovated warehouse in Little Tokyo, and stewards Michael Heizer's land-art work Double Negative in Nevada. Programming spans monographic and thematic exhibitions, education initiatives, publishing, and new-media engagement.

shows.title: Regime: Dramatis Personae
shows.description:
Alexander Apóstol's black-and-white portrait series casts LGBTQ+ activists in Caracas as stock characters from the theater of authoritarian power — the Dictator, the Masked Police Officer, the Ideological Tourist, the Propped-Up Paramilitarist — each posed with the studied body language of a political archetype rather than named as an individual. Shot in 2017 during a period of intense government repression in Venezuela, the ninety-image series draws on the artist's research into how gesture and posture get performed under populist and authoritarian rule, from independence-era heroes through the rise and fall of the Bolivarian Revolution.

Apóstol, a Venezuelan artist based in Madrid, frequently invokes the geometric abstraction of countrymen Carlos Cruz-Diez and Jesús Rafael Soto to needle at how national identity gets constructed and mythologized. By stripping his sitters of names in favor of social functions, he turns the portraits into a kind of civic taxonomy — a cast list for a political drama that keeps restaging itself. MOCA's presentation arrives as especially pointed given recent events in Venezuela, extending the work's original bite into an ongoing crisis.

This is a tightly focused, single-series exhibition rather than a full retrospective, well suited to close, patient looking at how photography can function as political theater criticism.

shows.title: Chapter 3: Interiors and Exteriors
shows.description:
The third installment in an ongoing series, Shanna Waddell's exhibition continues her project of building out an interior and exterior visual world in paint, moving between domestic scenes and the landscapes that frame them. As with the earlier chapters, the work reads as a kind of extended narrative told through discrete paintings rather than a single set of unrelated canvases.

Details on the specific works are still emerging as the show approaches its September opening, but Waddell's practice has consistently centered figuration grounded in everyday spaces — rooms, thresholds, the view through a window — treated with a painter's attention to how interior life and the built environment shape each other.

venue.name: Vielmetter Los Angeles
venue.about: Vielmetter Los Angeles is a contemporary art gallery in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles, located at 1700 S Santa Fe Avenue. It is owned and directed by Susanne Vielmetter and operates three exhibition spaces at that address. The gallery represents a multigenerational group of artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video, and installation, including figures such as Nicole Eisenman, Arlene Shechet, Mickalene Thomas, Wangechi Mutu, Mary Kelly, and the estate of William Pope.L. Represented artists have participated in major international biennials, museum surveys, and art fairs, and have received sustained critical attention in publications including The New York Times, Artforum, The Guardian, and Artnet. The gallery's program spans several decades of contemporary practice, with a consistent focus on socially engaged, figurative, and materially inventive work by artists based in Los Angeles, New York, and internationally.

shows.title: Views of Pagan, Burma, 1976-78
shows.description:
German photographer Ursula Schulz-Dornburg has spent decades documenting landscape and architecture at the edges of political and historical memory, and this show returns to some of her earliest sustained work: black-and-white photographs made in Pagan (Bagan), Burma between 1976 and 1978. The ancient temple field, one of the world's great concentrations of Buddhist monuments, becomes in her hands less a tourist monument than a study in erosion, silence, and scale.

These Pagan pictures — made decades before her better-known Cold War and Middle East bodies of work — show the same patient attention to structures left to time and weather. It's a quiet show, built for looking slowly.

shows.title: Julie Shafer | Jennifer Celio
shows.description:
as-is pairs two Southern California artists who both work at the boundary between document and invention. Julie Shafer is a photographer and educator whose practice examines the human imprint on landscape — she's made large-format work photographing industrially damaged terrain, and has spoken of her images as a way of walking through the ghosts a place leaves behind. Jennifer Celio, by contrast, works mostly in drawing and mixed media, mining the visual clutter of the built environment — vintage typefaces, mid-century design, personal ephemera — into dense, precise compositions that ask you to look slowly.

Both artists share a history with the loose Los Angeles network of artist-run spaces (Celio was a longtime member of Durden and Ray), and this isn't the first time their work has crossed paths at as-is — Shafer previously appeared there in a three-artist show built around politically engaged, lens-based practice. Pairing her photographic record of place with Celio's drawn accumulation of urban detail sets up a productive friction between the documentary and the invented.

as-is has built its reputation over more than a decade as one of downtown's steadiest small exhibition spaces, consistently giving veteran and mid-career Los Angeles artists tightly focused, single- or double-artist shows rather than sprawling group surveys — this one continues that pattern.

shows.title: Through the Tunnel
shows.description:
Ann Leda Shapiro has spent five decades making watercolors and works on paper that treat the body as a landscape of feeling — skin standing in for terrain, internal organs rendered as weather systems, psychological states given physical form. Her paintings move fluidly between the anatomical and the cosmic: a "Bonded Bodies" composition, a smoke-veiled tree at the edge of a fire, a spine drawn like a coiled snake. There's a loose, watery immediacy to her line that owes something to both feminist body art of the 1970s and older traditions of visionary and medical illustration.

"Through the Tunnel" gathers work spanning from the 1970s through her recent wildfire and tree paintings, tracing a long arc in which the personal (illness, aging, grief) keeps bumping up against the environmental (drought, fire, loss of habitat). Titles like "Smoke from Wildfires" and "Tornado" sit alongside earlier, more intimate pieces such as "Intestinal Distress" and "Holding On," suggesting a practice that has always used the body to talk about the world, and vice versa.

It's a chance to see how a career built on unguarded, visceral image-making holds up against, and speaks to, the present moment.

shows.title: Unordinary Days: Celebration as Resistance
shows.description:
This long-running exhibition revisits the Mary's Day celebrations that Corita Kent helped transform at Immaculate Heart College in the 1960s, when a quiet Catholic spring ritual became a campus-wide happening of music, dance, and Pop-inflected banners and installations. Rather than focusing solely on her famous serigraphs, the show treats collective celebration itself as a form of social practice — tracing how Kent and her students used costume, procession, and signage to fold anti-war and civil rights concerns into a religious observance, often putting the college at odds with a more conservative Church hierarchy.

The checklist draws on rare archival material alongside artwork: event flyers and programs from the Immaculate Heart College newspaper sit next to serigraphs like the two-part "tender be," in which Kent's shift away from figuration toward text-and-slogan compositions is on full view. These prints show her characteristic method of lifting language from advertising, pop songs, and scripture and recombining it into something closer to visual poetry, including her recurring, irreverent reimagining of the Virgin Mary as a figure of the everyday.

Installation photographs round out the presentation, giving a sense of how the original Mary's Day environments — box towers, banners, processional routes — transformed familiar campus spaces. For anyone who knows Kent mainly through her rainbow stripe or her LOVE stamp, this is a chance to see the more process-driven, collaborative side of her practice, and to understand how closely her graphic language was tied to a specific community and political moment.

shows.title: Clappers
shows.description:
Kathleen Henderson's drawings read like dispatches from an America that has stopped pretending things are fine. Working in oil stick and diluted oil on paper, she builds scenes where couples lie in bed together, clouds mass over flat land, and death shows up not as a specter but as one more figure going through the motions of daily life. The palette is often lurid — hot pinks, sickly greens — which only sharpens the sense that something has curdled beneath the domestic surface.

The suite grew out of a residency in Spoleto, Italy, where Henderson became fixated on the Marquis de Mores, a 19th-century French aristocrat-turned-rancher often cited as an early fascist, and traced a line from his failed cattle empire in the Dakotas to the rise of authoritarian violence in Europe. That research runs underneath the work as a kind of historical undertow, surfacing in titles and recurring motifs rather than literal illustration. The drawings are less about making an argument than about sitting with the queasy feeling that catastrophe has become ordinary.

Henderson's line has the loose, confident economy of someone who spent years painting sets and backdrops before turning to works on paper full-time, and that scene-painter's sense of staging shows up in how she blocks out space and light. This is her third solo show with Track 16, and it arrives as a tightly focused, formally assured body of work rather than a survey — worth a visit for anyone interested in how American painting is processing the current moment without resorting to easy slogans.

shows.title: Cute and Creepy 4 + Rising Stars of LA: Fall Edition
shows.description:
The Hive's October lineup pairs its recurring "Cute and Creepy" franchise, curated by Lady Beaver, with a "Rising Stars of LA" showcase spotlighting newer names in the gallery's pop-surrealist orbit. True to the title, the work swings between saccharine and unsettling — kawaii-adjacent character painting sitting next to grimier, more macabre imagery, with dozens of artists packed into the gallery's sprawling group-show format.

Featured artists Anka Yanovna and Colette Hussey anchor the show alongside a small-wall feature from Lorenzo Hall, while the Rising Stars wing gives a platform to newer contributors like NYX Garcia, Mariya Zaloznaya, and Vibrant Goth. This is very much the Hive's house style: a huge, democratic group show rather than a tightly curated statement, with dozens of artists represented across every wall and the gallery's trademark first-Saturday opening turned into a full event with DJs and performance.

It's not a show for viewers looking for a single thesis — it's a snapshot of the lowbrow/pop-surrealist scene that the Hive has championed in downtown LA for over two decades, cute mascots and creepy creatures crowding the same walls in roughly equal measure.

shows.title: Poster Pals
shows.description:
Poster Pals is a straightforward, fan-friendly pairing of two LA artists who built their names in music and poster graphics rather than the gallery system. MAZZA's contribution leans into dense, character-driven illustration with the kind of pop-culture-literate humor that made his prints popular well beyond the art world, while MUNK ONE shows the screen-printed concert posters and band artwork that have made him a go-to collaborator for musicians, alongside originals he hasn't shown before.

The show is less interested in making a critical argument than in celebrating the poster as its own legitimate art form — a medium built for reproduction and collecting rather than preciousness. Seeing the hand-drawn originals next to the editioned prints is the real value here, letting you compare the loose, direct mark-making underneath the more polished, mass-producible final images.

It's a good entry point for anyone curious about LA's poster-and-illustration scene, which runs parallel to the fine-art gallery world but rarely gets this kind of dedicated two-person spotlight.

shows.title: This Day, A Place in Time
shows.description:
Julian Tan's paintings and sculpture catch people mid-gesture, suspended in the gap between something happening and their ability to process it — a kind of sublime paralysis that Tan ties to living inside automated, algorithmically mediated systems. Figures here act without quite owning their actions, caught in loops of repetition that read as both comic and unsettling.

Tan, a second-generation Chinese American artist who moved to Los Angeles by way of Nashville, builds his images around the anxieties of a world where technology, capital, and alienation have become inseparable. The work sits at the intersection of narrative painting and object-making, using sculpture to extend the paintings' psychological space into the room rather than just illustrating it on canvas.

As a small, single-artist presentation in a project space run under Fulcrum Arts' EMERGE program, the show is a good chance to see a developing body of work up close, without the mediation of a larger survey — a snapshot of an artist working through very current unease in a sustained, serious way.

shows.title: 20th Anniversary Exhibition — September Edition
shows.description:
This group show is the second half of Corey Helford Gallery's two-part celebration of its twentieth year in business, bringing together an intergenerational roster of artists who have shaped the gallery's identity in New Contemporary and pop-surrealist art. Each participant made a new piece specifically for the occasion rather than contributing existing inventory, so the show functions less like a clip-reel retrospective and more like a fresh group statement from a shared lineage of artists.

Given CHG's two decades championing New Figurative Art, Pop Surrealism, and street-art-adjacent painting and sculpture, expect the show to range widely in style and medium — from tightly rendered figurative painting to mixed-media and sculptural work — unified mainly by the gallery's long-standing eye for narrative, craft, and pop-culture fluency rather than any single movement.

Seeing a show built entirely of new commissions from a gallery's extended family of artists is a useful way to take the temperature of where New Contemporary art stands two decades after CHG helped put the genre on the map in Los Angeles.

shows.title: Love, Death, & All Her Friends
shows.description:
Kelogsloops — the Melbourne-based digital-turned-traditional painter known for dreamy, watercolor-washed figures — brings a solo exhibition to CHG's Gallery 3 running alongside the gallery's 20th-anniversary group show. The work continues his signature mode: solitary figures and quiet emotional states rendered in soft gradients and atmospheric color, closer in spirit to melancholic illustration than to pop-surrealist bombast.

The title, pairing "Love" and "Death" with "All Her Friends," suggests a loosely narrative arc running through the body of work — relationships, loss, and the people who orbit both — treated with the understated, diaristic intimacy that built kelogsloops' large following well before he had gallery representation. It's a quieter, more interior counterpoint to the anniversary blowout happening elsewhere in the building.

For viewers who know kelogsloops primarily through prints and social media, this is a chance to see the paintings at full scale and in person, where the layered color work and soft edges read very differently than on a screen.

shows.title: Everybody's Perfect
shows.description:
Bradley Harms spent decades as a precise, hard-edged Canadian abstractionist, and Everybody's Perfect marks a deliberate break from that discipline. In its place he turns to domestic processes — cutting, dyeing, ironing, sewing, stuffing — building paintings that resist the machined perfection his earlier work pursued, with softened edges, irregular seams, and sculptural folds that make the canvases behave more like handled objects than windows onto an image.

The results sit in an uneasy, interesting zone between serious abstraction and familiar domestic things: a canvas might recall a stuffed toy or a worn sleeping bag, something half-remembered from childhood returned in strange form. That tension between a rigorous abstract painting tradition and soft, homemade construction is the engine of the whole show.

Underlying the shift is a real question about what's left for the human hand in an age when image-generating technology can manufacture "perfection" instantly — Harms answers by betting on intuition and the visible evidence of handling over mechanical consistency, work that stays interesting precisely because it refuses to resolve cleanly.

shows.title: The Paradise of Cyrus
shows.description:
Ladan Sedighi works in the lineage of Southern California minimalism — precise, geometric compositions in holographic film, vinyl wrap, and acrylic sheeting, materials borrowed from car culture and commercial signage rather than traditional painting. But the formal rigor is in service of something warmer than minimalism's usual austerity: she traces her real subject to the jeweled brooches and pins of her own Iranian heritage, prized not for their imagery but for the way light moves and flashes across them.

The show's title and structure come from the chahar bagh, the four-part Persian garden plan that runs from Cyrus the Great's garden at Pasargadae through Shiraz, the Alhambra, and the Taj Mahal — an architectural lineage of paradise gardens that Sedighi translates into columns, blocks, bands, and interrupted grids of industrial, light-catching material. It's an unusual move: using car-culture materials and a minimalist grid to carry centuries of Persian garden and textile history.

The effect she's after is joy without explanation — the shimmer of water and tile, the flash of a brooch, the grid's holographic surface collapsed into a single sensory hit. Worth seeing for anyone interested in how California finish/fetish and light-and-space traditions can be redirected toward an entirely different cultural inheritance.

shows.title: the sound i saw
shows.description:
Roy DeCarava spent the late 1940s through the 1960s photographing New York City's Black life with an eye tuned as much to sound as to sight, and this exhibition — curated by Ebony L. Haynes — reassembles the body of work he called the sound i saw. First put together as a handmade artist's book and later shown at the Studio Museum in Harlem in 1983, the project weaves images of jazz musicians on and off stage with pictures of everyday street life: deliverymen, kids playing, commuters waiting on a platform. DeCarava's silver gelatin prints are famous for their deep, controlled tonality, and the pairing of music-adjacent and street imagery is his way of asking viewers to notice the rhythm and improvisation already present in ordinary city life.

David Zwirner is pairing the photographs with a listening room built around DeCarava's own jazz record collection and playlists, an unusual curatorial move that leans into the show's audio-visual premise rather than just gesturing at it.

DeCarava's history in Los Angeles is thin, which is part of what makes this show notable: the gallery notes it's only the fourth time his work has been shown solo in the city, after a 1982 appearance at the Los Angeles Center for Photographic Studies, LACMA's 1996 retrospective, and a 2019 show at the Underground Museum. For a photographer this influential, that's a striking scarcity, and reason enough to make time for it.

venue.name: David Zwirner
venue.about: David Zwirner is an international contemporary and postwar art gallery with locations in New York, Los Angeles, London, Paris, and Hong Kong. It represents more than seventy artists and estates and is known for ambitious, cross-media exhibitions spanning painting, photography, sculpture, and installation, alongside active secondary-market dealing. The gallery was founded in 1993 in New York and expanded internationally over the following decades. Its Los Angeles presence debuted in 2023 with spaces in Melrose Hill, followed in 2024 by a standalone building designed, like all of the gallery's spaces, by Selldorf Architects. The Los Angeles gallery shares the program of the wider David Zwirner enterprise, presenting exhibitions by the gallery's international roster of established and emerging artists.

shows.title: Form Follows Feeling
shows.description:
Oliver Lee Jackson has spent six decades building paintings and sculptures around the human figure, and this show — Lisson's first with the Oakland-based artist at its Los Angeles space — brings together work from across that span rather than presenting a single recent series. Paintings built from spraypaint, chalk, enamel and oil stick sit alongside a rarer body of work: carved marble and mixed-media sculptures, some begun decades ago in Carrara and only now completed, that Jackson treats as slow accumulations of cloth, graphite, gold leaf and stone.

What ties the two mediums together is Jackson's refusal to let the figure resolve into simple likeness. Bodies appear crouched, in flight, or dissolving into their colored grounds, which are prepared for him by assistants without his knowledge beforehand, forcing an element of chance into every composition. The sculptures work similarly by accretion, with fresh material grafted onto old fragments so that a single totemic form can carry the residue of years of studio time.

It's a useful corrective for anyone who knows Jackson mainly through museum surveys at the National Gallery or the Saint Louis Art Museum: here the sculptural side of his practice, last seen publicly in a 2024 High Line commission, gets real room to breathe alongside the paintings that made his reputation.

venue.name: Lisson Gallery
venue.about: Lisson Gallery is an internationally established contemporary art gallery founded in 1967 by Nicholas Logsdail, with roots in Minimal and Conceptual art. Today it represents more than 70 artists spanning generations and geographies, from postwar figures like Carl Andre and Sol LeWitt to contemporary names such as Ai Weiwei, Marina Abramović and Hiroshi Sugimoto. Its Los Angeles space opened in 2023 in Hollywood's Sycamore District, occupying a standalone two-story building of over 8,000 square feet, with an inaugural exhibition of Carmen Herrera's Days of the Week series. The gallery also maintains spaces in London, New York and Shanghai, continuing its history of introducing international artists to new audiences.

shows.title: Hard Line Women
shows.description:
Nonaka-Hill gathers twelve Japanese women artists — among them Atsuko Tanaka, Rei Kawakubo, Kazuko Miyamoto, Tomie Ohtake and Kay Sekimachi — who each, at some point across six decades, worked in a hard-edged, geometric vocabulary that had little patience for softness or sentiment. The show spans painting, sculpture, textile, performance documentation and photography, and its animating idea is straightforward but rarely stated this plainly: that rigor and coolness were themselves a form of resistance for these artists, a way of working against the expressive, macho postures that dominated so much postwar art criticism.

Several of the artists included — Eiko Yamazawa, Aiko Miyawaki, Etsuko Nakatsuji, Shizuko Yoshikawa — also worked as graphic designers, and the show argues that this dual practice sharpened rather than diluted their formal thinking, feeding a shared interest in order and non-psychological composition. Pairing canonical names like Tanaka with far less exhibited figures like Sumie Aoki and Akiko Horio should make for a genuinely instructive walk through twentieth-century Japanese abstraction.

venue.name: Nonaka-Hill
venue.about: Nonaka-Hill is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles founded in 2018 by Rodney and Taka Nonaka-Hill, with a second space in Kyoto, Japan. The program centers on modern and contemporary Japanese art, presenting many artists for the first time on the West Coast, spanning painting, ceramics, sculpture, and photography from postwar and contemporary Japan alongside a smaller group of international artists. Located in Hollywood near the intersection of Melrose and Highland, the gallery sits among a cluster of established Los Angeles galleries. Nonaka-Hill represents the estate of Yōga painter Zenzaburo Kojima and has built a program bridging Japanese art history with contemporary practice, participating regularly in international art fairs including Frieze, Art Basel, and Art Collaboration Kyoto.

shows.title: Book of Sand
shows.description:
Elliott Hundley's seventh solo show with Regen Projects trades the Greek tragedies and Rilke sonnets that anchored his earlier bodies of work for something more interior. Book of Sand — titled after the Borges story about an infinite, unreadable book — takes its structural cue from Jungian sand-tray therapy, in which patients arrange miniature figures in sand to surface unconscious material. Several paintings here are bordered like a sand tray itself, turning the gallery into a kind of psychic stage where Hundley's signature accumulations of paper, pins, string and encaustic play the role of figurines.

The show's centerpiece sculptures continue Hundley's practice of building around personally resonant found objects: Palette (2024) fuses concrete, bone, rattan, feathers and other studio detritus into a totem-like column, while a large tapestry incorporates fabric from his mother's wedding veil. It's dense, accretive work that rewards close looking rather than a quick pass, consistent with an artist who trained at UCLA and has had museum surveys at the Nasher Sculpture Center, the Wexner Center and, most recently, the Santa Barbara Museum of Art.

Running concurrently in the gallery's viewing rooms is a focused selection of small watercolor-on-canvas paintings and studies by the late Silke Otto-Knapp (1970–2022), a former UCLA painting professor whose grayscale "erasure" technique — layering and scraping black watercolor to let a white ground emerge — offers a quieter, more austere counterpoint to Hundley's maximalism just steps away.

venue.name: Regen Projects
venue.about: Regen Projects is a contemporary art gallery on Santa Monica Boulevard in Los Angeles. The gallery represents an international roster of established and emerging artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, film, and installation. Its program has become known for supporting artists who engage with conceptual, social, and political concerns, spanning generations from pioneers of Conceptual and Minimal art to younger figures working in figuration and abstraction today. Regen Projects regularly organizes solo exhibitions for its artists in Los Angeles and participates in major international art fairs, while its artists are frequently included in biennials, museum surveys, and public commissions worldwide. The gallery also represents several artist estates, continuing the legacies of important late-twentieth-century figures.

shows.title: Who Needs Muscles If Nothing Is Heavy?
shows.description:
Bridget Mullen's fourth solo show with the gallery gathers fifteen paintings built around the idea of mutation: a shape or gesture in one canvas warps, migrates, and resurfaces transformed in the next, like a visual game of telephone. Hands grip empty sleeves, bulging eyes press against intestinal grids, and a figure descends a staircase split awkwardly across two abutting canvases — the seams and staggered panels are as much the subject as the imagery itself.

Mullen works without preliminary sketches, letting abstract marks and negative space calcify into figures and structures as she paints, so the pictures read as records of perception catching up with itself. That process gives the show its philosophical undertow (there are nods to Merleau-Ponty's idea that sensation is inseparable from the body doing the sensing) without ever feeling like an illustrated thesis; the paintings are strange, funny, and viscerally alive with pattern, hair, brick, and plumbing standing in for the membranes between inside and outside, body and object.

Mullen has had a serious decade of momentum — residencies at Skowhegan, MacDowell, and Yaddo, a Headlands Chiaro Award, and work now held by the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen and other institutions — and this exhibition, her most ambitious presentation of new work in Los Angeles yet, is a good chance to see how her language keeps mutating in real time.

venue.name: Nazarian / Curcio
venue.about: Nazarian / Curcio is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles, owned by Shulamit Nazarian and Seth Curcio. Nazarian founded the gallery in Venice, CA in 2012, initially focusing on artists from the greater Middle East. Curcio joined in 2016, and together they broadened the program to emerging, mid-career, and established artists whose work engages social and political issues through personal narrative. In 2017 the gallery moved to a 6,000-square-foot, two-story building on La Brea Avenue in Hollywood, with two exhibition spaces, a library, offices, and viewing rooms. The gallery represents artists based in the U.S. and abroad, with an emphasis on those working in Los Angeles, and regularly participates in major national and international art fairs.

shows.title: Desert Lenses
shows.description:
Ry Rocklen has spent years turning cast-off household objects into ceramic sculpture, and Desert Lenses points that habit of attention out toward the high desert. The show's title works as a pun: everyday things we can't do without — a sock, a slice of toast, a strip of Venetian blind — are recast in glazed ceramic using mold-making and photographic transfer, so that a mundane object becomes a kind of viewing device, a lens onto the wider landscape around it.

The "Absorption Panel" series is the clearest expression of that idea: flat ceramic panels bearing photo-real images of bread, candy, or a window pressed into three-dimensional relief, blurring the line between picture and object. Elsewhere, socks hang like curtains and everyday debris gets the reverent, slightly absurd treatment of a still-life painting. Rocklen has a long history of finding grandeur in domestic detritus — trophies made from furniture, shelving built from personal effects — and this show extends that sensibility into the wide-open, sun-bleached terrain of the Mojave and beyond, treating the desert less as scenery than as a mood that seeps into ordinary objects.

It's a show that rewards close looking: the ceramics photograph well but read very differently in person, where the glaze catches light and the illusion of photographic flatness gives way to the material reality of clay.

venue.name: Wilding Cran Gallery
venue.about: Wilding Cran Gallery is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles, founded in 2014 by Naomi Wilding and Anthony Cran. Now located at 607 N Western Avenue, the gallery represents a roster of emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, photography and mixed media, including Karon Davis, Fran Siegel, Ry Rocklen and Polly Borland. Its program has been featured at major international fairs such as Frieze Los Angeles, Frieze New York, Frieze London, The Armory Show, EXPO Chicago, FELIX Art Fair and NADA New York, and its exhibitions have drawn coverage from outlets including the Los Angeles Times, Artforum, The New York Times and The Guardian. The gallery is a member of the Gallery Association Los Angeles (GALA) and the New Art Dealers Alliance (NADA).

shows.title: Talk to Me
shows.description:
Vanessa Prager returns to Diane Rosenstein Gallery for her third solo show, an exhibition of new paintings that continues her long study of the human face pushed toward abstraction. Prager builds her portraits and figures out of thick, sculptural impasto, working the paint with palette knives until skin, hair, and background dissolve into ridges of pure pigment — you read the image at a distance and feel the material up close.

The Los Angeles-based artist has spent the past decade refining this push-pull between representation and mark-making, often returning to intimate subjects — lovers, friends, herself — rendered at a scale that makes the paint handling as much the subject as the sitter. Titles like "Affectionately" point to the emotional register she's after: warm, tactile, a little vulnerable.

For a gallery goer, this is a chance to see how far Prager has pushed her signature technique since her last outing here, and to catch a working method — thick paint laid on with tools rather than brushes — that photographs badly and rewards being seen in person.

venue.name: Diane Rosenstein Gallery
venue.about: Diane Rosenstein Gallery is a contemporary fine art gallery founded in 2012 by Diane Rosenstein, located in the Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles. The gallery represents emerging, midcareer, and established artists working across a wide range of media, including painting, drawing, photography, sculpture, and ceramics. Its program has featured artists such as Eleanor Antin, Julian Stanczak, Amir Zaki, and Terran Last Gun, reflecting an interest in both historical and contemporary practices. The gallery participates regularly in major art fairs, including Independent, Untitled Art, and Art Basel Miami Beach, and its artists' work is frequently reviewed in national art publications.

shows.title: Amadeo Luciano Lorenzato
shows.description:
Lorenzato (1900–1995) is one of the great outsider figures of Brazilian modernism: a house painter and itinerant laborer from Minas Gerais who didn't take up easel painting seriously until his sixties, after decades spent working in Brazil and briefly in Italy. This presentation, David Zwirner's fourth show devoted to the artist and his first ever in Los Angeles, gathers small-scale paintings of the everyday scenes around his hometown of Belo Horizonte — hillside houses, kitchen tables, potted plants, church façades — rendered in flattened, almost geometric blocks of saturated color.

What makes Lorenzato's paintings compelling is the tension between their modest subject matter and their sophisticated formal intelligence: thick, deliberately built-up surfaces (he often used a palette knife to lay paint on like plaster) turn ordinary domestic views into something closer to abstraction. There's a kinship with self-taught painters like Bonnard's more naive cousins, but also a direct line to the color logic of Brazilian concretism, despite Lorenzato never being formally part of that movement.

For Los Angeles audiences this is a rare chance to see a substantial body of work by an artist far better known in Brazil than in the U.S., and one whose reputation has grown steadily since his rediscovery late in life. Expect landscapes, interiors, and still lifes that reward close, slow looking.

shows.title: Manzanita
shows.description:
Daniel Gibson's third solo show with the gallery is built around eleven modestly scaled oil pastel paintings on linen, hung close together along the wall so they read almost like pages of a single unfolding book. The works move between the observed and the invented — desert rock formations, wildflower fields, granite morteros once used by the Kumeyaay to grind seeds — filtered through a loose, automatic drawing process that lets forms surface intuitively rather than by plan.

The title refers to a plot of land Gibson owns near the Mexican border in San Diego County, and to one of the Kumeyaay tribal bands whose history is woven into the imagery of stone and desert. Recurring throughout is the painter's palette itself, appearing as landscape feature, held aloft like a talisman, or merged with a figure's head — a symbol, in Gibson's words, of painting as a means of getting through uncertainty.

Gibson, who lives and works in Los Angeles, has spent the last several years developing a distinctive visual vocabulary around the California and Baja desert — a mix of folk-art flatness, hallucinatory color, and personal mythology. With his recent transition into fatherhood surfacing as a quiet undercurrent (a desert dove named for his daughter recurs in several works), Manzanita reads as a meditation on inheritance, memory, and the desert as a site where deep time and personal history overlap.

shows.title: Silke Otto-Knapp
shows.description:
Presented in Regen Projects' viewing rooms alongside Elliott Hundley's main-gallery exhibition, this focused selection of small paintings and studies revisits the singular watercolor-on-canvas technique of Silke Otto-Knapp (1970–2022), the German-born, Los Angeles-based painter and longtime UCLA professor who died in 2022. Many of the works are being shown publicly for the first time.

Otto-Knapp built her paintings through a process of controlled erasure: layers of black watercolor applied to canvas, sprayed with water, then scrubbed and scraped away to let the white primer beneath emerge as figure and light. The results hover between representation and abstraction — grayscale dancers, stage sets, and landscapes that draw on her wide-ranging enthusiasms, from Bronislava Nijinska's choreography to Georgia O'Keeffe, Ingmar Bergman, and the coastal light of Fogo Island.

Because several works on view are preparatory studies for larger, later paintings, the exhibition doubles as a window into Otto-Knapp's process — how an intimate, exploratory mark could scale up into the monumental multi-panel works for which she's best known. For anyone who has encountered her paintings in museum collections from LACMA to MoMA and Tate, this is a rare chance to see the workings behind them.
