The gallery also represents several artist estates, continuing the legacies of important late-twentieth-century figures.

shows.title: Open Sesame
shows.description:
Alexa Guariglia paints tightly composed interiors and figure studies in gouache, watercolor, and ink on paper, a combination that gives her scenes an odd, matte flatness even as the imagery leans theatrical and cinematic. Chairs, drapery, and figures caught mid-gesture recur across her compositions, staged with the lighting and framing of a stopped film still — a sensibility that fits a show titled Open Sesame, with its implication of a door swinging open onto some private, slightly heightened world.

Guariglia builds her larger paper works — some reaching five or six feet across — the way a painter might build a canvas, layering washes and opaque gouache passages until the paper takes on real weight and shadow, quite a feat on a support usually reserved for something lighter and more immediate. That tension between the modesty of the material and the ambition of the scale is a big part of what makes her work distinctive.

This is a two-person hang at Moskowitz Bayse, paired with Franziska Goes's Seeds and Circles in the gallery's adjoining space — worth the trip to see both bodies of work in dialogue, one rooted in figuration and narrative, the other in geometric abstraction.

shows.title: Seeds and Circles
shows.description:
Franziska Goes makes hard-edge abstractions built from grids, dots, and repeated geometric units — paintings that read at first like exercises in systematic color logic before you notice how much she lets the system wobble. A grid tilts, a color runs slightly warmer than its neighbor should allow, sand and modeling paste rough up an otherwise smooth acrylic surface. It's abstraction with an engineer's structure and a painter's appetite for friction.

The German-born, LA-based artist's canvases in this show span from crisp, brightly colored grid paintings to newer, more textured works that incorporate sand and paste into the acrylic, giving the surface a tactile, almost topographic quality that photographs can't quite capture — worth seeing in person for that reason alone.

Seeds and Circles hangs alongside Alexa Guariglia's Open Sesame at Moskowitz Bayse, setting Goes's cool geometric vocabulary against Guariglia's theatrical figuration — two very different ways of using structure to organize a picture.

shows.title: Come When Mi Call Yu
shows.description:
Lenworth McIntosh's first solo exhibition with OCHI imagines a Black commune in a lush rural valley, bracing for a storm that reads as both weather and spiritual reckoning. Working from his childhood memories of Jamaica and the visual grammar of animation, McIntosh renders ghostly ancestral presences moving alongside the living: a man ladling soup for the group, elderly women singing in a circle of light, figures dissolving into cloud and color.

The paintings draw specifically on the Caribbean "Nine Nights" wake tradition, in which mourners gather for nine nights of food, music and storytelling to send a loved one's spirit onward. McIntosh translates that communal, celebratory mourning into an earthy, saturated palette and loose, cartoon-inflected figuration that keeps the work feeling alive rather than elegiac.

McIntosh, who lives and works in Los Angeles, follows up a 2025 solo presentation at Frieze Los Angeles with this debut gallery show. It's a good entry point for viewers curious about how diasporic memory and folklore get reworked through a very contemporary, animation-adjacent painting language.

shows.title: She who sits
shows.description:
Adrienne Elise Tarver's paintings center on Vera Otis, a fictional matriarch the artist built over a decade of work after finding an unnamed woman's photo in a secondhand shop. Otis is styled after mid-century Black screen icons like Dorothy Dandridge and Eartha Kitt, but instead of performing for the camera, she simply sits — resting, watching, taking up space without asking permission. That stillness is the whole argument of the show: rest as agency, not passivity.

These particular paintings began as a much larger public project — a Public Art Fund commission that put Otis's image on some 300 bus shelters and newsstands across New York, Boston and Chicago in 2024. Seeing the paintings themselves, rather than the billboard versions, lets you sit with the layered source material Tarver works from: family snapshots, found photographs, and clippings from vintage Ebony and Jet magazines collaged into an invented but historically textured biography.

Tarver, who teaches at Pratt and lives in Brooklyn, has shown at institutions including the Aldrich Museum and Atlanta Contemporary; this is her latest outing with OCHI, which represents her.

shows.title: Sangam
shows.description:
Raghav Babbar spent time at the 2025 Maha Kumbh, the Hindu pilgrimage that drew what's been described as the largest religious gathering ever recorded, and this show is his attempt to paint his way through that scale. Rather than a single hero or holy figure, Babbar's canvases dissolve individual pilgrims into a churning, nocturnal crowd — bodies caught mid-gesture between exhaustion, ecstasy and prayer, rendered in a muted, earthen palette that owes an evident debt to European history painting.

That's a deliberate move on Babbar's part: he's spoken of wanting to bridge Goya-style crowd painting with the specific, documentary reality of a contemporary Indian pilgrimage. It's a shift for an artist who built his early reputation on intimate portraiture — here the crowd itself becomes the subject, with darkness functioning less as absence than as a shared, primal space.

This is Babbar's first US solo exhibition, staged simultaneously with a booth at New York's Armory Show. Born in Rohtak, India and now based in London, Babbar has had a fast rise — a 2025 Arts Council England Global Talent Visa, a spot on Forbes' 30 Under 30 Asia list, and works already in the permanent collections of ICA Miami and the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art. Worth seeing for anyone interested in how a young painter handles mass spectacle without losing the individual.

venue.name: Rajiv Menon Contemporary
venue.about: Rajiv Menon Contemporary is a Los Angeles gallery founded in 2023 by gallerist Rajiv Menon, who holds a PhD from New York University in global media and visual culture. The program centers on emerging and diasporic South Asian artists, aiming to expand collecting audiences within diasporic communities and to place new voices into museums and private collections. Initially operating from a Sunset Boulevard space, the gallery opened a permanent home on North Highland Avenue in 2025. Exhibitions have included thematic group shows exploring South Asian regional identity, such as a Kerala-focused Onam exhibition, alongside presentations at international art fairs. The gallery positions itself as a hub connecting South Asia and its diaspora with the broader Los Angeles art world, emphasizing education and connoisseurship alongside commercial representation.

shows.title: Rough Ways of The Delicate Ones
shows.description:
Emmanuel Louisnord Desir works across painting, assemblage and sculpture to dig into colonialism, spirituality and the long shadow of biblical narrative — particularly the Abrahamic traditions and how they echo across diasporic history. The works on view (with titles like "Fury of the Saints," "Hellenization of Jacob," and "SOS Radio Telescope") suggest an artist reaching for cosmic and scriptural language to talk about displacement and inherited belief.

Desir's assemblage pieces incorporate found and industrial materials — engine parts, radio components — alongside more traditional painted surfaces, giving the biblical references a scavenged, present-tense grounding rather than treating them as historical illustration. The effect is less devotional than interrogative: sacred stories reframed through the wreckage of contemporary material culture.

This is a Los Angeles solo outing for the gallery's program, running alongside a concurrent Herman Cherry exhibition at Sebastian Gladstone's New York space — a reminder of how this young transatlantic gallery is building out its roster on both coasts.

shows.title: Black Florals
shows.description:
Henri Paul Broyard's second solo show with Tyler Park Presents is built around a single, deceptively narrow idea: painting flowers and houseplants entirely in black. Broyard has circled floral still life throughout his career but always avoided the genre's cozy, domestic connotations; rendering the plants in black strips out the sentimentality and turns them into graphic, almost architectural silhouettes that hover between the viewer and a richly colored ground.

The paintings build outward from total abstraction — blocks of color, stripes, grids — before Broyard lets figuration emerge, and he'll sometimes paint back over a resolved image to return it to abstraction, leaving traces of the erased picture underneath. Alongside the paintings, the show continues his series of repaired terracotta and Bauer pots, mended with construction adhesive and metal brackets in a blunt, American riff on kintsugi — vessels that stay visibly broken even as they're made whole again.

Broyard, a Los Angeles native trained at CCA and in Peter Doig's class at Düsseldorf's Kunstakademie, has shown at 12.26 in Dallas, Post Gallery in Zurich and Foreland in the Catskills; his work sits in the collections of the Portland Museum of Art and the California African American Museum.

venue.name: Tyler Park Presents
venue.about: Tyler Park Presents is a contemporary art gallery founded in September 2020 by Tyler Park, originally housed in a converted apartment in Los Angeles's Silver Lake neighborhood. The gallery represents and exhibits emerging and established artists working across painting, photography, sculpture, and mixed media, staging six to seven exhibitions a year, including solo and group presentations. It has built a track record of organizing artists' first solo exhibitions in Los Angeles, with nearly half of its solo shows marking such debuts. The gallery participates regularly in art fairs including NADA, Future Fair, Material Art Fair, Felix Art Fair, and Frieze Los Angeles, and is a member of the New Art Dealers Alliance. It is planning to relocate to the Melrose Hill neighborhood in September 2026.

shows.title: Remains of the Day
shows.description:
Michel Auder has spent more than sixty years pointing a camera at whatever was in front of him — friends, lovers, hotel rooms, television screens, the inside of his own apartment — and this show pulls together the photographic side of that restless archive. Auder was one of the first artists to treat portable video as a real medium rather than a novelty, and the black-and-white and color photographs here function less like discrete artworks than like frames pulled out of a much longer continuous take. Alongside the stills, moving-image works extend the same logic into time.

Auder's decades of documenting Warhol-era downtown New York (he crossed paths with Alice Neel, Cindy Sherman, Hannah Wilke, and Larry Rivers, among others) give the work a specific historical weight, but the images on view are presented as an open-ended visual archive rather than a greatest-hits survey — records of looking as much as records of who was in the room.

The exhibition is accompanied by a book of the same title, treated as an extension of the show rather than a catalogue afterthought, with tactile photographs on the wall placed in dialogue with the printed page. Opening day includes a 3pm conversation between Auder and curator Hamza Walker, followed by a reception.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 5-7pm (artist talk with Hamza Walker at 3pm)

shows.title: No Center No Above No Below
shows.description:
Ernesto Burgos builds his sculptural paintings the way a boxer builds a body of work — through repetition, impact, and accumulated damage. He starts with cardboard, bends and tears it into gestural forms, then locks that gesture in place with fiberglass and resin before working the surface over with spray paint, oil stick, lacquer, and charcoal. The result sits somewhere between a frozen brushstroke and an actual object, a piece of abstract expressionism that has been given a spine.

This new body of work, titled "No Center No Above No Below," continues Burgos's interest in forms that resist a single fixed viewpoint — pieces that shift character as you walk around them, refusing to settle into a stable front or back. The Chilean-American artist, who splits his biography between Santa Clara, Viña del Mar, and New York, has shown at galleries from Stockholm to Seoul to London, and exhibited previously at Fernberger as part of a 2025 group show alongside Grant Falardeau and Brett Goodroad.

Expect large, wall-mounted or freestanding pieces that read at a distance like gestural paintings and up close like geological cross-sections — evidence of a slow, physical process of building, cutting, and repainting. It's sculpture made with a painter's instincts, and worth seeing in person for the way light catches the layered, scarred surfaces.

venue.name: Fernberger
venue.about: Fernberger is a Los Angeles gallery founded by Emma Fernberger in January 2024. Located on North Western Avenue, it presents an intergenerational program of artists with a global outlook, placing particular emphasis on women-identifying practitioners. The program is unified by a sense of intensity and immediacy, favoring work that produces an instant visceral reaction while remaining thoughtful and historically grounded. Fernberger has described an interest in art's transformative and unifying potential, seeking pieces that are high-impact yet cerebral. The gallery has participated in major art fairs and been the subject of coverage in international publications, reflecting a growing profile within the Los Angeles gallery scene, particularly around the Melrose Hill area.

shows.title: Dream Factory
shows.description:
Jessie Stevenson's first California exhibition gathers new oil paintings made after the London-based artist's inaugural trip to the state, with plein-air sketches done in Ojai, Hollywood, Venice, and San Diego later worked up into finished canvases back in her studio. Stevenson builds her surfaces with an unusual egg-oil-titanium ground that mimics the tooth of a sketchbook page, then layers semi-transparent oil glazes over it — a technique she developed during her fellowship at the Slade School of Fine Art.

The paintings sit at the hinge between British Romantic landscape painting (Constable, Turner) and American traditions of depicting the West, from Bierstadt's grandeur to Agnes Pelton's more mystical visions. Freeway interchanges, coastal bluffs, and chaparral hillsides appear rendered with the same trembling, atmospheric touch Stevenson usually reserves for the English countryside, pushed toward abstraction and inflected by a recurring iridescent blue.

It's a quietly ambitious debut: a British painter's outsider view of Southern California landscape, filtered through art-historical memory and accompanied by a small poetry publication illustrated with her own sketches and photographs.

shows.title: Trevor Shimizu
shows.description:
Trevor Shimizu's paintings work a deliberately awkward, loose-handed style — thin washes, visible drips, and a knowingly "bad painting" sensibility — to depict subjects that range from still lifes and landscapes to bodybuilders and golf courses, always with a dry, self-aware humor about painting's own conventions. The promotional image for this show, of dahlias and tulips, suggests a return to still life, a genre Shimizu has used before to needle expectations about beauty and skill in painting.

Shimizu, who has shown widely in New York and internationally, brings a very different sensibility to Matthew Brown's program than the gallery's other September opening (Carroll Dunham) — trading Dunham's maximalist, high-color figuration for something flatter, funnier, and more diaristic. Seeing the two shows on view around the same time offers a useful contrast in how contemporary painters handle the body, subject matter, and technical bravado.

Worth a visit for anyone interested in painting that treats its own limitations as subject matter rather than something to be smoothed over.

shows.title: All Unfinished
shows.description:
Nic Gregory's solo show at ace/121 Gallery takes its title from a state most artists know intimately: the not-quite-resolved painting, the piece that keeps changing hands between finished and in-progress. Working in acrylic on wood panel, Gregory builds surfaces with a rough, worked-over quality — visible layering, exposed grain, and passages that look deliberately left raw alongside more resolved sections.

The result is painting that treats incompleteness as subject matter rather than a flaw to be corrected, asking viewers to consider process and provisionality as part of the finished object. It's a fitting complement to ace/121's program, which Glendale Arts uses to spotlight Los Angeles-based painters and sculptors in an intimate, artist-colony setting.

This is the gallery's first exhibition of its fall season, opening in late September after a summer show by Leah Knecht, and it continues ace/121's pattern of tightly focused, single-artist presentations that give each body of work room to breathe in the gallery's modest footprint.

shows.title: Artifacts from an Unborn Empire
shows.description:
Timed to land on the 250th anniversary of the United States, this group exhibition turns a skeptical eye on the myths nations tell about their own founding. Curators Jason Jenn and Vojislav Radovanović have assembled more than twenty Los Angeles-based artists — including Ben Cuevas, Elana Mann, Gina Herrera, Rubén Esparza, Kristine Schomaker, and Marcus Kuiland-Nazario — working across knit sculpture, ceramics, photography, installation, and performance documentation to ask who gets to write history and whose symbols survive it.

The work on view ranges from intimate to spectacular: a skull knitted from acrylic yarn, hand-drawn maps of imagined cities labeled in overlapping languages, a nude fiberglass figure inked in dark patterns, and an installation of clear crystalline forms suspended over a hardwood floor. Photographic documentation of performance and costume work — including a startling image of a performer under a stoplight in an Elizabethan gown built from egg cartons — sits alongside spray-painted text works and painted wood assemblages, giving the show a restless, materially inventive feel.

Brand Library & Art Center's gallery, a light-filled space attached to a public library devoted to art and music, has a long history of hosting ambitious, community-minded group shows, and this one continues that tradition by pairing serious conceptual ambition with genuine visual variety. It's a fitting way to mark a fraught national anniversary — not with celebration, but with inquiry into empire, colonial legacy, and the stories a culture chooses to keep.

venue.name: Brand Library & Art Center
venue.about: Brand Library & Art Center occupies the restored 1904 Miradero mansion, the former Glendale estate of civic figure Leslie C. Brand, whose Indo-Islamic-styled house was donated to the city upon his death in 1925 and converted into a public library that opened in 1956. A 1969 addition added a gallery and recital hall, and the whole complex was renovated and reopened in 2014. Operated as a branch of the City of Glendale Library, Arts & Culture Department, it combines a specialized visual-arts and music library collection with rotating exhibitions, concerts, dance performances, lectures and community arts programs, serving as a cultural and historic landmark at the base of the Verdugo Mountains.

shows.title: Promised Lands: California's Unratified Treaties and Native Resilience
shows.description:
In the 1850s, federal commissioners negotiated eighteen treaties with California tribal nations promising reservation lands in exchange for ceding territory — treaties the U.S. Senate then quietly refused to ratify, leaving those promises legally void while the land was already gone. This traveling exhibition, developed with the National Museum of the American Indian and the Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service, uses archival documents, protest ephemera, and contemporary Native-made objects to walk through that history and its long aftermath.

Objects on view include things like a spray-painted "Honor the Treaties" protest sign from 2017 and a coiled horsehair basket by Chumash artist Linda Aguilar that incorporates beads, shells, and even scavenged bingo markers and credit-card fragments — a piece that folds present-day material culture into a traditional basketry form. That mix of hard historical documentation and living contemporary art practice is the show's throughline: California's unratified treaties aren't a closed legal footnote, they're a condition Native communities in the state are still working within and responding to.

It's a smaller, more issue-driven show than the Autry's big collection surveys, built around a specific and under-told piece of California history. Worth planning around its late-September opening in the Samuel & Minna Grodin Gallery.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: You and I
shows.description:
Kwame Brathwaite (1938–2023) was the photographer behind the "Black Is Beautiful" movement of the 1960s, documenting Harlem's jazz clubs, the Grandassa Models, and the cultural politics of natural hair and Black self-image alongside his brother's African Jazz-Art Society and Studios collective. This exhibition, co-curated by actor and activist Jesse Williams with the artist's son Kwame S. Brathwaite (director of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive), pulls together vintage and later prints spanning self-portraiture, fashion, and street photography.

The works on view move between the intimate and the iconic: a self-portrait of Brathwaite with his Argus C3 camera sits alongside images of models like Sikolo in ruffled dress, a jazz quartet caught mid-performance, and children on a Harlem swing set. Together they trace how Brathwaite's camera doubled as an instrument of cultural advocacy — turning fashion and portrait photography into a visual argument for Black pride well before the phrase became a slogan.

Having represented the Brathwaite archive for several years, Philip Martin Gallery continues to give this pivotal but still under-recognized photographer serious gallery treatment in Los Angeles, pairing rarely seen prints with the historical framing that Williams and Brathwaite's son bring as co-curators.

venue.name: Philip Martin Gallery
venue.about: Philip Martin Gallery is a contemporary art gallery based in Los Angeles that presents innovative, experimental and ambitious artworks in all media, both at its own space and at art fairs in the United States and abroad. In January 2023 the gallery moved into a new 4,000-square-foot location at 3342 Verdugo Road in Los Angeles. The gallery represents a roster of artists working across painting, photography, video, sculpture and textile, including figures such as Ericka Beckman, Kwame Brathwaite, Brian Bress and Carl Cheng, alongside a group of emerging and mid-career painters and sculptors. The gallery has a history that traces back to its earlier incarnation as Cherry and Martin.

shows.title: 40 Year Anniversary Exhibition
shows.dates_note: Page presents this as two consecutive shows: "Part One: Oct 2nd – Nov 1st" and "Part Two: Nov 6th – Nov 29th," saved here as one continuous run through Nov 29.
shows.description:
La Luz de Jesus marks four decades in business with a two-part anniversary exhibition, split into back-to-back installments each with its own opening reception.

Given the milestone, expect the anniversary show to function as something of a highlight reel — likely drawing on the gallery's deep artist roster and past exhibition history rather than presenting a single new body of work. The two-part structure (with a changeover and second opening in early November) suggests a rotating cast of contributors across the eight-week run.

For longtime followers of the lowbrow and pop-surrealist scenes, this is a rare chance to see the gallery reflect on its own history in real time, with two separate opening nights to catch different configurations of the show.
shows.reception: Friday, October 2 and Friday, November 6, 7-11pm each night

venue.name: La Luz de Jesus Gallery
venue.about: La Luz de Jesus Gallery is a Los Angeles gallery founded in 1986 by entrepreneur and art collector Billy Shire. Housed inside the Soap Plant/Wacko complex on Hollywood Boulevard, the gallery is credited with helping foster what became known as the Lowbrow or Pop Surrealist movement in California art. Its program favors figurative, narrative painting and unconventional sculpture, with content spanning folk, outsider, religious, and sexually charged themes. The gallery states its mission is to bring underground art and counter-culture to a wider audience, and it also operates an Art Advisor Service connecting collectors, curators, and designers with contemporary artists worldwide.

shows.title: discrepancies with E.S. (in company): The Neutra VDL House
shows.description:
Leonor Antunes turns the Neutra VDL House itself into her material, threading a suite of new sculptures through Richard Neutra's glass-walled studio and residence. Rather than simply installing objects in the space, she measures and re-derives forms from the furniture and architecture of Elizabeth Scheu Close, a Viennese-Jewish émigré architect who moved in the same circles as Neutra but was turned away from his office decades ago. The result is a quiet historical correction disguised as abstract sculpture: hanging cedar forms strung from stainless steel poles in the upstairs living room, curved acrylic-and-brass screens echoing a childproofing gesture Close made in her own house, and a leather floor piece patterned after her brick pathways.

Antunes has spent years building a body of work out of the overlooked designs of modernist women — this show also folds in earlier pieces referencing Cuban designer Clara Porset and French designer Charlotte Perriand. Seeing the work installed inside an actual mid-century house, rather than a white-box gallery, gives the project unusual stakes: viewers can compare Antunes's abstracted "measurements" directly against the real staircases, sun louvers and pocket gardens that inspired them.

Given Antunes's exhibition history — Venice Biennale representation, and surveys at SFMOMA, the New Consequence Museum, and Kunsthalle Basel — this is a rare chance to see her work in Los Angeles, and specifically in dialogue with the city's own architectural history.

shows.title: Stalking the Wild Pendulum
shows.description:
Ramiro Hernandez paints in a soft-focus, technicolor haze that reads at once as nostalgic and unsettling — sun-bleached beach scenes hang beside images of weaponry and police equipment, all rendered in the same hazy, Richter-adjacent glow. The Oakland-based painter takes his exhibition's title from Itzhak Bentov's 1977 book on consciousness and holograms, using the idea that "every ripple can mechanically be traced back to the source" as a loose organizing metaphor for a body of work that moves between violence and calm without much visual distinction between the two.

It's a show about how images flatten difference: an idyllic day at the beach and a piece of military hardware can occupy the same fuzzy, sentimental register once they're run through Hernandez's palette. He's showing recently at galleries like Massey Klein and Harkawik in New York and BOZOMAG in LA — this is his first solo outing at Dominique Porter.

venue.name: Dominique Porter Gallery
venue.about: Dominique Porter Gallery is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles presenting emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, and installation. Established in 2026, the gallery supports practices marked by sustained material exploration, formal invention, and individual vision. Its program is built around exhibitions, projects, and collaborations intended to give artists room to develop ambitious work and to engage in dialogue with one another and with wider cultural conversations. The gallery describes its approach as artist-centered, bringing together a range of practices while keeping exhibition-making thoughtful and considered rather than driven by a single house style.

shows.title: Control X
shows.description:
Tala Madani returns to her longtime Los Angeles gallery with a new suite of paintings and video animation that continues her interrogation of power, bodies, and the slippery line between creation and destruction. The Iranian-born, LA-based artist has built her reputation on a scabrous, funny, and often unsettling cartoon language, using loose brushwork and simplified male figures to needle at authority, shame, and domestic absurdity. This show pushes that language into new territory with a series of "mountain portraits" that swell human subjects into landscape-scale forms, riffing on the grandiosity of Romantic painting while still handling paint with an intimate, almost bodily touch.

The centerpiece is reportedly Madani's most ambitious video to date, an animated work built from painted, drawn, and photographed source material and scored by artist Nathaniel Mellors, in which renegade letters of the alphabet escape the page and start remaking the world in their own image — a fable about language, domination, and the way symbols calcify into systems of control. It's a natural extension of Madani's long-running interest in animation as a sibling practice to her paintings, and it gives the show its title's double meaning: control as command, and "X" as erasure.

Madani has had a genuinely international decade, with solo museum shows at MOCA Los Angeles, the Mori Art Museum, Secession Vienna, and most recently the Henry Art Gallery in Seattle, plus inclusion in the Istanbul and Whitney Biennials. Seeing new work in her home city, in the gallery that has represented her for years, is a chance to track an artist still actively complicating a visual vocabulary that has already become widely influential.

venue.name: David Kordansky Gallery
venue.about: David Kordansky Gallery is a contemporary art gallery founded in 2003 in Los Angeles's Chinatown neighborhood as an incubator for emerging artists. It moved to Culver City in 2008 and now operates a 20,000-square-foot campus in Mid-City Los Angeles, alongside a 5,000-square-foot space in Chelsea, New York. The Los Angeles site comprises three exhibition spaces across two buildings with a courtyard, allowing simultaneous shows and programming that includes performance, film, and outdoor sculpture. The gallery represents artists working across all media, emphasizing individuality over a shared aesthetic, and situates its program within the history of postwar Los Angeles art while engaging global contemporary practice. It regularly participates in major international art fairs and produces exhibition catalogues and artist's books.

shows.title: Tacita Dean: FILM
shows.description:
Marciano reopens after its summer install break with the U.S. debut of one of Tacita Dean's signature works: FILM, an 11-minute, silent 35mm installation originally commissioned by Tate Modern for its Turbine Hall in 2011. Dean projects the piece onto a vertical screen so that a strip of film seems to rise straight up out of the gallery floor, sprocket holes and all, turning the physical apparatus of analog cinema into the actual subject of the image.

Inside that towering frame, Dean intercuts a private visual vocabulary — a waterfall, a street clock, a pine tree, an ostrich egg, a flickering bulb — with glimpses of the Turbine Hall's industrial architecture, using century-old in-camera tricks like glass matte painting and multiple exposure rather than digital effects. It's a monument to photochemical film built at a moment when the medium's survival was genuinely in question, and Dean has said as much herself: her practice treats celluloid as something closer to poetry than to mere image-capture.

Seeing FILM at Marciano also means seeing the building itself, a former Scottish Rite Masonic temple that gives the piece's monolithic verticality an unusually theatrical setting. The show opens alongside Pierre Leguillon's Ads & Brands and continues Marciano's rotation of collection-based and single-artist installations throughout its Wilshire Boulevard galleries.

shows.title: To Hell and Back
shows.description:
New York-based artist Margaret MacLean makes her Los Angeles solo debut at induction gallery with this show, which the gallery describes as opening a new chapter for the space following Severin Hallauer's inaugural-season exhibition. Details on the work itself are sparse ahead of the opening, but the single released image — a close, textured view of a painted surface — suggests a practice grounded in material and mark-making rather than pure image-making.

Induction is a small project space tucked into a Westlake apartment building, the kind of low-overhead room where an artist's first LA showing can feel appropriately intimate rather than overproduced. Worth a visit for anyone tracking which emerging painters are getting their first foothold on the West Coast.

venue.name: induction gallery
venue.about: induction gallery is a Los Angeles gallery founded and directed by artist and curator John Zinonos. Located at 672 S. La Fayette Park Place in the city's Westlake area, the space works by appointment and presents a roster of emerging and mid-career artists working across painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, collage, and new media. The program reflects Zinonos's own multidisciplinary curatorial interests, bringing together Los Angeles-based and out-of-state artists whose practices engage material experimentation, personal narrative, and technology-driven or ecological themes.

shows.title: Textile Alchemy: The Art of Reiko Sudō and NUNO
shows.description:
For more than forty years Reiko Sudō has run NUNO, a Japanese textile collective that treats fabric-making as a kind of alchemy — fusing traditional handicraft with industrial technology and unlikely materials to produce cloth that architects and designers around the world have sought out. This is billed as the largest retrospective of her work to date, with more than a hundred limited-edition textiles shown alongside the drawings, sketches, tools, and prototypes that reveal how each piece actually gets made.

What comes through is Sudō's collaborative process: she works constantly with independent artisans and regional workshops across Japan, and the exhibition frames her practice as much about preserving disappearing craft traditions as about producing beautiful objects. For anyone who thinks of textiles as a secondary art form, this show makes the case that Sudō's inventive material experiments belong in the same conversation as painting or sculpture.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
venue.about: LACMA is the largest art museum in the western United States, holding some 155,000 objects spanning 6,000 years of global art history. It traces its roots to the Los Angeles County Museum of History, Science, and Art (1910) and became an independent institution in 1961, opening on Wilshire Boulevard in 1965. The campus has grown through additions including the Anderson/Art of the Americas Building, the Pavilion for Japanese Art, BCAM, and the Resnick Pavilion, culminating in the 2026 opening of the Peter Zumthor-designed David Geffen Galleries. Located on Wilshire Boulevard in the Miracle Mile, LACMA presents rotating exhibitions across its global collection alongside public programs, education initiatives, and community partnerships, including a gallery at Charles White Elementary School.

shows.title: Home of the Future, 1925–1985: Designing Domestic Utopias
shows.description:
Between 1925 and 1985, American designers and manufacturers kept promising that a better life was one gadget away — self-cleaning kitchens, plastic houses that could be assembled in a day, push-button appliances, and eventually the desktop computer. This exhibition gathers the architectural models, drawings, films, and consumer objects — everything from kitchen sinks to television sets — that sold those visions of domestic utopia to the American public.

What's most interesting is the exhibition's stated interest in who got left out of these futures and who imagined alternatives to them; a show about mid-century optimism that also asks pointed questions about whose home was actually being designed for whom. It's a great pick for anyone into design history, postwar consumer culture, or the strange gap between advertised futures and lived reality.

venue.about: LACMA is the largest art museum in the western United States, holding some 155,000 objects spanning 6,000 years of global art history. The campus has grown through additions including the Anderson/Art of the Americas Building, the Pavilion for Japanese Art, BCAM, and the Resnick Pavilion, culminating in the 2026 opening of the Peter Zumthor-designed David Geffen Galleries. shows.title: The Kitchen and Its Discontents
shows.description:
Two landmark kitchens from LACMA's design collection anchor this compact show: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky's efficiency-driven 1926–30 "Frankfurt Kitchen," designed for German social housing, and Charlotte Perriand and Le Corbusier's 1948–50 kitchen for the Marseille Unité d'Habitation. Both were engineered around modernist ideals of order and labor-saving design, built explicitly with women's domestic work in mind.

Photographs, prints, and advertisements from the collection complicate that tidy modernist narrative, showing the mess, friction, and unpaid labor that these "rational" kitchens didn't actually eliminate. Presented alongside the concurrent Home of the Future, it's a sharp, feminist-inflected footnote to that larger survey — proof that the history of domestic design is also a history of whose comfort was being engineered, and at what cost to whom.

shows.title: Keith Sonnier: Inside Light, 1968–1970
shows.description:
This is a focused historical survey of the earliest, most experimental years of Keith Sonnier's career, honing in on 1968 to 1970, when the Louisiana-born artist first began bending neon and argon gas into sculpture. Sonnier, who died in 2020, is remembered as one of the great postwar American sculptors, and this show captures the moment he found his signature material: glowing tube light paired with the raw fixtures, transformers, and wiring that power it. Works like the two-tone "Arced Neon" pieces from 1968 show him testing single gestures in colored light, while the later, more elaborate "Neon Wrapping Incandescent V" (1970) shows a fast-maturing vocabulary of layered, multicolor form.

What makes this body of work compelling beyond its historical importance is how physical it still feels — these are sculptures that depend on their walls and corners the way a painting depends on its stretcher bars, casting shadow and colored light into the room and implicating the viewer's own silhouette in the composition. Sonnier arrived at these ideas while still a student, in dialogue with contemporaries like Eva Hesse and Bruce Nauman, and this exhibition makes the case for how radical that dialogue with industrial materials and immaterial light really was.

It's a tightly scoped, jewel-box kind of show rather than a full retrospective, but for anyone interested in postminimalism, the history of light as sculptural material, or just wanting to see real neon glow in person, it's worth the visit.

It regularly participates in major international art fairs and produces exhibition catalogues and artist's books.

shows.title: Pierre Leguillon: Ads & Brands
shows.description:
Pierre Leguillon is less a traditional artist than a career-long collector and re-arranger, and this two-part presentation across the Marciano's Window Gallery and Library makes his archival instincts the whole show. In "Ads," he draws from decades of advertisements in which artists — Marina Abramović, Andy Warhol, Joseph Beuys, Salvador Dalí, among many others — appear as models or brand ambassadors, an ongoing collection of over 250 images that's been curated here specifically for Los Angeles. Seeing artists sell McDonald's, Dior, and liquor next to each other says a lot about how celebrity and cultural capital operate outside the gallery walls.

The second half, "Brands," transplants a piece of Leguillon's own Brussels institution The Museum of Mistakes into the MAF Library — a sprawling, non-hierarchical accumulation of ephemera, printed matter, and oddities (a painted pair of Doc Martens shows up alongside a sock collection) that treats the museum itself as a kind of book, and the book as a museum. It's a strange, funny, research-driven show about how images and objects circulate and gain meaning through display and repetition rather than through any single masterpiece.

Leguillon has shown at the Louvre, WIELS, and the ICA Boston, and his cataloguing sensibility rewards patient, close looking rather than a quick walkthrough — budget real time if advertising, art-world mythology, or archival art practice interests you.

shows.title: Jon Ching (new work)
shows.description:
Jon Ching paints hyperrealist, symbolically loaded scenes that fuse the human figure with plant and animal life — skin sprouting ferns, hands cradling anemones, faces dissolving into coral and fungus. It's a style that sits at the intersection of natural history illustration and surrealism, built on meticulous oil-painting technique and a recurring interest in ecological fragility and interconnectedness.

This new exhibition at KP Projects (also known as Merry Karnowsky Gallery) continues that body of work; based on the gallery's past presentations of Ching's paintings, expect densely detailed, jewel-toned compositions of hybrid creatures and human/nature mergers, rendered with a naturalist's precision. Ching has built a substantial following for this niche of botanical-surrealist realism, and past shows here have sold out quickly, so the opening reception is the moment to see the work in person before it disperses into private collections.

shows.title: As the Moonbird Flies
shows.artist: Shane Cotton, Simone Griffin, Fiona Pardington
shows.description:
1301PE brings together three New Zealand artists — Shane Cotton, Simone Griffin and Fiona Pardington — whose work, in different mediums, keeps returning to questions of land, ancestry and the natural world as seen through a distinctly Māori and Pacific lens. Cotton is known for layered, symbolically dense paintings that mix Māori motifs, birds and colonial-era imagery into unsettled historical landscapes; Pardington works primarily in photography, often turning her lens on natural history specimens and taonga (treasured objects) to meditate on loss, memory and colonial collecting practices.

The show's title nods to migration and flight — apt for a gallery pairing that gathers three distinct practices under one roof and asks them to speak to a shared set of concerns about place and passage. It's a rare chance for Los Angeles audiences to see contemporary New Zealand art in depth, since none of these three shows regularly on the West Coast.

Given 1301PE's history of championing under-recognized international artists (Uta Barth, Diana Thater and others got early support here), this show is worth catching both for the work itself and as a signal of where the gallery's attention is turning next.

shows.title: David Lynch: LA
shows.description:
This is the first showing of David Lynch's photography in his adopted home city since his death in 2025, and Pace has built it around the atmosphere he spent fifty years chasing on film and canvas alike. Five bodies of work from 1979 to 2008 are brought together: the large-scale Figures and Smoke portraits of women mid-exhale, black-and-white nude studies that abstract the body into topography, the layered, blurred Couch Series riffing on the art-historical odalisque, deadpan architectural "portraits" of LA's industrial edges, and the wry Kits photographs documenting disassembled fish, chicken, and duck like model-airplane instructions gone uncanny.

None of this is separate from Lynch the filmmaker — the same eye that composed Eraserhead's stables-era Los Angeles or Mulholland Drive's dream logic is visibly at work in these frames, where smoke, mystery, and psychological unease do a lot of quiet work. The show leans on the idea that Lynch's photography, painting, and cinema were parallel outputs of one sensibility rather than separate hobbies.

Given that LACMA is reportedly in early discussions for a full Lynch retrospective, this gallery show functions as a first, tightly focused look at an artist whose visual art has been comparatively little seen next to his film work — worth catching before the bigger survey inevitably arrives.

venue.name: Pace Gallery
venue.about: Pace's Los Angeles gallery is the West Coast flagship of Pace Gallery, an international gallery founded by Arne Glimcher in Boston in 1960. Pace has had a presence in California for six decades and opened this dedicated LA space, on La Brea Avenue, in 2022. As part of Pace's global program, the Los Angeles gallery presents an intergenerational mix of contemporary and modern artists, connecting newer voices with long-represented figures and legacy estates. The gallery's program reflects Pace's broader emphasis on dialogue between contemporary practice and twentieth-century art, including strong historical ties to the Light and Space movement associated with Southern California.

shows.title: Summoning Cleo
shows.description:
Mia Middleton's second solo show with Roberts Projects builds surreal tableaux out of anonymous vintage photographs and late-19th-century theatrical staging, translated into oil paintings that mix intimate, tightly cropped scenes with much larger, more theatrical canvases. Her palette narrows to theatrical reds and archival greys, and her cast of recurring characters — a faceless figure in a wide-brimmed hat, a man with a coin for an eye, a woman swallowed in light — keep appearing and disappearing across the work without ever cohering into a single narrative.

The show's title character, Cleo, never actually appears in any painting; she's evoked rather than depicted, a device Middleton uses to talk about presence, absence, and what representation can't hold onto. There's also a sustained interest in surveillance and the unease of being watched without consent, which gives the theatrical, cropped compositions an edge of contemporary anxiety underneath their vintage-photography surface.

Middleton, who is based in Lisbon and has shown recently at Rodolphe Janssen and the Liverpool Powerhouse Museum, works in a register that rewards slow looking — these are paintings built from omission, and the show is best approached as a set of open questions rather than a story with an ending.

venue.name: Roberts Projects
venue.about: Roberts Projects is a Los Angeles gallery representing mid-career, established, and emerging artists working across drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, film, and performance. Founded in 1999 as Roberts & Tilton by Bennett Roberts, Julie Roberts, and Jack Tilton, the gallery occupied the Miracle Mile's 6150 Gallery Complex, then a converted coffee-roasting factory in Culver City, before taking its name Roberts Projects in 2018 following Tilton's passing. In 2023 the gallery relocated to a converted 1948 automobile showroom on South La Brea Avenue in Mid-Wilshire. The program emphasizes museum-quality, installation-based exhibitions and periodic historical surveys, spanning multiple generations and continents. The gallery also runs a publications division producing artist books and catalogues, and maintains a permanent site-specific niche installation by artist Betye Saar.

shows.title: Objective Truths
shows.description:
This group show pulls together six artists from the Roberts Projects roster — Aaron Glasson, Chris Johanson, Suchitra Mattai, Evan Nesbit, Wendy Red Star, and Brenna Youngblood — around a loose, useful premise: that abstraction and material process can carry meaning representation can't quite reach. Glasson's paintings, built from natural pigment, sand, and beeswax, read as records of time spent in wilderness; Johanson's color-saturated compositions nod to frescoes and mandalas while staying grounded in everyday contemporary life.

Mattai's mixed-media textile works fold found objects and rich color into revisionist histories, while Nesbit pushes paint into thick, textured surfaces that blur where painting ends and object begins. Red Star's bishkisché series translates research into Apsáalooke rawhide case-making into geometric works on paper that double as both art object and cultural record, and Youngblood's impasto-heavy canvases treat abstraction as a way of processing American material culture.

None of these artists work in the same visual language, which is exactly the exhibition's point — six distinct routes toward the same idea that meaning in painting doesn't require a picture of anything in particular.

shows.title: "Perfect Lovers" (Untitled)
shows.description:
Michelle Jane Lee's exhibition takes its title from Felix Gonzalez-Torres's iconic 1991 "Untitled" (Perfect Lovers) — two identical clocks ticking in sync until they inevitably drift apart — and uses that piece's quiet meditation on intimacy, time, and loss as a jumping-off point for new work.

Lee's practice typically works through accumulation and repair: assembling found and fragmented materials into surfaces that read as both mended and still visibly broken. Read against the Gonzalez-Torres reference, the work here seems to ask what happens after synchrony fails — what's left to hold onto once two things that once moved together start keeping different time.

It's a tightly focused solo presentation from an artist attentive to the emotional weight objects can carry, staged in Rusha & Co.'s compact Leimert Park-adjacent space.

shows.title: Olympia
shows.description:
Paul Pfeiffer built his reputation on taking apart the machinery of spectacle — cropping and looping broadcast footage of boxing matches and basketball games until the athletes dissolve and only the roar of the crowd and the glow of the stadium lights remain. Olympia pushes that inquiry outward from the screen into architecture itself, using Los Angeles's run-up to the 2028 Olympics as its occasion. The centerpiece is an expanded version of Pfeiffer's 2008 piece Vitruvian Figure, in which a scale model of a stadium becomes an absurdist monument; here he blows the idea up again, training it on the L.A. Memorial Coliseum, the 1923 landmark that is about to host its third Olympic Games.

The exhibition surrounds that architectural meditation with Pfeiffer's long-running fascination with celebrity as a kind of public infrastructure — bodies broken into fragments and recirculated as image, half monument and half debris. Expect large-scale photographic and sculptural works that ask what it means to build (and rebuild) a stage for the world to watch, and what's left over once the cameras move on.

This is Pfeiffer's first Los Angeles gallery show since his acclaimed 2023–24 survey at MOCA, and it finds him working at a genuinely civic scale — looking at a city gearing up to perform for the world again, and asking what gets flattened in the process.

shows.title: Ai: Rain Drawings in Natural Indigo
shows.description:
Miya Ando spent the pandemic years compiling a visual dictionary of rain — two thousand Japanese words for every conceivable way water can fall from the sky, each one paired with a drawing made in natural indigo, graphite, and pure silver powder on handmade paper. That project became her book Water of the Sky, published by MIT Press, and this exhibition pulls a generous selection of the original artworks off the page and onto the gallery wall: fourteen large-scale indigo drawings plus two hundred smaller works from a related series, 498 Aspects of the Rainy Moon, that layers rain against moonlight and the turning seasons.

The material itself carries centuries of weight. Indigo dyeing, or aizome, has been used in Japan since the sixth century, and Ando leans into that history rather than updating it — her blues are plant-dyed and variable, her silver hand-applied, her paper made in the traditional kozo method. The effect is quiet and cumulative: drawing after drawing of near-identical gestures that turn out, on close looking, to each be rendering a distinct, specific kind of rain, from the barely-there mist of early spring to the violent cloudbursts of typhoon season.

Ando, who was born in Los Angeles and has shown at the Noguchi Museum and the Venice Biennale, treats rain less as weather than as a form of attention — a way of noticing time passing in increments too small to otherwise register. Seeing dozens of these drawings together, rather than as isolated book illustrations, makes the scale of that attention much clearer, and turns a project about language into one that's unmistakably about looking.

shows.title: Thomas Demand
shows.description:
Thomas Demand builds his photographs before he ever picks up a camera. The German artist recreates scenes from memory, media images, or historical objects entirely out of paper and cardboard, photographs the fragile constructions under exacting studio light, and then destroys them — so the print is the only trace of the sculpture that made it. This new body of work turns to the miniature theater: eighteenth- and nineteenth-century opera and ballet set models held in museum collections in Vienna, Monaco, and Munich, originally built for productions of Wagner's Tannhäuser and Rossini's Guillaume Tell. Demand photographed these tiny stages with a periscope threaded into their interiors, turning toy-sized scenography into images of genuine theatrical scale and shadow.

Alongside the model photographs, the show includes newer images of Demand's own invented tableaux — an overstuffed bookshelf, reeds catching light on a pond's surface — printed directly onto copper sheets, a material choice that nods back to Renaissance panel painting and early printmaking. It's a quieter, more intimate register for an artist best known for reconstructing scenes of political and historical consequence.

Demand's photographs sit in the collections of MoMA and the Neue Nationalgalerie, and he represented Germany at the São Paulo Bienal in 2004; a related survey of this same body of work, "Rooms That Dream of the Past," is currently on view at Vienna's MAK museum. Seeing the Los Angeles show alongside that context underscores how deliberately Demand blurs the line between document and fabrication — every image here looks like straightforward reportage until you remember that none of what's pictured actually exists anymore.

venue.name: Matthew Marks Gallery
venue.about: Matthew Marks Gallery was founded in New York in 1991 and today represents thirty-five artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, and printmaking. The gallery has grown to five exhibition spaces—three in New York and two in Los Angeles—totaling more than 18,000 square feet, and mounts between thirteen and fifteen exhibitions each year, often accompanied by original publications. Its program spans multiple generations of artists and a broad range of media, reflecting a long-standing commitment to both established and younger practitioners.

shows.title: worthless serpentine
shows.description:
Marley Freeman builds her paintings the way a weaver builds cloth: layer by layer, thread of color over thread of color, until an image emerges that feels less composed than grown. For "worthless serpentine," her latest solo show at Parker Gallery, she brings a new group of canvases that continue her long study of abstraction rooted in the structure of textiles — warp and weft translated into hand-mixed gesso and shifting fields of oil and acrylic.

Freeman's forms hover at the edge of recognition: biomorphic shapes, loose grids, and soft-edged color blocks that seem to pulse against one another rather than sit still. The paintings reward slow looking, the kind you'd give a piece of fabric held up to the light — noticing where colors bleed into their neighbors and where a hard edge suddenly appears. It's intimate, handmade work, made by an artist whose paintings already hang in the collections of LACMA and the Hammer.

Freeman — based between New York and Massachusetts but deeply tied to the gallery's history (this is her fourth solo show there since 2018) — continues to develop the language she's built over years of showing with Parker. This show is a good chance to see how her work has evolved since her last outing here in 2023.

shows.title: Hothouse
shows.description:
Randy Wray's new paintings continue his long engagement with organic, almost bodily abstraction — biomorphic forms rendered in thick, tactile oil paint that suggest flowers, cells, and swollen fruit all at once. His large canvas "Flower," worked over two years, gives a sense of the buildup and revision typical of his process: layers of paint accumulate like sediment until the image feels grown rather than composed.

Wray has spent decades working at the boundary between sculpture and painting, and that sculptural sensibility shows even in two dimensions — his forms have real weight and volume, pressing against the edges of the canvas. "Hothouse" suggests both greenhouse cultivation and fevered intensity, an apt frame for paintings that feel simultaneously nurtured and combustible.

shows.title: Felipe Suzuki
shows.description:
This untitled solo presentation brings Brazilian painter Felipe Suzuki's small, densely worked panels to Karma's Los Angeles space. Working in oil on canvas mounted on wood at an intimate scale, Suzuki builds still lifes and interior scenes that hover between representation and abstraction, with a compressed, almost jewel-like density of color and mark.

Suzuki has shown primarily in South America to date, and this marks a notable West Coast outing for an artist whose small-format paintings reward close, patient viewing rather than the sweeping glance a bigger canvas invites.

shows.title: Dancing in the Pocket
shows.description:
Gabriel Slavitt makes paintings and reliefs out of house paint, drywall mud, and wood filler — hardware-store materials pushed into the register of fine-art surface. Working in Los Angeles, he hand-carves wood panels to match the contours of his own sketchbook drawings, then stretches or wraps canvas over them and builds up the image mark by mark, often with improvised tools like chopsticks or sewing needles standing in for brushes. The result sits somewhere between painting, relief sculpture, and drawing — surfaces that read as loose, doodled gestures until you notice how laboriously they were constructed.

Dancing in the Pocket is Slavitt's newest body of work at Babst, following prior solo and group presentations at the gallery including What Is Wrapped in Heart Cloth and The Loss That Shapes the Image. His pieces have circulated through a mix of contexts — from academic project spaces to L.A. galleries like Vielmetter — and consistently return to the same questions: what a mark retains of the hand and material that made it, and how a domestic, unglamorous palette (house paint, drywall compound) can still carry real feeling.

Expect a continuation of Slavitt's carved-panel paintings alongside ink drawings on paper, the two bodies of work he tends to develop in tandem — sculptural pieces built slowly over weeks and spontaneous sumi or India ink drawings made in a single sitting. Worth a visit for anyone interested in artists who treat construction materials as a legitimate painting medium.

shows.title: The Hour of the Pearl
shows.description:
Jonathan Ryan takes his exhibition's title from a line in Steinbeck's Cannery Row describing the hush of early morning before the sun rises — a threshold moment between night and day that becomes the show's governing mood. Ryan, a Buffalo-born, LA-based painter with an MFA from Tyler School of Art, has built a body of work around exactly these liminal states: light that hasn't decided what it is yet, figures caught in transitional interiors, the strange clarity that appears right before ordinary vision resumes.

Ryan's paintings tend to work in hazy, saturated color and soft-edged forms, giving even mundane domestic scenes an charged, almost hallucinatory quality. He has shown previously at the Landing in LA and Hesse Flatow in New York, and was recently included in a group show at the Utah Museum of Contemporary Art, signaling a painter whose quiet, atmospheric canvases are gaining wider institutional notice.

This is one of three concurrent solo presentations opening the same week at Megan Mulrooney's Santa Monica Boulevard space.

venue.name: Megan Mulrooney
venue.about: Megan Mulrooney is a contemporary art gallery on Santa Monica Boulevard in Los Angeles, founded in 2024 by Megan Mulrooney, a lifelong Angeleno and former senior director at Nino Mier Gallery. The gallery represents emerging and mid-career artists from Los Angeles and abroad, staging solo exhibitions alongside artist-curated group presentations that encourage artists to participate in curatorial discourse. Its program blends a traditional commercial model with a collaborative, artist-forward ethos historically associated with the LA art scene, fostering cross-generational dialogue across two to three exhibitions per cycle. The gallery occupies a space formerly run by Nino Mier Gallery and has quickly built a presence on the national art fair circuit.

shows.title: The End of a Long Line
shows.description:
Omaha-based painter Falon Stutzman returns to Megan Mulrooney following her 2025 debut solo show there, Woman Having a Hard Time, which introduced her flattened, cartoon-inflected figures caught in states of quiet emotional overload — waiting tables, curled up with a dog, stalled mid-gesture. The End of a Long Line looks to continue that project of turning everyday female personhood into something both comic and faintly tragic.

Stutzman paints in oil and flashe, building scenes with bruised, queasy color and spatial distortions borrowed from animation and New Wave film stills. Her figures are archetypes rather than portraits — generic enough to be anyone, particular enough to sting. She's a Columbus College of Art and Design graduate whose work has appeared in New American Paintings, and this second LA solo suggests a gallery relationship still very much building momentum.

The show opens alongside two other solos at Megan Mulrooney.

shows.title: Conjuror
shows.description:
Tommy May's Conjuror is the third of three solo shows opening simultaneously at Megan Mulrooney this September, filling out the gallery's rotating three-room format. May works as a painter whose practice leans toward invented, theatrical imagery — the title itself points to sleight-of-hand, transformation, and the idea of pulling something unexpected out of ordinary materials.

Details on the specific works are still emerging as the show approaches its opening, but May's inclusion alongside Jonathan Ryan and Falon Stutzman continues Megan Mulrooney's pattern of pairing painters with distinct, often uncanny takes on figuration and atmosphere within a single exhibition cycle.

Visitors can expect to see all three shows in one visit to the gallery's Santa Monica Boulevard space, a format that has become a signature of how Megan Mulrooney programs its calendar since opening in 2024.
