shows.title: Michael LeVell: Salient Forms
shows.description:
Michael LeVell has been drawing and painting architecture and interiors for nearly forty years, working out of Tierra del Sol's Claremont studio program since its founding in 1989. His signature medium is layered colored pencil and acrylic on paper, rendering rooms, facades, and furniture pulled loosely from the pages of design and architecture magazines. The forms come out geometric and saturated — flattened planes of color that snap into believable perspective even as they dissolve into pattern and texture built from repeated, obsessive mark-making. He extends the same vocabulary into clay, producing rough-hewn slab sculptures that read as three-dimensional companions to the works on paper.

Billed by the gallery as a survey of five decades of his output, this show pulls together drawings, paintings, and ceramic pieces spanning LeVell's career, tracing how his handling of interior space has shifted from tightly bordered architectural studies toward looser, more abstracted geometric fields. The recurring hand-drawn borders and frames that edge many of his pieces give the flat compositions an odd sculptural presence, as if each drawing were also a small building.

LeVell's work has traveled well beyond the gallery that represents him — group showings at Outsider Art Fair and Felix Art Fair, and past recognition from mainstream critics — and this exhibition is a rare chance to see the arc of his practice assembled in one room rather than in single-artist snapshots.

venue.name: Tierra Del Sol Gallery
venue.about: Tierra del Sol Gallery is the exhibition space of the Tierra del Sol Foundation, a Los Angeles-area nonprofit founded in 1971 that supports artists with disabilities through studio space, career development, and materials. A dedicated gallery opened in West Hollywood in 2019 to expand the foundation's programming and connect its artists with a wider audience. The gallery organizes year-round exhibitions and events, frequently inviting guest curators such as Alison Saar, Darren Romanelli, and jill moniz. Its program centers on drawing, painting, ceramics, and textile work by self-taught and outsider artists, with pieces acquired by institutions including MoMA, the American Folk Art Museum, and El Museo del Barrio. Proceeds from sales support the artists and the broader foundation.

shows.title: Scenes From Elsewhere
shows.artist: Sally West, Carlos Gamez de Francisco, Phoebe Brunner
shows.description:
Three painters with very different subjects — Australian plein-air seascapes, theatrical figuration, and Southern California landscape — are brought together here under the idea that beauty can be a deliberate, almost maximalist artistic strategy rather than a lapse into prettiness. The connective tissue is generosity of surface: thick, tactile paint handling that asks to be seen in person rather than on a screen.

Sally West's harbor and coastal studies are built from loaded, confident brushwork that turns boats, light, and water into near-abstract fields of color. Carlos Gamez de Francisco supplies the show's most ornate register, with sharply painted figures dressed in florid, theatrical costume that nods to classical portraiture while staying rooted in a contemporary, slightly camp sensibility. Phoebe Brunner's large-format landscapes of California coastline and open terrain round out the group, using saturated color and sweeping composition to give familiar scenery an almost heightened, cinematic glow.

As a program note, it's worth seeing for the contrast in technique alone — West's impasto, Gamez de Francisco's crisp illustrative line, and Brunner's atmospheric scale sit side by side and make a case for painterly abundance as a legitimate, even urgent, approach to contemporary representational painting.

shows.title: Outside The Gamut
shows.artist: Amber Goldhammer, Cynthia Coulombe-Bégin, Naguy Claude, Danny Brown, Gary John
shows.description:
Five artists working in the overlap between street art and pop abstraction fill this gallery with high-saturation color and instantly legible imagery — hearts, cartoon references, fashion logos, graphic text. The point isn't subtlety; it's the way bold, familiar visual language gets bent toward personal and sometimes confrontational ends.

Amber Goldhammer's paintings turn affection into a graphic, almost sloganeering visual vocabulary, while Cynthia Coulombe-Bégin builds thickly worked, sculptural canvases out of recurring motifs like hearts and butterflies, treating accumulated paint as a physical stand-in for emotional weight. Danny Brown's mixed-media panels — drawing on his background in fashion and graffiti — recontextualize luxury-brand imagery into something more pointed about identity and self-presentation, and Gary John's found-surface paintings, developed from his years working on the Venice Beach boardwalk, keep a scrappy, improvisational edge that the rest of the show's polish doesn't quite have.

It's a loud, color-forward show best taken as a survey of how different artists metabolize the same visual sources — advertising, cartoons, street graphics — into distinct personal languages.

shows.title: Backstage Pass
shows.description:
Backstage Pass pulls from Morrison Hotel Gallery's deep archive of rock photography to ask a simple question: who are music's biggest stars when the show is over and the cameras supposedly stop? The images here come from the green rooms, tour buses, and off-stage downtime that photographers like Lynn Goldsmith, Bob Gruen, Jerry Schatzberg, Henry Diltz, Ethan Russell, and Danny Clinch were granted rare access to across five decades of rock history.

The throughline is proximity rather than performance — candid, unguarded frames of Beatlemania-era chaos, the Rolling Stones between sets, and decades of arena-rock figures caught in quieter, more human moments. It's a bi-coastal exhibition, running concurrently at Morrison Hotel Gallery's Soho location, which gives West Coast visitors a chance to see prints that don't always make it out to the gallery's Sunset Marquis outpost.

For anyone whose interest in rock photography runs toward the mythology of fame as much as the music itself, this is a dense, image-packed survey worth the visit before it comes down in mid-October.

venue.name: Morrison Hotel Gallery
venue.address_detail: In the lobby of the Sunset Marquis Hotel

shows.title: Chris Lux
shows.description:
Los Angeles painter and ceramicist Chris Lux returns to GGLA for a solo turn after a run of collaborative and group appearances at the gallery, including 2024's Revel Hall installed inside a derelict Mt. Washington house. Lux works in a flattened, ultra-bright register — often using Flashe vinyl paint — that borrows the graphic punch of stained glass and early-20th-century woodblock prints while staying rooted in a distinctly Southern Californian strain of outsider-adjacent figuration.

His recurring cast of frog-people, saints, and domestic still lifes reads like folklore rewritten for a skate shop: cooperation, adoration, and low-grade menace all play out in flat, saturated color fields outlined in confident black line. Lux extends the same sensibility into glazed ceramic lamps and objects, treating functional forms with the same cartoon-mythic seriousness as his paintings.

Given his history of installing work in unconventional settings, expect this show at GGLA's Glassell Park space to lean into both the paintings and the sculptural lamp works that have become a signature of his practice.

shows.title: A Human Pace
shows.description:
Paolo Ventura builds miniature worlds and then photographs them as though they were full-scale film sets, and A Human Pace finds him turning that method toward Paris. His pictures conjure a city suspended between memory and invention: deserted streets, lone figures under streetlamps, and interiors that feel like stage sets abandoned mid-scene. The mood is melancholic and theatrical rather than documentary — this is a Paris assembled from nostalgia and imagination as much as from observation.

Ventura, an Italian photographer known for meticulously constructed dioramas populated with handmade figures, has built a career on blurring the line between staged fiction and lived history, and this body of work continues that practice at a more intimate, human scale.

For viewers who know Ventura's earlier war-haunted tableaux, A Human Pace is a gentler register — closer to reverie than reckoning — but it retains his signature patience: every shadow and prop placed with the deliberateness of a diorama-builder rather than a street photographer.

shows.title: our sharp line of sight
shows.description:
Fabiola Menchelli works without a camera, using photosensitive paper and light itself as raw material to build images that sit somewhere between photograph, sculpture and painting. For her third solo show at Marshall Gallery, the Mexico City-based artist turns exclusively to the prismatic, camera-less chromogenic prints that have dominated her practice over the past two years, folding each of two dozen unique works into a custom color-matched shadowbox frame.

The presentation borrows its atmosphere from Menchelli's 2024–25 museum show at the Norton Museum of Art, with dimly lit, magenta-hued walls meant to intensify the saturated color fields in the work. Titles like "green supercell" and "fire wire" point to the elemental, almost meteorological quality of her abstractions — fields of color that read as light caught mid-event rather than fixed on paper.

Menchelli has spent over a decade investigating what a photograph can be once you remove the lens, and this exhibition arrives at a moment of wider institutional attention to her work, including a recent Getty Museum acquisition from her Queer Horizons series. Seeing two dozen of these intimate, glowing objects together in one room is a rare chance to watch a single idea — light as material — worked through in quiet, obsessive variation.
shows.reception: Opening reception with the artist: Friday, September 11, 2026, 5:00-8:00 pm

venue.name: Marshall Gallery
venue.about: Marshall Gallery is a Santa Monica photography gallery founded in 2018 by Douglas Marshall and opened to the public in 2021 at Bergamot Station Arts Center. The program centers on contemporary and 20th-century lens-based art, with particular attention to experimental processes, printmaking craft and conceptual approaches to photography and video. In recent years the roster has increasingly explored the intersection of photographic practice with painting and sculpture. Alongside a regular schedule of exhibitions, the gallery hosts artist conversations and community events and participates in art fairs internationally, positioning itself within ongoing conversations about photography's evolving role in contemporary art and collective memory.

shows.title: Familiars
shows.description:
Von Wolfe's paintings stage a menagerie of animals — crocodiles, night creatures, watchful predators — rendered in rich, glossy oil on canvas that gives even a small study the weight of a history painting. "Familiars" brings together new canvases ranging from an intimate 55 x 55 cm close-up to a large 180 x 180 cm centerpiece, "Night Visitor," suggesting a show built around scale as much as subject.

There's a storybook menace to the work: animals rendered with enough anatomical specificity to feel real, but staged and lit like symbols or omens rather than straightforward wildlife studies. For anyone who likes their painting a little uncanny, this is a tightly focused, visually punchy show.

venue.name: Richard Heller Gallery
venue.about: Richard Heller Gallery is a contemporary art space in Santa Monica, California, run by director and owner Richard Heller with associate director Barry Belkin. Established in 1997, the gallery presents a program centered on figurative and narrative painting, drawing, ceramics, and photography by an international roster of emerging and mid-career artists. Known for supporting artists early in their careers—several of whom went on to significant critical attention—the gallery has built a reputation for eclectic, often humor-inflected exhibitions spanning painting, sculpture, and works on paper. Located at Bergamot Station, the gallery regularly participates in major art fairs and has been the subject of numerous press features on its artists in publications such as the Los Angeles Times, Juxtapoz, and Artillery.

shows.title: White Fence, Los Cholos
shows.description:
In 1986, on assignment for the documentary project "A Day in the Life of America," the great Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide spent a day in a Boyle Heights household connected to the White Fence gang, one of East LA's oldest and most storied. What began as a brief assignment turned into an ongoing relationship that Iturbide returned to over more than three decades; this exhibition presents the photographs from that first 1986 visit, many never widely exhibited.

The pictures are notable for what they don't do: rather than sensationalizing gang life, Iturbide's black-and-white images register tenderness, domesticity and communal bonds, complicated by the fact that many of her subjects, including Rosario, Liza and Cristina, were Deaf as a result of the mid-1960s rubella epidemic and communicated through sign language — hand gestures that can look like coded signs but are, in fact, ordinary conversation.

Iturbide is one of the most significant documentary photographers of the past half-century. This show is a chance to see a tightly focused, historically rich body of work that treats a stigmatized Los Angeles community with unusual patience and respect.

venue.name: ROSEGALLERY
venue.about: ROSEGALLERY is a Los Angeles-area gallery founded in 1991 by Rose Shoshana at the Bergamot Station Arts Center in Santa Monica. The program centers on modern and contemporary photography, spanning works that draw on the medium's history as well as contemporary photo-based art. Shoshana, who trained at Art Center College of Design and worked in editorial photography before opening the gallery, has built relationships with artists such as William Eggleston, Bruce Davidson, and Graciela Iturbide, and has collaborated with institutions including the Getty Museum and Tate Modern. The gallery represents a roster of established and emerging photographers and lens-based artists, and regularly presents work at international art fairs including Paris Photo and Photo London.

shows.title: What's Goin' On
shows.description:
Greg Miller has spent more than three decades mining the visual debris of American popular culture — advertisements, comic panels, magazine clippings, movie stills, signage — and reassembling it into densely collaged paintings that read like scrambled transmissions from the postwar id. What's Goin' On is his latest body of work in that vein, combining photorealist passages with gestural abstraction and cut-and-pasted found material so that faces, logos, and fragments of text keep surfacing and receding within the same canvas.

The work sits at the intersection of nostalgia and unease: the imagery Miller pulls from is glamorous and familiar, but he distresses and interrupts it enough that the comfort curdles into something closer to cultural archaeology. It's less about a single narrative than about the accumulation of half-legible signals — the same overload of mediated memory that gave the 1960s and '70s their look, filtered through a contemporary hand.

Miller has particular history with this gallery: he was William Turner Gallery's first artist when it opened its doors in Venice in 1991, and this show marks another chapter in a relationship now well into its fourth decade. A longtime Venice resident who now splits time between Los Angeles and Austin, his paintings sit in the collections of LACMA, the Laguna Art Museum, the Crocker Art Museum and the Weisman Foundation, among others — a track record that gives this new work the weight of a career-long project still very much in motion rather than a victory lap.

shows.title: The Shape of What Remains
shows.description:
Katherine Flynn is a Los Angeles-based photographer known for chasing forgotten places — motels with the vacancy sign still glowing, boats abandoned mid-lagoon, cars bleached by desert sun. This solo show at bG Gallery, her latest with the space after past exhibitions there, gathers new photographic work built around the same sensibility: color-saturated, slightly surreal scenes that read as documentary but feel staged by time itself.

Flynn has previously shown work that reframed found objects, including a series of photographs set into salvaged Volkswagen car doors, and that instinct for repurposing the discarded runs through this body of work too. Her images of empty swimming pools, roadside motels, and stranded vehicles turn the residue of American car culture and desert leisure into quiet, painterly compositions — evidence of past use now standing still.

The title, "The Shape of What Remains," points to what unites the pictures: an interest in the outline something leaves behind after its original purpose has drained away. It's an approachable but melancholic show, well suited to a gallery known for artists who work at the border of documentary and staged imagination.

shows.title: Spiritus Animales
shows.description:
Lara Kempke (also known professionally as Lara Eve Kempke) paints animals as if they were emissaries from another register of experience — birds, big cats and other creatures rendered in layered, richly textured mixed media that leans toward the mystical rather than the naturalistic. A Southern California artist with a background in fashion design, she brings a maximalist, pattern-driven sensibility to her canvases, building up surfaces with paint, collage and gilding until the animal subjects feel iconic, almost devotional.

"Spiritus Animales" (spirit animals) gathers this body of work at bG Gallery's Bergamot Station space. Expect vividly colored, densely worked compositions where a peacock, raven or big cat becomes a kind of totem — a stand-in for instinct, intuition, and the parts of ourselves we don't fully control. Kempke has described her practice as deeply intertwined with process and impulse, and that improvisational energy comes through in surfaces that reward close, slow looking.

Kempke's paintings are unapologetically decorative, emotionally direct, and easy to enjoy without a lot of art-historical throat-clearing.

shows.title: A Human Pace: Robert Doisneau
shows.description:
Robert Doisneau spent more than five decades photographing Paris at street level, and this survey pulls together a wide swath of that career — lovers stealing kisses on rainy sidewalks, children turning gutters and stairwells into playgrounds, dogs waiting patiently outside cafés, and the ordinary tradespeople, musicians and strangers who populated his frame. It's the kind of material that made Doisneau one of the central figures of French humanist photography, working alongside contemporaries like Cartier-Bresson and Willy Ronis but with a gentler, more whimsical eye.

The checklist ranges from the 1930s through the 1970s and includes several portraits of fellow artists — Picasso with Françoise Gilot, filmmaker Jacques Tati — alongside the anonymous Parisians who make up the bulk of his archive. Doisneau worked mostly in gelatin silver, and the prints on view include both vintage and later prints pulled from his estate, giving a sense of how his negatives have continued to be revisited since his death in 1994.

What holds the show together is Doisneau's insistence that the street itself was the best director: chance encounters, caught at the right moment, outperform anything staged. For visitors who know him only from the famous kiss photographs, this is a chance to see how consistent and generous that vision was across an entire career, and why his pictures of postwar Paris remain some of the most beloved images in twentieth-century photography.

venue.name: Peter Fetterman Gallery
venue.about: Peter Fetterman Gallery is a Santa Monica photography gallery founded by Peter Fetterman, a London-born collector and former filmmaker who opened his first gallery in 1988 and became one of the original tenants of Bergamot Station when it opened in 1994. The gallery holds one of the largest inventories of classic twentieth-century photography in the United States, with particular depth in humanist photography. Its holdings include work by figures such as Henri Cartier-Bresson, Sebastião Salgado, Steve McCurry, Ansel Adams, Paul Caponigro, Willy Ronis, Michael Kenna, André Kertész, Manuel Alvarez Bravo, Lillian Bassman, Pentti Sammallahti, Sarah Moon and Jeffrey Conley. The gallery presents this work in an intimate, salon-style setting intended to promote appreciation of the photographic medium.

shows.title: Joseph + Melinda Ostraff
shows.description:
Nüart Gallery's Santa Monica outpost pairs husband-and-wife artists Joseph and Melinda Ostraff for a two-person show of new work. Joseph Ostraff, a longtime Brigham Young University professor and three-time Utah Arts Council fellowship recipient, makes richly patterned, densely layered paintings that read as a kind of personal cartography — abstracted shapes and architectural motifs that track how people convert raw space into meaningful place. Melinda Ostraff, who holds a PhD in environmental science and human geography, brings a research-driven eye to her own practice, and the pairing sets his painterly abstraction against her more systematic investigations of landscape and place.

Joseph Ostraff was born in Santa Monica, giving this Bergamot Station presentation a homecoming undertone, and his gradated, patterned canvases — with titles referencing places from Berlin to the Lofoten Islands — suggest an artist still mapping his own relationship to geography decades into a well-traveled career.

This is a compact, one-month run, timed for Nüart's fall Santa Monica program, and offers a chance to see two connected but distinct sensibilities in dialogue in the gallery's Bergamot Station space.

venue.name: Nüart Gallery
venue.about: Nüart Gallery was established in Santa Fe at the start of the 21st century and has grown into a 3,000-square-foot, ten-room space on Canyon Road showing contemporary abstract and figurative art. Over more than two decades it has mounted upwards of 250 solo and group exhibitions, introducing many artists to the U.S. market and shipping worldwide. In 2023 the gallery expanded with a second 3,000-square-foot location at Bergamot Station in Santa Monica, extending its reach into the Los Angeles market. The program represents around 40 artists working locally and internationally, with works held in major museum collections such as MoMA, LACMA, the Getty, and the Tate Modern. The gallery also carries limited inventory from blue-chip artists.

shows.title: Living Echoes
shows.description:
Living Echoes is this year's faculty exhibition at Santa Monica College's Barrett Gallery, with an unusual twist: the show was researched, curated, and installed entirely by students in the department's gallery-practice courses rather than by outside curators or the faculty themselves. The result is a survey of twenty-seven working artists who also teach at SMC, shown through the eyes of the students who study alongside them.

The work spans painting, sculpture, photography, installation, and mixed media, loosely organized around questions of memory, identity, material, and place — themes that let a sprawling faculty roster cohere into something resembling a conversation rather than a group portrait. Expect real variation in approach and generation, from longtime studio painters to artists working in more conceptual and installation-based registers.

What makes the show worth a visit beyond its merits as art is the pedagogical frame: it's a rare chance to see a gallery exhibition built from the ground up by students learning the mechanics of exhibition-making, at a free, publicly accessible campus gallery that doesn't get the foot traffic of the commercial galleries nearby. The opening reception on October 13 is a good moment to see the work alongside the artists and the students who organized it.

venue.name: SMC's Pete and Susan Barrett Art Gallery

shows.title: Arreglos Artificiales
shows.description:
Salvador Domínguez opens de boer's fall season with "Arreglos Artificiales" — "artificial arrangements" — a title that plays on the Spanish term for silk-flower bouquets and points toward a practice built on staged, synthetic tableaux. Domínguez, an LA-based painter, works in a hyper-saturated, faintly surreal figurative mode, often placing solitary or paired figures inside interiors thick with pattern, drapery, and decorative objects that feel simultaneously domestic and theatrical.

Based on the works available ahead of the opening, the show looks to continue his interest in the artifice of everyday staging — flowers that don't wilt, rooms arranged for effect rather than comfort — using it as a lens on inherited Latino domestic aesthetics and the performance of hospitality and care. It's a promising follow-up slot after the gallery's summer run of Kash Ford, and a chance to catch an emerging painter's work in a single, focused presentation before the fall art-fair circuit picks up.

venue.name: de boer
venue.address: 3311 E Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90023

shows.title: GREMLIN: Museum of Commerce
shows.description:
Nick Herman has spent two decades making sculpture, photography, and books that treat industrial materials and structural systems as raw poetic material — fat solids cast into a lunar-looking frieze, hand-tied nets that sag under their own logic, antennas that double as myth machines. Museum of Commerce, his solo turn at FOYER-LA titled GREMLIN, promises more of that same sleight of hand: taking the leftover vocabulary of manufacturing, retail, and technology and bending it toward something stranger and more bodily.

FOYER-LA is exactly the kind of space this work needs. Herman's MFA is in sculpture from Yale, and his exhibition history runs through Socrates Sculpture Park, LAXART, and the Chinati Foundation's collection, so a project-space outing lets him work at a scale and speed that bigger institutions don't allow.

Given the title's nod to commerce and gremlins alike, expect a show that pokes at consumer culture and the "traumatic residue" — Herman's own phrase — that industry and technology leave on both land and body. It's a compact, single-artist project, which makes it an easy, quick stop for anyone curious about one of LA's more understated sculptor-writers.

venue.name: FOYER-LA
venue.about: FOYER-LA is an artist-run exhibition space in Los Angeles, founded in 2019 by artist Connie Walsh. Set behind a courtyard in front of Walsh's own studio, it describes itself as an in-between space for experimentation, dialogue, and collaboration. Since opening, the gallery has presented more than thirty projects, ranging from solo debuts to conceptually driven installations across sculpture, drawing, and performance. Its program has included artists such as Ellie Krakow, Michael Ashkin, Ana Maria Devis, and James Rose, alongside Walsh's own work. The space favors small-scale, provocative shows that explore themes of intimacy, transition, and the body, positioning itself as a laboratory for experimentation rather than a conventional commercial gallery.

shows.title: Charles Dickson: Select Works, 1965-2026
shows.description:
Charles Dickson has been carving since he was five years old, whittling toy knives under the blankets in South Central Los Angeles, and this survey at Parrasch Heijnen compresses sixty years of that practice into one gallery. Select Works, 1966-2026 pulls from across his career — wood, bronze, concrete, metal, glass, acrylic — tracking a self-taught sculptor who came up alongside Noah Purifoy and John Outterbridge in the Watts arts scene of the late 1960s and never really left it, becoming the longtime artist-in-residence at the Watts Towers Arts Center and groundskeeper of the Towers themselves.

What unites the wildly different materials in Dickson's work is a consistent visual language drawn from African sculptural tradition — masks, totemic forms, ritual tools — repurposed to catalog and honor Black life and history in Los Angeles specifically. He's best known publicly for civic commissions like the Mariposa Metro Green Line station and the Martin Luther King Jr. memorial in Watts, but this gallery presentation gets at the more intimate, studio-based side of his output: carved reliefs, assemblages, and figures that read like a private notebook kept over six decades.

A show spanning 1966 to 2026 is essentially a mini-retrospective, and it's a notable get for a Boyle Heights gallery to present a Los Angeles art-world elder statesman whose work usually turns up in museums and public plazas rather than commercial spaces. Worth seeing both for the sculpture itself and as a rare chance to see this much of Dickson's range in one room.

venue.name: Parrasch Heijnen
venue.about: Parrasch heijnen is a gallery in the Boyle Heights neighborhood of Los Angeles. Its program brings together postwar Los Angeles Light and Space and geometric abstraction, work by artists associated with the historic Brockman Gallery and the Black Arts Council, and a roster of contemporary painters and sculptors working in abstraction and assemblage. The gallery represents several artist estates, including those of Peter Alexander, Tony DeLap, Forrest Bess, Marcia Hafif and Alonzo Davis, alongside living artists such as Anne Appleby, Edith Baumann, Alteronce Gumby, Xylor Jane, Kristy Luck, Mildred Howard and Christine Howard Sandoval. The gallery participates regularly in international art fairs, including Frieze, Art Basel Miami Beach, NADA, Independent and the Dallas Art/Invitational fairs, and has organized historical group presentations such as 'Brockman Days' surveying the artists of the pioneering Black-owned Brockman Gallery.

shows.title: Dye Trace
shows.artist: Abby Flanagan, Hai-Wen Lin, and Marina Darcy Weiner
shows.description:
Dye Trace brings together three artists — Abby Flanagan, Hai-Wen Lin, and Marina Darcy Weiner — for a group exhibition at IZZY LEE, the Chinatown gallery formerly known as North Loop West. The gallery has spent the past several years cultivating a roster that moves fluidly between Los Angeles and the Northeast (it grew out of a project space in Williamstown, Massachusetts), and this show continues that cross-country conversation with new work from each artist.

While the gallery has not yet published a checklist, the title points to processes of saturation, staining, and residue — the kind of slow chemical or material transformation that recurs across a lot of the painters and object-makers this space has shown before, from Beverly Acha's mineral-toned abstractions to Andrew Holmquist's layered geometries. Expect an exhibition built around close looking at surface and process rather than a single unifying subject.

Dye Trace opens after the gallery's usual August closure, marking its first show back on Chung King Road for the fall season. It's worth a stop both for the work itself and as a chance to see how the gallery's identity is settling under its new name.

shows.title: Darren Cortez and Tanya Brodsky
shows.description:
This two-person exhibition pairs Darren Cortez, whose paintings often traffic in gothic, folkloric imagery — crows, blades, ritual objects rendered with a graphic, tattoo-flash intensity — with Tanya Brodsky, an LA sculptor who reworks found urban hardware (security bars, bed frames, rolling gates) into wry, body-conscious objects. Both artists share an interest in taking materials loaded with menace or utility and bending them toward something stranger: Cortez through image-making steeped in memento-mori symbolism, Brodsky through a sculptural practice that sandblasts and re-chromes the architecture of domestic security into objects that read as almost tender.

Brodsky, who was born in Kyiv and trained at RISD and UC San Diego, has spent years mining the visual language of window bars and fences — devices meant to keep bodies out or in — and turning them into sculptures that flirt with humor, vulnerability, and camp; her public commission "Yolki Palki" carried that same colorful, industrial-materials sensibility into a West Hollywood streetscape. Cortez's paintings, seen in NOON's recent group shows, favor a stark, illustrative style that draws on tattoo culture and outlaw iconography.

Pairing the two suggests a show interested in toughness as a surface that can be cut into, softened, or reclaimed. Expect a mix of wall-based painting and object-sculpture that plays off each other's hard materials and soft undertones.

venue.name: NOON Projects
venue.about: NOON Projects is a contemporary art gallery in Chinatown, Los Angeles, founded by Ryan Noon in 2022. The program presents emerging and historical artists working across painting, sculpture, performance, craft, and sound, with a focus on spirituality, eroticism, the natural world, queerness, and social practice. The gallery is known for close, collaborative relationships with its artists and an interdisciplinary curatorial approach that pairs exhibitions with a regular schedule of community programming, including concerts, lectures, dinners, workshops, salons, and performances. Noon brings a background in fashion and creative direction, having worked with Alexander McQueen and Henrik Vibskov and built a design studio and think tank at Nike, which informs the gallery's artist-centered, experimental sensibility and emphasis on long-term collaboration and dialogue between artists and audiences.

shows.title: Untitled Exhibition
shows.description:
Seasons opens its next exhibition on September 12 with a presentation of work by Malerie Marder. Marder is a Los Angeles-based photographer long associated with the staged, psychologically charged domestic tableaux that emerged from the Yale MFA program in the 1990s alongside artists like Gregory Crewdson and Justine Kurland — work that treats the family photograph and the snapshot's intimacy as a subject for careful, often unsettling reconstruction.

Seasons has not yet published a title, checklist, or statement for the show.

Given Marder's history of exhibiting internationally, this is a show worth watching for as the date approaches, even with details still thin.

shows.title: Joy is a Puppet
shows.description:
Isabelle Frances McGuire's first solo turn at Bel Ami arrives on the heels of a large-scale installation in the 2026 Whitney Biennial, and it keeps faith with the Chicago-based artist's signature move: taking the language of mass-produced objects — toys, mascots, consumer packaging — and recasting it in bronze and other durable, art-historical materials. The title work, a small bronze puppet in a cloth bonnet, typifies McGuire's interest in things that perform cuteness or utility while quietly withholding their own agency; the puppet is both a plaything and an uncanny effigy, animated by absence rather than by a hidden hand.

McGuire's practice moves fluidly between sculpture, sound, and video, often built from research into how toys, games, and domestic objects train bodies and expectations. Showing at Bel Ami puts this new body of work in conversation with the gallery's roster of artists who treat the vernacular — consumer goods, genre fiction, car culture — as material for serious formal and conceptual investigation.

Given McGuire's growing institutional profile, including a 2024 solo at Chicago's Renaissance Society and a recent Artadia Award, this compact gallery presentation offers an intimate, close-up look at a practice usually encountered at much larger scale.

shows.title: Novel
shows.description:
Ian Miyamura's first solo exhibition at Bel Ami is a deliberately unstable mix of registers: geometric paintings that fake symmetry, text pictures built on puns, sunken relief sculptures, and small, almost fussy tableaux populated by painted miniatures lifted from the tabletop game Warhammer. Rather than settle into one voice, Miyamura treats the gallery like a novel with multiple narrators, each piece a different kind of sentence testing out what a picture can say.

The Brooklyn-based painter, who trained at SAIC and MICA, has built a reputation in recent New York and Los Angeles survey shows for a restless, genre-hopping approach to painting that resists easy categorization — one work might read as hard-edged abstraction, the next as fantasy-nerd curio cabinet. That tension between control and collectible kitsch is the show's real subject: Miyamura is less interested in resolving his many styles than in letting the friction between them generate meaning, daring the viewer to detect a hidden order.

It's a show that rewards close, patient looking — small works that ask to be read almost like clues, accumulating into a bigger and more elusive picture the longer you stay with them.

shows.title: Worlds within Worlds
shows.artist: Jasser Membreno, Jian Lee, FADNAT, Jenn Lima, Ricardo Garcia
shows.description:
Curated by Los Angeles artist Jasser Membreno, this five-person show gathers painters, an illustrator, and a ceramicist who each build self-contained visual worlds out of fantasy, memory, and myth. Membreno's own monster-inflected paintings draw on Latin American and European folklore; animator and CalArts-trained painter Jian Lee works augmented reality into traditional media; FADNAT's intuitive, freestyle process conjures uncanny creatures out of abstract starting shapes; Jenn Lima hand-builds kawaii-inflected clay figures steeped in Mexican folk art and the supernatural; and Ricardo Garcia paints bold, abstracted portraits of Los Angeles and its people.

What unites the group is less a shared style than a shared method — each artist starts from intuition or chance and lets a distinct, personal cosmology take shape on the page, canvas, or kiln shelf. The result is a show about world-building in miniature: five different entry points into the strange, the playful, and the dreamlike, installed together at Keystone Art Space's Lincoln Heights studio complex.

It's a modest, short run (just over a week) but a good excuse to see a cross-section of the working artists based at Keystone, a no-frills industrial studio building that doubles as an exhibition space for its own resident community.

shows.title: On the Consideration of the Curve
shows.description:
Dorothea Rockburne built her art out of mathematics, and this survey — spanning five decades of her career — makes that case with unusual clarity. The earliest works here, graphite-and-kraft-paper pieces like "2, 4, 6, 8" and "Drop/Fold" from 1969-70, show her using gravity, folding, and repetition to let the material itself generate the composition, a method she developed after studying topology with mathematician Max Dehn at Black Mountain College in the early 1950s.

The show then traces how that structural logic evolved: the Golden Section paintings of the mid-1970s apply Renaissance proportional systems to chalk, varnish, and gesso on linen, while the translucent vellum "Musician Angel" works from the early 1980s, made after Rockburne encountered Giotto's frescoes in Padua, bring a new warmth and luminosity to her geometric vocabulary. Later watercolors like "Northern Sky; Southern Sky" and "Star Structure" push the same ideas toward cosmology, treating the picture plane as a map of celestial order.

It's a rare chance to see an artist's governing idea stay constant while its expression keeps changing — rigorous drawings giving way to glowing, astronomically-minded paintings without ever abandoning the underlying logic of folding, measuring, and marking. For anyone interested in how postwar American abstraction absorbed science and structure without losing feeling, this is an exceptionally focused introduction to a chronically under-recognized artist.

venue.name: Marc Selwyn Fine Art
hours: Tue - Sat 11am to 6pm, or by appointment

shows.title: Describing Clouds
shows.description:
Jordan Nassar's fifth solo show with Anat Ebgi pairs two bodies of work rooted in Palestinian craft: large multi-panel embroideries worked in tatreez, the traditional cross-stitch technique usually found on clothing and domestic textiles, and a new mosaic made from smalti tile. The embroidered pieces are built from geometric modules — diamonds, pentagons, hexagons — that can be rehung in different configurations, so the imagined horizons and hillsides they depict are never quite fixed. The modularity nods openly to Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian's mirror sculptures, another case of a regional craft tradition pushed toward abstraction.

The show's centerpiece is the mosaic Jabalia, which reconstructs, tessera by tessera, imagery from the mosaic floors of a fifth-century Byzantine church excavated at a Gaza archaeological site whose current condition is unknown after years of bombardment. Nassar doesn't editorialize this directly in the work, but the choice to spend painstaking hours reassembling a damaged or possibly destroyed site's imagery, animal by animal, carries its own argument about preservation and loss. The exhibition's title comes from a Mahmoud Darwish poem about clouds that resist fixed description, gathering and dispersing — an apt metaphor for how Nassar treats inherited pattern and symbol as something always being reassembled rather than settled.

It's quiet, formally rigorous work that rewards close looking: the embroidery is dense and exacting, and the mosaic's color shifts reward standing in front of it rather than viewing it in reproduction. Nassar's pieces are in the collections of the Whitney, LACMA, and MOCA LA among others, and this body of work is being shown concurrently in a two-part presentation with The Third Line at Frieze London.

shows.title: Private Life
shows.description:
P. Staff's work has long used light and chemical process to put pressure on the body — in past projects, caustic gas and color-saturated video have stood in for the pain of medical transition and institutional control. Private Life takes a more intimate route into similar territory. The press materials for the show take the form of a letter addressed to the artist, describing a dream about bodily rupture, and the works themselves center on a series titled Property: Polaroid images of anonymous genitals and bodies, shot on green- and purple-tinted film that pulses between abstraction and explicitness.

The polaroid format matters here — it's the camera of amateur intimacy, of pictures taken by and for friends and lovers rather than for an audience. Staff is reportedly handing the camera to friends to document themselves, which turns the show into something closer to a collective, consensual archive of desire than a single artist's statement about it. The discordant lighting schemes the artist is known for do their usual work of visually overwhelming the viewer, making bodies that are otherwise rendered with documentary plainness harder to settle into.

It's a show about the parts of ourselves that are shown "in action" being shown instead at rest — asses, genitals, hair, all slowed down and given a different kind of attention. For an artist whose practice usually operates at an institutional scale (Staff represented the UK at the 2024 Whitney Biennial and has had museum surveys at the ICA Philadelphia and MASS MoCA), this is a tighter, more interior turn.

shows.title: Vessels
shows.description:
Nicole Coson's practice starts from printmaking but keeps expanding outward — she's known for taking the humble industrial objects of the global food supply chain, like styrofoam fruit netting and stackable plastic shipping crates, and translating their textures into large-scale impressions on linen and canvas. Vessels, organized in collaboration with Silverlens, continues that line of work, using the crate and its grid-like geometry as a recurring motif that nods to Bauhaus design history even as it points to the more mundane, global logistics of how food and goods actually move.

Coson is a Filipino artist based between Manila and London, and the "vessel" of the title does double duty: it's the shipping container that carries produce across oceans, and it's a metaphor she's used elsewhere for the body and for home itself, drawing on Ursula K. Le Guin's "carrier bag theory" of culture as something built from containers and gathering rather than from conquest. The resulting works sit somewhere between abstraction and index — monochrome fields that reveal, on closer inspection, the exact grooves and ridges of the industrial objects that made them.

It's a show about diaspora and trade routes approached through material process rather than narrative, which fits Coson's reputation as a close observer of how global supply chains leave physical traces on the objects — and the people — that pass through them.

shows.title: Secret Agent Woman (SAW) presents: Crownsprouting
shows.description:
Gogo Graham is best known as a fashion designer who has built garments specifically for trans women's bodies, showing collections that treat clothing as a direct tool of gender self-determination rather than a neutral covering. Crownsprouting, organized under Commonwealth and Council's Secret Agent Woman (SAW) series (itself presented by fellow gallery artist P. Staff), brings that sensibility into the space of the gallery rather than the runway.

The title suggests growth breaking through from the top down — a crown sprouting rather than a root — which tracks with Graham's broader interest in bodies that generate their own forms of adornment and transformation on their own terms, outside of conventional fashion-industry structures. Expect garment-based or textile work that carries the hand-built, improvisational quality Graham has become known for, made for bodies the mainstream fashion world has historically ignored.

As a SAW presentation, this show is also a statement about how Commonwealth and Council uses its program to platform artists adjacent to its core roster — in this case bringing a designer's practice into dialogue with the gallery's longstanding interest in queer and trans makers.

shows.title: AAAgent presents: Past Time
shows.description:
Maryrose Cobarrubias Mendoza has spent her career using scale manipulation and cultural critique to examine assimilation — what it costs and what it looks like for a Filipino immigrant family to pursue "the American dream," as she's described her own parents' motivations for leaving Manila for Los Angeles in 1970. Past Time, presented under the gallery's AAAgent banner, brings that long-running inquiry to Commonwealth and Council.

A Guggenheim Fellow and longtime drawing coordinator at Pasadena City College, Mendoza works across drawing and object-based installation, often taking ordinary domestic or everyday items and distorting their scale to defamiliarize them — a strategy that turns the mundane props of assimilated life into objects worth stopping to examine. The title's double meaning, a nostalgic "past time" and a sense of time having passed, points to a show concerned with memory, inheritance, and the slow accumulation of a life built between two cultures.

It's a quieter, less widely covered show than some of the gallery's bigger names, which makes it a good entry point into an artist whose decades of steady, personal work on immigrant identity deserve more attention than they typically get.

shows.title: Seeing Through: Jia Aili's Parallel Paintings
shows.description:
Jia Aili, one of the most closely watched painters to emerge from contemporary China, brings a new body of work to Beverly Hills that pushes his signature apocalyptic-romantic landscapes into a more layered, almost sculptural register. The show takes its title from a concept he calls "parallel painting" — canvases paired with acrylic-pen drawing on plexiglass set in deep artist-made frames, so that a painted image and a drawn one hover at different depths and seem to shift against each other as you move past them. The effect splits his usual single flat plane into overlapping strata, turning familiar motifs — swirling waves, diagonal slashes, solitary figures, spiraling horizon lines — into compositions that resist settling into one fixed reading.

Alongside these hybrid works are more straightforward oils on linen, square-format paintings built from the same vocabulary of wind-scoured color fields and fractured brushwork that made Jia's reputation: vast, weather-beaten spaces populated by isolated figures that read as stand-ins for a disoriented contemporary consciousness. Titles like "Wayfarer," "Cross," and "The Barque of Dante" signal his continued interest in art-historical and literary reference points, filtered through a painterly language indebted equally to Chinese ink traditions and to Northern Romantic landscape painting.

This is Jia's first solo presentation at Gagosian's Beverly Hills space and his first solo project with the gallery since 2019, making it a useful checkpoint for anyone tracking how his work has developed — the parallel-painting device in particular feels like a genuine formal leap rather than a stylistic tweak. Worth seeing before it closes October 10.

shows.title: Ovum
shows.description:
Roxanne Jackson's ceramic menagerie of hybrid, half-fossilized creatures lands at The Pit for what the gallery describes as her first solo presentation in her home state of California. The new sculptures grew out of a residency at Cal State Long Beach's Center for Contemporary Ceramics, and the ambition of that time in the studio shows: large-scale creatures share the room with smaller, more intimate objects, all circling around the idea of the egg as an origin point for wild, unstable life.

Jackson treats clay less as a medium than as living tissue — glazes and lusters read like scale, bark, or bone, and every piece keeps visible traces of the kiln's unpredictability rather than smoothing them away. A serpent wraps around a vessel, a bird's body splits open, a harpy hoards silver treasure in her nest; the show works a rich seam of natural history and myth without settling into either.

It's a good showcase for an artist whose work sits at the noisy end of the current wave of figurative ceramics — funnier, grosser, and more unruly than most, with a real command of glaze as a tool for storytelling rather than decoration.

venue.name: The Pit
venue.about: The Pit is a contemporary art gallery in Los Angeles founded in 2014 by artists Adam D. Miller and Devon Oder. It began as an artist-run, artist-curated project space in a former mechanics garage in Glendale before relocating, after a decade, to a larger complex in Atwater Village designed by JK & Co. The gallery represents and exhibits emerging, mid-career and established artists across generations, with a program grounded in dialogue with historical California art traditions, emphasizing material exploration, design, and counterculture influences. The Pit participates in major national and international art fairs and is a member of several art-dealer associations.

shows.title: Life on Earth
shows.description:
Chase Biado's new paintings mark a shift away from the invented fantasy worlds of his earlier work toward scenes drawn from ordinary life — a figure reading the newspaper, a drive through smoke-hazed air, a walk through an orchard — rendered with just enough distance to feel like half-remembered dreams rather than documentary. Desaturated color and loose, atmospheric brushwork do a lot of the talking; a single stroke stands in for rain, a smear for a passing car, so the paintings read as much as records of weather and motion as they do as pictures of people.

Showing alongside Roxanne Jackson's ceramics in The Pit's Atwater Village space, Biado's quieter, more melancholic paintings offer a contrast in temperature and material while sharing an interest in transformation and impermanence.

shows.title: Benjamin Echeverria
shows.description:
This is a solo presentation of new paintings by Benjamin Echeverria, installed across Overduin & Co.'s Sunset Boulevard space. The installation views show canvases of varying scale hung in open, evenly lit rooms, giving each piece room to be read on its own rather than crowded into a salon hang — a curatorial choice that suggests confidence in the individual works carrying the room.

Without a press release to lean on, the paintings themselves are the clearest guide to what Echeverria is after: a handling of surface and color that favors accumulation and layering over single gestures, built up in a way that rewards close looking as much as a view from across the gallery. The works read as part of a younger generation of LA painters working through abstraction's recent history — material, process-driven, unafraid of a messy edge — while keeping enough restraint in composition that the paintings don't tip into pure gesture.

It's a tightly installed show and a good opportunity to see an artist's recent output gathered in one place, in a gallery that has built its reputation on exactly this kind of close attention to younger and under-the-radar painters.

shows.title: (Almost) Every Year: Sixty Years of Printmaking at Gemini G.E.L.
shows.description:
For its sixtieth anniversary, Gemini G.E.L. opens its archive rather than mounting a monograph on any single artist. Curators Susan Dackerman and Helen Molesworth have pulled a work or two from nearly every year of the workshop's history since 1966, building a loose chronological survey of what collaborative printmaking in Los Angeles has looked like across six decades. The result reads like a cross-section of postwar American art: a Josef Albers color study, Jasper Johns' lead relief Light Bulb, Claes Oldenburg's molded-polyurethane Profile Airflow, Richard Serra etchings, and a brand-new 2026 lithograph by Analia Saban sit in the same rooms as prints by Rauschenberg, Lichtenstein, Diebenkorn, and Julie Mehretu.

What makes the show more than a victory lap is its structure: rather than grouping by artist or theme, it leans on the calendar itself, letting viewers watch technique and style shift year to year as the workshop's master printers worked out new ways to get an artist's hand onto a plate or stone. Sculptural and object-based editions — Jonathan Borofsky's photo-etched copper Foot Print, Ken Price's glazed earthenware cup, Edward and Nancy Kienholz's lens-fitted Econo-Can — sit alongside flat work, underlining that Gemini's definition of a "print" has always been elastic.

It's a rare chance to see the breadth of a single publisher's output in one place, from a 1966 Man Ray lithograph to Analia Saban's 2026 E-Trash, and a useful reminder of how much of the look of American printmaking since the 1960s was quite literally made in this building on Melrose Avenue.

shows.title: Tête-bêche
shows.artist: Aleza Zheng, Daniel Wang, Tianlian Liu, Xiangxi Zhang, John Wu, Studio Paul Chan x Jeremy Kim, Yuri Yuan
shows.description:
Tête-bêche brings together seven Los Angeles-based artists and designers — painters, a sculptor, and a furniture studio — who each grew up somewhere else and carry a private stock of images from Hong Kong cinema and Japanese film and animation. None of them is working on the same subject, but that shared visual inheritance surfaces obliquely throughout: in a lacquered credenza built like a stage set, in Xiangxi Zhang's mixed-media assemblages built around a television and a toaster oven, in the quiet domestic scenes of Daniel Wang and John Wu.

The show's title, a printing term for pages bound head-to-tail, is a fitting metaphor for a group exhibition built on inversion and echo rather than a unifying theme. Tianlian Liu's large pigment-on-silk piece and Yuri Yuan's oil painting September anchor the show's more painterly register, while Studio Paul Chan's collaboration with designer Jeremy Kim pulls the exhibition toward functional object and interior design, with washi-paper furniture that doubles as sculpture.

It's a loosely woven but visually rich group show, worth seeing for the range of media — oil, acrylic, silk, mahogany, found objects — under one conceptual umbrella of imported memory.

shows.title: Where Willows Rise
shows.description:
Katya Labowe-Stoll's debut solo show imagines a world after a great flood has receded, leaving behind scarred, alluvial land where willows — plants built for water but stranded on dry ground — become a stand-in for resilience under pressure. The seven oil paintings on view, most of them sizable canvases built around a single mountain landscape seen at different hours, move through a tight, shifting palette: grey mornings, arctic blue, smoky sienna, ochre red.

Labowe-Stoll, who trained at RISD and is based in Los Angeles, builds scenes that hover between the specific and the hallucinatory — holographic bubbles, mirror-maze reflections, reeds that read like waving tentacles. The work draws loosely on nineteenth-century landscape painters like Frederic Church and on the high-desert terrain near her Mount Washington studio, but the effect is closer to a fever dream than a plein-air record, inflected by the flood narrative from the Torah and her own Jewish upbringing.

As a first gallery outing, the show is a confident, cohesive statement: a small body of work that commits fully to one atmosphere and one color logic, and rewards the slower looking the artist is clearly asking for.

shows.title: Periphery Dreaming
shows.description:
Xingzi Gu paints people in suspended states — adolescents caught between childhood and adulthood, couples unsure whether a gesture is affection arriving or leaving, solitary figures parked in an unnamed mood. The reference point, made explicit by a line from Beckett's Waiting for Godot on the gallery wall text, is waiting itself as a condition rather than a prelude to something else.

That slowness is built into the paintings' making as much as their subject: Gu works in thin layers of acrylic and oil that can take over a year to resolve, treating the canvas as what they call a "recording machine" for small shifts in opacity, expression, and surface over that time. The nine large-scale works on view — bedrooms, nocturnes, figures folded into soft, ambiguous light — share a muted, candlelit palette that makes the waiting feel less like stasis and more like a held breath.

Gu, who splits their training between SAIC and NYU, has a growing reputation for this kind of patient, interior figuration, and this show (timed alongside the gallery's presence at Frieze Seoul) is a strong, cohesive introduction to the mood and method behind the work.

shows.title: Memnosphere
shows.description:
Erin Wright trained as an architect before she trained as a painter, and it shows: her canvases render tile grout, wood grain, upholstery and skin with the flat, exacting clarity of an architectural rendering or a staged product shot. For Memnosphere, her second solo show with the gallery, she builds that precision toward an impossible target — smell — populating her tightly controlled domestic interiors with the things that trigger it: a magnolia cutting by a sofa, moths over a flowering cactus, a worn t-shirt on a door hook.

The show's three built kitchenettes are the most ambitious gesture here: full-scale, constructed on site, complete with upholstered banquettes you can actually sit on, but with cupboards that don't open and sinks that aren't plumbed. They sit in the uncanny space between stage set and architectural model, extending into three dimensions the same just-short-of-real quality that defines her paintings, which stop a fraction of an inch before the canvas edge. A loose-leaf catalogue in each kitchenette — Wright's own writing mixed with recipes, quotations, and ephemera, modeled loosely on John Cage's Rolywholyover catalogue for MOCA — gives viewers scattered, nonlinear routes into the stories behind individual paintings.

Wright has said the show is meant to unfold the way a fragrance does, developing over its three-month run as paintings rotate in and out — so a visit in September won't show quite the same thing as one in December. It's a smart, understated show from an LA-based artist and Woodbury University architecture professor whose work sits at an interesting hinge between built space and painted illusion.

shows.title: A Pacific Line
shows.description:
Teruko Yokoi (1924–2020) belongs to the generation of postwar Japanese artists who crossed the Pacific to study and exhibit in the United States, training at the Art Students League in New York and later studying with Hans Hofmann before marrying the painter Sam Francis. This exhibition gathers paintings and works on paper from the 1950s, the period when Yokoi was absorbing the gestural vocabulary of Abstract Expressionism while folding in the brushwork, flattened space, and calligraphic rhythm of her training in Japan.

The works on view — loosely figured compositions like "Pose" alongside more abstract, untitled canvases from 1957–58 — show an artist working out how to reconcile two visual languages at once. Color sits in flat, almost ink-wash fields; forms are built from quick, loaded brush gestures rather than outline. It's a body of work that reads as both of its American moment and distinctly apart from it, closer in spirit to the Gutai and Mono-ha painters working concurrently in Japan than to her Hofmann School peers.

Yokoi's reputation has been slowly catching up to her historical importance over the past decade, as curators and galleries revisit the women and non-Western artists who were present in New York's midcentury avant-garde but written out of its first histories. This show, concentrated on a tight run of 1950s pictures, is a good entry point: small enough to take in the particulars of her hand, substantial enough to make the case for a rediscovery.

shows.title: Ynez Johnston: In Search of the Oracle
shows.description:
Ynez Johnston spent more than six decades building a visual vocabulary all her own, one that borrowed as freely from ancient maps, textiles, and hieroglyphs as from the gestural abstraction she absorbed coming up in postwar Los Angeles. This survey gathers paintings and works on paper that show her restless, maze-like compositions at full strength: dense fields of invented glyphs, totemic figures, and winding pathways rendered in jewel-toned color that reward close, unhurried looking.

The "oracle" of the title is apt. Johnston's pictures read like coded messages or divinatory objects, less interested in describing a place than in conjuring one from half-remembered travels and imagined cosmologies. She trained at Berkeley and in Paris under André Lhote, then spent a Fulbright-funded year in Guatemala whose textiles and ruins left a permanent mark on her forms, and her gallery's current program of estate shows has steadily made the case for her as one of the era's more idiosyncratic and under-recognized painters.

For a gallery built around the legacy of California hard-edge and mid-century abstraction, Johnston is something of an outlier, closer to Klee or Dubuffet than to the geometric clarity of her Los Angeles peers, and that friction is part of what makes the show worth a visit. The installation draws from multiple decades of her output, letting visitors trace how her symbolic language thickened and loosened over time without ever losing its handmade, obsessive density.

shows.title: Suns, Stars, and Story Systems
shows.description:
Shar Tui'asoa returns to Thinkspace for her second solo show with the gallery, arriving right after her debut museum exhibition opened in her home state of Hawai'i. The new paintings extend her signature style — bold, flattened color fields and statuesque female figures rooted in Pacific Islander iconography — into territory explicitly about oral storytelling, tracing a line from cosmology and oration down to the voices of everyday speakers and elders.

Tui'asoa, who is of Tongan descent and runs her own illustration studio, has built a visual language instantly recognizable from commercial work for clients like Disney, Pixar, and The New York Times, but her gallery paintings do something different: they slow that same graphic confidence down into devotional, almost totemic portraits. This body of work reads as a continuation of her ongoing project of centering Pacific Islander culture and womanhood within a contemporary painting practice, made for an audience that includes her own community as much as the gallery-going public.

It's a strong show for anyone interested in how an artist moves between commercial illustration and fine-art painting without losing the clarity of her graphic voice.

shows.title: Nocturnos: Painted Midnight Poems
shows.description:
This is RJ Quiralta's debut solo show with Thinkspace, bringing sixteen new paintings and works on paper and found objects from the self-taught, small-town Mexican artist. Quiralta came to painting late, after years away from drawing, and his "Nocturnos" series channels that late-night, self-taught energy directly: vintage-inflected imagery, mythological and romantic pairings, and a theatrical, stage-lit quality that treats each canvas like a small scene caught mid-performance.

The work leans into whimsy and melancholy in roughly equal measure — characters that feel plucked from old storybooks or silent film, rendered with a dark, slightly surreal humor. Because Quiralta works across canvas, paper, and found objects, the show should have a varied, handmade feel rather than a uniform painting-only presentation.

For a gallery known for polished pop-surrealism, this show offers something rougher-edged and more personal — worth seeking out if you're curious about self-taught narrative painters working outside the MFA pipeline.

shows.title: Going Direct
shows.description:
Susanna Coffey has spent four decades painting her own face in a mirror hung above her palette, turning self-portraiture into a lifelong study of symmetry, identity, and the body politics of looking. Alongside that practice she keeps a second, looser body of work: small night paintings made en plein air, landscapes and cityscapes built from direct observation after dark. Going Direct brings these two strands together at Serious Topics, pairing recent self-portraits with nocturnal landscapes and still lifes that share the same insistence on working straight from life rather than from photographs or memory.

The title is a quiet joke and a statement of method. Coffey, who taught painting for decades at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, has long argued that observation is itself a discipline, a way of discovering meaning rather than illustrating it. Seeing her luminous, close-cropped heads next to small dark-toned nocturnes lets you track a single sensibility moving between two very different kinds of looking: the unblinking confrontation of the mirror and the slower, more atmospheric attention demanded by a landscape at night.

For a gallery that has long championed figurative painters working outside the mainstream art-market spotlight, a show by an artist of Coffey's stature and critical pedigree (her work sits in the collections of the Whitney, the Met, and the National Portrait Gallery) is a notable draw, and a chance to see new work from a painter still, by her own account, happily obsessed with the problem of how to render a face.

shows.title: Taking Stock: The Gym
shows.description:
Michael Mandiberg scraped and analyzed some 130 million stock photographs for Taking Stock, an ongoing project that treats the anonymous image bank underlying advertising, AI training data, and everyday visual culture as raw material for art. Machine-learning tools sorted the images by pose, gesture, and theme, and Mandiberg's code then fused clusters of near-identical photos — the same forced smile, the same pointing hand — into single composite images and looping videos, producing eerie, blurred composites of people who never quite existed as photographed.

The Gym, the chapter of the project on view at Gattopardo, narrows the lens to stock imagery's favorite fiction of wellness: the generic gym-goer, flexing, stretching, mid-rep, endlessly interchangeable. By averaging thousands of these images together, Mandiberg turns a genre built on aspirational sameness into something closer to a statistical ghost — a portrait of nobody that is also, uncomfortably, a portrait of an entire industry's idea of a body.

Mandiberg has spent two decades making work about information systems and the ideologies hidden inside them, from the 7,473-volume Print Wikipedia to earlier chapters of Taking Stock shown at Heft Gallery and Paris Photo. This installment keeps that same deadpan, research-driven method but turns it toward a more intimate, bodily subject — the pictures that are supposed to make us want to be someone else.
