shows.title: The Transcendence of Memory
shows.artist: Melinda Braathen, Ji Won Cha, Cheung Tsz Hin, Paul Lam, Anna Lugovska, H.E. Morris, Liz Stringer, Alixe Turner, Jiatong Yuan
shows.description:
This nine-artist group show inaugurates Baert Gallery's new Melrose Hill location, and it's organized around a loose but coherent idea: memory as something felt in the body rather than just recalled in the mind. The works on view move between landscape and figure, often blurring the two — Anna Lugovska's layered, atmospheric canvases read as much as interior weather systems as outdoor views, while Melinda Braathen and H.E. Morris paint the human form and the natural world as if they're made of the same substance.

Ceramics give the show its physical counterweight. Liz Stringer's glazed and foil-wrapped sculptures and Paul Lam's earthenware pieces bring a bodily, almost ritualistic presence into a room otherwise dominated by painting, while Alixe Turner's charcoal-and-plaster panels split the difference, pulling drawing into relief. Ji Won Cha's oils of blossoms and animals and Jiatong Yuan's heavily worked, wax-and-oilstick canvas add two more distinct registers of mark-making to a show that's less about a unified style than a shared preoccupation with how the past lodges in materials.

It's a strong opening statement for the gallery's new space: ambitious in scale, wide-ranging in media, and worth a slow look given how much is packed into the nine practices on view.

shows.title: SKZ Centimeter Studies Classroom
shows.description:
Dan Levenson has spent well over a decade building out the State Art Academy, Zürich — SKZ for short — a wholly invented Bauhaus-adjacent art school whose non-existent students supposedly produced the paintings, storage furniture, and classroom props that make up his actual studio practice. This new installment, a "Centimeter Studies Classroom," continues that project with small-format, metrically-sized paintings and the plywood fixtures built to house them, all aged and worn to look like relics of a defunct institution.

The joke is dry and the craft is real: Levenson's formalist exercises — rigid grids, standardized proportions, geometric color studies — are a sly way of interrogating how art schools teach creativity by drilling rules into students, and what gets lost or found in that process. He's shown pieces of the SKZ saga at the Hammer Museum, Vielmetter, Honor Fraser, and Praz-Delavallade, among others, and has returned to this gallery before with 2023's "In That Far Corner."

This is a return engagement of sorts for an artist whose entire body of work is itself one long-running fiction, and the centimeter-scale studies promise a more intimate, classroom-supply-closet version of a world he's been elaborating since 2008.

shows.title: Oneiria
shows.description:
French street artist ABYS (Julien Brouand) makes his North American solo debut here with seventeen new acrylic paintings, translating characters built for large-scale murals down onto canvas. Brouand came up through graffiti and collective street-painting crews before developing his own cast of stylized, large-than-life figures around 2015, and "Oneiria" is essentially a gallery-scale showcase of that invented universe — characters, lettering, and setting combined into dense, narrative compositions.

The work sits at the intersection of animation and street art: precise, almost cartoon-clean linework carrying expressive, lived-in color, with his figures staged like frames from a story rather than isolated portraits. For an artist whose primary canvas has been walls and public space, seeing this vocabulary compressed into paintings meant for close viewing is the real draw of the show.

It's a solid pick for fans of graffiti-rooted painting looking for someone newer to the US gallery circuit.

shows.title: The Fresh Series (Session Eighteen): Spotlight on Local Creatives
shows.artist: Timothy Smith, Steve Montiglio, Marina Claire
shows.description:
The Fresh Series is Thinkspace's recurring slot for emerging local talent, rotating in a fresh trio of Los Angeles-area artists each month for a smaller-scale, lower-stakes showcase alongside the gallery's main solo exhibitions. Session Eighteen brings together Timothy Smith, Steve Montiglio, and Marina Claire — three area artists getting gallery wall space without the full build-out of a solo show.

Because the series deliberately favors newer and lesser-known names over established gallery artists, it functions as a kind of farm system for the broader Thinkspace program and a way for visitors to see who might be getting a solo show here a year or two down the line.

Worth a look if you want a read on what's percolating in LA's current illustrative and pop-surrealist painting scene outside the artists who already have name recognition.

shows.title: Everything I See I Swallow
shows.description:
Alessandra Acierno's first solo outing at Sea View gathers a tight body of new paintings built around the idea of the double — faces and figures that seem to repeat or split across the canvas, as if a single sitter were caught twice in the same frame. The palette throughout is deliberately dim: murky greens, bruised browns, and glowing patches of light that pick out a shoulder or a jaw while leaving the rest of the composition to dissolve into shadow.

Several works openly quote art history — a nude borrowed from Matisse's Bathers with a Turtle, a sleeping figure that nods to Fuseli's The Nightmare — but Acierno bends those references toward something closer to Gauguin's flattened, symbol-heavy color fields than to straight homage. Her young, often topless subjects don't perform for the viewer so much as resist being looked at, which gives the whole room a quietly confrontational charge.

It's a small, focused show — a mix of intimate oils on board and a handful of larger canvases — but it rewards slow looking. Acierno is still an emerging name, and this is a good opportunity to see a distinct, slightly unsettling painterly voice take shape in person, in one of Hollywood's more tucked-away project spaces.

shows.title: Virtual Erasure
shows.description:
David Rappeneau is one of the more unusual figures in contemporary drawing: a French artist represented by a major gallery who refuses interviews, skips his own openings, and is barely known even to his own dealers. Virtual Erasure gathers a new body of his pen, pencil, marker, and acrylic drawings, continuing a practice built on hyper-rendered, androgynous figures that hover somewhere between adolescence and something post-human.

The works typically depict youth absorbed in private, almost narcotic states — gaming, smoking, dressed in logo-heavy streetwear — rendered with a density of line that recalls Albrecht Dürer and Egon Schiele filtered through anime and internet image culture. Bodies warp and dissolve at the edges, a visual correlate to the show's title: figures caught mid-erasure, flickering between presence and digital abstraction.

It's a tightly focused solo presentation in a small project space, fitting for an artist whose cult following has been built entirely on the strength of the images themselves rather than any public persona — there is, notably, no studio visit or artist statement to lean on here, just the drawings.

shows.title: Life
shows.description:
Jacob Fenton paints with the internet's leftovers: the half-recognized faces, news fragments, and conspiratorial debris that circulate online until they stop meaning anything in particular. In "Life," his pictures treat that churn as raw material, smearing and recomposing familiar imagery until legibility becomes a kind of flicker — you catch a figure or a headline, then lose it again in the paint.

Fenton, a young LA-born painter fresh off his BA from UCLA, works in a city whose whole identity is bound up with image-making and self-invention, and that context sits just under the surface of this work. There's a Hollywood-adjacent unease to his handling of celebrity and spectacle, less a critique than an immersion in how thoroughly our sense of what's real has been scrambled by repetition and recontextualization.

This is his gallery's current exhibition and follows a run of attention that's included a London solo show and a presentation at Frieze Los Angeles — a fast rise for an artist barely out of school, and a good reason to see the paintings in person before the conversation around them gets any louder.

shows.title: Politics & Theatre
shows.description:
Ariel Parkinson spent more than five decades moving between painting, drawing, and stage design, working in the orbit of Berkeley's postwar poets and writers — Robert Duncan, Jack Spicer, Jess — while designing sets and costumes for productions ranging from Shakespeare's The Tempest to Carmina Burana. This is House of Seiko's second show devoted to her, and it zeroes in on the overlap between her two most sustained preoccupations: left political engagement and the theater.

The checklist bears that out literally. Costume sketches for The Tempest hang near ink posters made for the Ecology Center and the Berkeley Barb, protest ephemera rendered with the same theatrical exaggeration Parkinson brought to her scenography. A large six-panel oil-on-masonite altarpiece, Rilke Angel, anchors the show alongside smaller ink-and-oil studies for productions like Pelléas and Mélisande and The Knight of the Burning Pestle, plus vintage chromogenic prints documenting her set and mask designs.

What emerges is less a survey than an argument: that for Parkinson, the stage and the street were never separate registers. Vietnam-era protest imagery and Shakespearean costume design share the same hand and the same appetite for spectacle, and seeing them together clarifies an artist who used theater's heightened language to process the political turbulence of her own era. For anyone who only knows Parkinson's name from the Berkeley Bunch footnotes, this is a chance to see the actual work.

shows.title: Donning Armor
shows.description:
Ethan Shaw builds sculptures out of the stripped-down vocabulary of hardware and uniform: steel, foam, paint, towels, cast aluminum, and found doorknobs assembled into objects that read like clothing or armor that has given up on its job. Titles pulled from loose, lyrical couplets — scraps of language about buttons, seams, and shoes that have lost interest in walking — sit alongside each piece, treating the work less as discrete sculpture than as fragments of a running internal monologue about utility and exhaustion.

This is Shaw's first show at Giovanni's Room, and it reads as a survey of one idea worked through many registers: a court-gated steel door fitted with brass knobs, wall-hung steel "garments" named for fabrics like chambray and seersucker, and a shared stoneware piece made with fellow artist Spencer Russell. Shaw, a RISD graduate now an MFA candidate at UCLA, is interested in the moment function curdles into something more vulnerable and self-referential — a blue-collar aesthetic pushed until the objects stop working and start merely existing.

It's a tightly conceived solo debut, heavy on wall-based steel works that reward close looking at welds, hardware, and the small absurdist gestures (a toppled shoe, a railroad beam) that keep the show from reading as purely formal.

shows.title: Marlon Mullen
shows.description:
Marlon Mullen paints directly from the printed page: covers and spreads of art magazines like Artforum and Juxtapoz, rendered in thick, loose, almost abstracted acrylic that flattens photographs, typography, and advertising copy into a single pictorial surface. Letters dissolve into brushy approximations of themselves, masthead logos become smears of color, and the original image is often only legible as a ghost beneath the paint. The effect is a strange feedback loop — art-world ephemera translated into the very kind of expressive, textured painting those magazines exist to cover.

Mullen, who is autistic and has worked for decades out of NIAD Art Center in Richmond, California, has had a markedly late-career rise, with institutional attention only catching up to a practice built steadily since the 1980s. This show at Hoffman Donahue's Beverly Hills space gathers a group of these magazine paintings, offering a concentrated look at an artist whose flattening, almost illegible take on art-media imagery has become one of the more distinctive bodies of outsider-adjacent painting working today.

It's a tight, single-location presentation, well suited to the gallery's smaller Beverly Hills space, and worth seeing for how insistently physical Mullen's paint handling is in person — reproductions flatten the very thing his work is about.

shows.title: TOUCHPOINTS
shows.artist: Amiee Byrne, Hartwick Hanson, Lauren Miranda, Meg Jorgenson, Michael Laed
shows.description:
TOUCHPOINTS gathers five Los Angeles-based artists whose work shares a tactile, handmade intimacy — ceramics, incandescent light fixtures, textile, and salvaged wood and fiber construction. The show was timed to LA Design Week/end, and it reads accordingly like a conversation between craft and design: objects meant to be touched, worn, sat near, or lived with, rather than only looked at.

Amiee Byrne contributes her hyper-realistic ceramic renderings of discarded everyday objects — the kind of trompe-l'oeil clay work that asks viewers to look twice at what seems like trash elevated to relic. Hartwick Hanson, a sculptor and woodworker who works primarily with salvaged lumber, brings a rougher, more primitive sensibility in wood, playing off the smoother ceramic and textile pieces around it. Rounding out the group are Lauren Miranda, Meg Jorgenson, and Michael Laed, whose ceramic, fiber, and weaving practices extend the show's throughline of materials shaped by hand and marked by human connection.

Taken together, the exhibition functions less like a themed survey and more like a cross-section of LA's current studio-craft scene — artists who move fluidly between fine art and functional design, each contributing a distinct material voice to a show about the points where people and objects meet. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about where ceramics and wood-based sculpture are headed outside the gallery mainstream.

shows.title: MAW
shows.dates_note: Venue's own exhibition page (reisigandtaylorcontemporary.com/exhibitions/maw) confirms the show via its dedicated press image, but its text/dates render only via JavaScript our fetch tools could not execute; exact run (Sep 25–Oct 24, 2026) is corroborated by MutualArt's gallery listing.
shows.description:
Anna Wittenberg's solo show MAW arrives at Reisig and Taylor Contemporary's new Western Avenue space as a close study of bodies in extremis — the title itself nodding to the gaping, consuming mouth. Wittenberg, an LA-based interdisciplinary artist who works across video, sculpture, and drawing, has built a practice out of staring hard at human and animal bodies, at junk, and at the mechanics of cinema itself, and this exhibition continues that line of inquiry with a dark, almost claustrophobic install.

The press image and promotional material for the show lean into high-contrast black silhouettes and void-like forms, suggesting sculptural or installation elements that play with absence as much as presence — a hole that isn't there, a shape defined by what's cut away. It reads as a tighter, more concentrated gesture than a typical gallery survey: fewer objects, more pressure per square foot.

This is a good show for anyone tracking the current crop of LA artists working in the uneasy space between sculpture and moving image — Wittenberg has shown at LAXART, Human Resources, and other artist-driven spaces around the city, and MAW is a chance to see her research into bodily and mechanical excess distilled into a single, tightly wound gallery presentation.

shows.title: Samantha Fields + Barbara Strasen
shows.description:
Billis/Williams pairs two Los Angeles painters whose work turns heavily atmospheric subject matter into something more psychological than descriptive. Samantha Fields has long painted fog, smoke, and haze rolling across California landscapes and highways, using photorealist technique to dissolve solid ground into something closer to memory or dream. Her canvases often withhold as much as they show, letting a a guardrail or rockface emerge from a wall of mist.

Barbara Strasen works in the opposite register, building dense, collaged compositions where fragments of appropriated imagery, pattern, and color are layered into busy, jewel-toned surfaces. Where Fields empties the picture out, Strasen fills it to the brim, and the show's pairing sets up a conversation between reduction and accumulation. A small feature of new work by Carol Charney rounds out the exhibition.

This is a gallery built around traditional painting craft, and the show continues Billis/Williams' pattern of putting mid-career California painters with distinct, fully worked-out visual languages into dialogue with one another rather than presenting a single unified theme.

venue.name: Billis/Williams Gallery
venue.about: Billis/Williams Gallery is a painting-focused gallery in the Culver City Arts District of Los Angeles, led by partner Tressa Williams. The program is technique-driven, spanning figurative, abstract, and still-life painting by a roster of California-based and national artists working primarily in oil and mixed media. Recurring themes include California landscapes and cityscapes, portraiture, domestic and still-life subjects, and meditative or abstract explorations of memory and place. The gallery participates regularly in national art fairs, including the Seattle Art Fair, San Francisco Art Fair, SCOPE Miami Beach, Intersect Palm Springs, and Palm Springs Modernism, and its artists are frequently covered in art press, interviews, and podcasts. The gallery describes itself as woman-owned.

shows.title: Cast Shadows
shows.artist: David Vega and Andy Montiel Phillips
shows.description:
Cast Shadows brings together David Vega's large-scale paintings and Andy Montiel Phillips' sculptures around a shared interest in how bright, cartoonish, instantly recognizable imagery can carry darker historical and psychological weight. Vega's paintings draw on vibrant color and crisp graphic patterning to address Indigenous displacement, cultural erasure, and the friction between ancestral identity and imposed religious frameworks.

Montiel Phillips works with a reduced, cartoon-like vocabulary — most notably the white picket fence — to explore nostalgia as both a comforting and politically loaded device, freezing a mid-century American symbol into a flattened, stage-set facade that shifts as the viewer moves around it.

Together the two bodies of work use familiar, almost pop-inflected surfaces as an entry point into questions about who gets to record history and how collective memory distorts over time.

venue.name: Currency Exchange
venue.about: Currency Exchange (CXLA) is a Los Angeles gallery and community arts space that pairs its exhibition schedule with social-practice programming. Rather than functioning as a conventional white-box gallery, it uses its ground-floor space—situated within affordable housing along the West Washington corridor in Mid-City—as a gathering point for artists, residents, and neighbors. Alongside rotating exhibitions, CXLA runs Community Feeds tied to each show's closing, karaoke nights during exhibitions, artist talks, workshops, and a Beauty Salon series developed with Transformation Arts and the Agape Artist Residency. It also produces a neighborhood zine documenting Mid-City businesses and stories, and invites residents to create collaborative lobby artworks. The organization frames its programming as an investment in the surrounding community's social fabric.

shows.title: Shapeshifters
shows.description:
Two South Bay sculptors share the gallery this fall for a show built around the idea of transformation — bodies, materials, and meanings all shifting shape under pressure. Karena Massengill, who works out of a 2,500-square-foot San Pedro studio, contributes stainless and mild-steel figures built up from welded sheet and recycled found metal, her forms swinging between recognizable figuration and pure abstraction; she's the kind of public-art sculptor whose work you've probably already walked past without knowing her name, having placed large commissions around Southern California and Canada.

Dave Clark's contribution leans stranger and more playful: hybrid 2D-and-3D pieces that mix dyes, plaster, wood, acrylic, and wire into objects that refuse to sit still as either painting or sculpture, including functional-art tables that double as abstract compositions. Clark has said he's more interested in what viewers project onto the work than in dictating its meaning, and that loose, open-ended quality is the real throughline of the show.

Together the two practices make a good pairing — Massengill's polished, gestural steel against Clark's rougher, mixed-media constructions — united by a shared interest in how form can twist, fold, and read differently depending on where you stand. The gallery is hosting an opening reception and closing artist talk bookending the run, giving visitors two chances to hear directly from the artists about how these pieces come together.

venue.name: Diversions Fine Arts
venue.address: 1069 N Aviation Blvd, Manhattan Beach, CA 90266

shows.title: Countervision
shows.description:
Monica Majoli built this body of new drawings out of archival digging: years of research into the Ovulars, a string of photography workshops held between 1979 and 1983 at Rootworks, a lesbian feminist commune in rural Oregon, led by photographers Joan E. Biren, Tee A. Corinne, Honey Lee Cottrell, and Ruth Mountaingrove. Working from their photographs of nude women collaborating and creating together, Majoli renders the images in intimate, unframed drawings that are installed, deliberately, so visitors can handle them directly out of a custom flat file rather than view them behind glass.

What makes the show unusual is where it lives. Rather than a white-cube gallery, the drawings are embedded directly inside the Mazer's archive, alongside material Majoli curated from the collection of the long-closed Sisterhood Bookstore, the Westwood feminist hub where she first encountered lesbian life in print as a teenager. The result folds a contemporary artist's new work into the same shelves and files that hold the primary-source history she's drawing on, blurring the line between artwork and archival object.

Presented by Los Angeles Nomadic Division (LAND), "Countervision" is one of several exhibitions around the city this fall giving overdue institutional attention to lesbian and queer women artists, and it's a rare chance to see Majoli's work in direct conversation with the community history that shaped it. Visits are by appointment, Thursday through Saturday.

venue.name: June L. Mazer Lesbian Archives
hours: Thu - Sat 11am to 5pm by appointment (Countervision exhibition)

shows.title: Images, Afterimages
shows.artist: Em Davenport, Christian John Munks, Leah Ke Yi Zheng, Calvin Miceli Nelson, Mary Stephenson, Peter Tomka
shows.description:
This six-artist group show is built around a shared preoccupation: what happens to an image after it has already been seen, copied, or half-remembered. Rather than depicting subjects directly, each artist works through a kind of residue — a picture that has already passed through some other process (a screenprint, a home video, a family snapshot, a darkroom accident) and come out the other side altered, softened, or scrambled.

The range of media is wide but the mood is consistent. Em Davenport hand-paints recognizable pop-culture images — Jane Birkin, a punk album sleeve — so they mimic the flatness of mechanical reproduction, hiding her own touch inside a surface that reads as printed rather than painted. Leah Ke Yi Zheng's canvases refuse the rectangle outright, with stretched silk that buckles at the edges and dissolves gears and bolts into fields of color. Christian John Munks builds his paintings through layers of construction and erasure, letting earlier pentimenti haunt what's visible on top, while Calvin Miceli Nelson strips his figures of narrative until only an archetypal charge remains.

Mary Stephenson's oil paintings on rabbit-skin-glue-primed canvas seep and pool unevenly, treating the image as something built and rebuilt rather than fixed in one pass. Peter Tomka's contribution is the most literal translation of the show's premise into process: he converts his own photo archive into negatives and exposes them through a homemade enlarger built from the frame and cut-open mattress of his bed, so each print carries the noise and drift of its own strange darkroom.

Taken together the show reads less like a survey of young painters and more like a meditation on how images degrade, circulate, and come back changed — appropriate territory for a gallery occupying the quiet, historic Hollywoodland Realty building, tucked away from LA's more conventional gallery circuits.

shows.title: Idols In Bloom
shows.description:
Rafael Megall's paintings work a rich, jewel-toned register somewhere between religious icon and botanical still life, with figures and floral motifs rendered in the flattened, gilded planes of devotional art. Idols In Bloom leans into that vocabulary directly, pairing the language of veneration with the fragility and excess of flowers in full bloom — worship and decay held in the same frame.

This show looks to be a good showcase for Megall's particular fusion of the sacred and the decorative, ornate surfaces built up with the patience of an icon painter but aimed at very contemporary anxieties about beauty and impermanence.

venue.name: Mek Contemporary
venue.about: Mek Contemporary is a Los Angeles–based gallery presenting contemporary artists working across disciplines and geographies. The program pays particular attention to work engaging memory, migration, displacement, place, identity, and cultural inheritance, favoring artists with distinctive approaches to form, material, and image. The gallery emphasizes close attention to each artist and body of work, developing focused exhibitions and publications alongside sustained relationships with artists, collectors, institutions, and audiences. Through this approach, Mek aims to extend conversations sparked by the work beyond the exhibition space itself, treating each show as part of an ongoing dialogue rather than an isolated event.

shows.title: The Poetics of Place
shows.description:
ATLA's fall two-person show pairs Vamba Bility and Shun Kadohashi under the banner of "place" — how a maker's surroundings, materials, and inherited traditions surface in the work. ATLA has built its program around craft-forward practices that bridge East and West, and this exhibition continues that thread, setting two artists with very different vocabularies in dialogue inside the gallery's small Kenmore Avenue storefront.

Without a full checklist yet available, the specifics of medium and scale are still emerging, but ATLA's track record — recent solo shows built around ceramics, textile, and object-based work — suggests visitors should expect handmade, materially attentive pieces rather than large-scale spectacle. The gallery's exhibitions typically reward a slow look at surface and technique.

This is ATLA at its most typical: an intimate, appointment-friendly gallery in a converted Los Feliz-adjacent storefront, showing artists who take the long view on making things by hand.

venue.name: ATLA
venue.about: ATLA is a contemporary gallery in Los Angeles focused on craft-based work, particularly ceramics, that brings together East and West artistic traditions. Its program explores themes of intersectionality, history, heritage, politics, and identity through skilled making. The gallery's name references the Japanese word 'atara,' evoking the sorrow of losing something beautiful, and reflects ATLA's commitment to celebrating endurance and resisting disposability of work, experience, and attention. The gallery operates from a space on Kenmore Avenue and presents exhibitions featuring a wide roster of ceramic and multidisciplinary artists.

shows.title: Rest Stops
shows.description:
After the Eaton Fire destroyed her family's home and studio in Altadena, Kenturah Davis turned toward the scorched landscape itself as material. Rest Stops, co-presented with Destination Crenshaw, shows the prototypes and drawings behind a three-year project to build a network of sensory gardens on burned residential lots — adaptive, fire-resilient plantings meant to support soil remediation while giving displaced families a place to sit with what's been lost.

Davis is best known for large-scale figurative drawings that incorporate debossed text — literary excerpts, legal transcripts, sheet music — pressed into the paper beneath carbon-pencil rubbings of bodies in motion. Here that same interest in inscription and memory gets applied to landscape design: her drawings for the gardens borrow structural logic from Black quilting traditions, treating planting plans like pieced fabric, stitching individual lots into a larger communal pattern.

The show is less a conventional art exhibition than a working document of a long-term public project, grounded in Davis's own history in this stretch of Los Angeles — she's also the artist behind the 2019 mural at the Downtown Inglewood Metro station. Seeing the drawings and prototypes at Crenshaw Dairy Mart, an Inglewood gallery built around art as community repair work, underscores how closely the project's aesthetic and civic ambitions are entwined.

shows.title: Neither Land Nor Water
shows.description:
Amy MacKay makes paintings out of other people's memories of an evening she staged. In 2023 she restaged the Irish play By the Bog of Cats — Marina Carr's bog-set retelling of the Medea myth — as a private performance around a heated Pasadena pool, with a cast, a cinematographer, and an invited audience all documenting the night from different vantage points. Those competing, imperfect records of a single live event are the raw material she translates into oil paint.

The result is a body of work built through layering and erasure: thin veils of oil paint wiped back with spirits, clouds of white gesso sanded down to a ghostly residue, surfaces that accumulate and dissolve in the same gesture. Figures and settings surface and recede — a coat, a changing room, the shape of a dancer mid-turn — never quite resolving into a single fixed image, which is the point. MacKay is less interested in what happened than in how memory distorts, multiplies, and fades every time it's retold.

This is MacKay's second solo show with la BEAST built from the same source material, following her 2024 exhibition To the Bog of Cats I One Day Will Return. Where that show tracked the paintings closely to the text of the play, Neither Land Nor Water pushes further into the subjective experience of the performers and audience members themselves, with works ranging from small, intimate studies to large sculptural panels. It's a show about the unreliable, generative space between an event and its retelling — fitting territory for a painter who treats documentation itself as a kind of drawing.

venue.name: la BEAST gallery
hours: Thu - Sat 12pm to 6pm, or by appointment

shows.title: Global Fugitivity: UCLA New Wight International Biennial Exhibition 2026
shows.description:
Every two years, UCLA's graduate art students curate the New Wight Biennial by traveling to studio programs around the world and selecting work from a rising generation of MFA candidates. This edition, organized by student-curators Sabaah Folayan, tunmi da silva, and Luke Francis Austin, takes "fugitivity" as its theme — art-world shorthand for practices of escape, refusal, and self-determination that run through Black studies and diaspora theory.

Expect a wide-ranging, multimedia group show: the biennial has historically mixed painting, video, sculpture, and installation from art schools across North America and abroad, giving Los Angeles audiences an early look at artists who haven't yet had gallery representation. Because it's juried through studio visits rather than an open submission, the show tends to have a sharper, more considered feel than a typical student exhibition.

The New Wight Gallery is a teaching space as much as an exhibition venue, tucked into the ground floor of the Broad Art Center just north of the Murphy Sculpture Garden, and this biennial is one of the few times each cycle that its program looks outward past UCLA's own graduate cohort.

shows.title: Energetic Connections: The Ki Paintings of Yoshio Ikezaki
shows.description:
Yoshio Ikezaki works with sumi ink, water, and handmade washi paper, letting the interaction of liquid and fiber do much of the compositional work. He grinds his own ink and makes his own paper, and his paintings read less like fixed images than records of a physical event — ink blooming, pooling, and drying according to forces he guides but doesn't fully control. The results range from stormy, atmospheric landscapes to near-abstract fields of tone that hover between painting and residue.

The show's title points to the Japanese concept of ki, the life-force energy that Ikezaki treats as both subject and method: he describes using water as an active agent to steer the ink, so that intention and accident collide on the paper's surface. Trained in traditional Japanese papermaking and steeped in Buddhist practice from childhood, Ikezaki has spent decades translating ideas of emptiness and impermanence into a distinctly physical, process-driven body of work.

Shumei Hall Gallery, a small nonprofit space in Pasadena devoted to art with a contemplative bent, is a fitting home for this material — expect a quiet, meditative installation of ink paintings that reward slow looking.

shows.title: Eat Happy
shows.description:
Narsiso Martinez's fourth solo show with Charlie James turns the grocery bag into a painting surface. Known for portraits of farmworkers drawn on discarded produce boxes, Martinez here mounts branded paper bags from Whole Foods, Trader Joe's, Ralphs, Lazy Acres and Javier's onto wood panels and canvas, then paints pickers and packers into, around and over the logos. The premium brands are the point: their promises of health and indulgence sit right beside the people whose labor fills the shelves.

Some of the best moments are small collisions between figure and print. A worker emptying a sack of fruit seems to laugh at a "Live Healthy, Eat Well" slogan; another glances down at cartoon kids asking about recycling. Others are simply shown resting, eating lunch or looking straight back at the viewer, given the dignity of a portrait rather than the anonymity of a supply chain.

Alongside the bag series are large works on canvas and painted produce boxes, berry flats and grape crates, some built out with plastic fruit into small sculptural assemblages. Martinez, who worked nine harvest seasons in Washington state before art school, draws on 1930s Social Realism, and the show reads as a pointed, often wry look at who pays for abundance.

venue.name: Charlie James Gallery
venue.about: Charlie James Gallery opened in 2008 in Los Angeles' Chinatown and has built a program centered on emerging and established artists with distinct, often political voices. The gallery works across painting, sculpture, textile, installation, and new media, with particular attention to marginalized perspectives and narratives touching on identity, race, gender, and broader socio-political concerns. Under gallery director Ever Velasquez, the program has become known for thoughtful, provocative curatorial approaches, including annual group exhibitions, and for close collaboration with museums and academics to help place artists' work within broader critical and historical conversations. The gallery now operates two adjoining spaces on historic Chung King Road.

shows.title: Food and Beyond, Beyond Food
shows.description:
Running alongside his solo show Eat Happy, Food and Beyond, Beyond Food is a group exhibition curated by Narsiso Martinez that gathers four women artists from different backgrounds around food and what it means to be nourished. Andrea Bersaglieri, Ashley Jose-Isip, Jessy Slim and Karen Tepaz each come at the subject sideways, so the show is less about meals than about land, memory, identity and care.

Bersaglieri's large black-and-white charcoal drawings of soil treat fertile ground as something finite that has to be looked after. Slim paints with chickpeas, an unexpected material that doubles as a link to her homeland in Lebanon. Jose-Isip pulls in fast-food interiors, artificial sweets and dinner plates to probe Filipino-American identity and the artificiality of what ends up on our plates. Tepaz's organic, abstract ceramics point toward motherhood and the body as a first source of nourishment.

Seen next to Martinez's paintings of farm labor, the group show widens the conversation from how food is produced to how it shapes who we are.

shows.title: Spotlight: Brittney Leeanne Williams
shows.description:
Vielmetter's viewing room Spotlight gives Los Angeles painter Brittney Leeanne Williams a focused showing of new oil paintings and works on paper. The pieces are built on saturated color gradients, from which forms emerge that read as eyes, tulip blossoms, mountains and curled bodies, their edges dissolving into fine, pointillist dots of color.

Williams describes the works as talismans or icons, devotional images meant to be looked at and through at the same time. The eye is a recurring center, sometimes projecting from a crouched figure, and each piece is organized around a "pupil," either a black point or a gap left unpainted. The tulip acts as a kind of architecture: its domed blossom suggests a huddle of women bowed together, enclosing the red/Black figure at its heart.

The work draws on Hilma af Klint, whose residency program Williams recently inaugurated in Sweden, and on Laura Aguilar's desert portraits, and it treats the Black female body as a shapeshifting site between the physical and the mystical. Small in scale and intense in color, it rewards close, slow looking.

venue.name: Vielmetter Los Angeles
venue.about: Vielmetter Los Angeles is a contemporary art gallery in the Arts District of downtown Los Angeles, located at 1700 S Santa Fe Avenue. It is owned and directed by Susanne Vielmetter and operates three exhibition spaces at that address. The gallery represents a multigenerational group of artists working across painting, sculpture, photography, video, and installation, including figures such as Nicole Eisenman, Arlene Shechet, Mickalene Thomas, Wangechi Mutu, Mary Kelly, and the estate of William Pope.L. Represented artists have participated in major international biennials, museum surveys, and art fairs, and have received sustained critical attention in publications including The New York Times, Artforum, The Guardian, and Artnet. The gallery's program spans several decades of contemporary practice, with a consistent focus on socially engaged, figurative, and materially inventive work by artists based in Los Angeles, New York, and internationally.
